root.stem: A 36-year-old woman who is 22 weeks pregnant has had burning behind the breastbone for 8 years. It comes within an hour of large, fried meals and when she lies flat, and she tastes sour fluid at the back of her throat. Last winter, before the pregnancy, her symptoms broke through while she was eating much larger holiday meals and drinking more alcohol. Now antacids no longer help. Swallowing is painless and has never been difficult, she has not lost weight, and she takes no daily medicines. Her examination is normal. An upper endoscopy before the pregnancy showed redness and shallow erosions of the lower esophagus without white plaques, and a biopsy showed a thickened basal layer of the squamous lining with long papillae, no goblet cells and no atypical cells.
root.oneliner: 36F + 22 weeks pregnant + 8 years of burning behind the breastbone after large fried meals and lying flat + sour taste + flare with large holiday meals and alcohol before pregnancy + antacids failing + painless, easy swallowing + no weight loss + no daily medicines + erosions of the lower esophagus, no white plaques + biopsy with basal layer thickening, long papillae, no goblet cells, no atypical cells
highlight: burning behind the breastbone for 8 years
larger holiday meals and drinking more alcohol
thickened basal layer of the squamous lining with long papillae

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Stomach contents flow back into the lower esophagus and inflame it. The clincher: **burning behind the breastbone after large or fatty meals and when lying flat, with sour regurgitation, and no trouble swallowing or weight loss**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Same disease when the lining is inflamed; the exam may name it by the biopsy finding rather than the symptom.

nodes.q: What failure at the lower end of the esophagus lets stomach contents back up?
nodes.a: Transient (inappropriate) relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter
nodes.note: Most reflux comes from transient relaxations that are not triggered by swallowing; a low resting sphincter tone and a sliding hiatal hernia (which pulls the sphincter above the diaphragm) add to it. Scleroderma (CREST) causes reflux by weakening the sphincter muscle.

nodes.q: Which nerve triggers these relaxations?
nodes.note: A vagal reflex set off by stretch of the stomach after a large meal relaxes the sphincter (nitric oxide is the mediator).

nodes.q: Before the pregnancy, which drink she took more of, besides eating larger meals, relaxed the sphincter?
nodes.note: Fatty foods, chocolate, caffeine, peppermint and smoking do the same. A very full stomach also raises the pressure inside and pushes the sphincter open, which is why symptoms can break through even on treatment.

nodes.q: Which hormone of pregnancy lowers the tone of the sphincter?
nodes.note: It relaxes smooth muscle; the growing uterus also raises the pressure inside the abdomen. Symptoms usually go away after delivery.

nodes.q: Which drug that protects the stomach lining is contraindicated in pregnancy because it raises the risk of spontaneous abortion?
nodes.note: A prostaglandin E1 analog that makes the uterus contract. Antacids, sucralfate, famotidine and omeprazole are acceptable choices in pregnancy.

nodes.q: Which stomach cells make the acid that injures the esophageal lining?
nodes.note: They secrete hydrochloric acid; chief cells add pepsin, which injures the lining too.

nodes.q: Which white blood cell, in small numbers, is characteristic in the squamous lining in reflux esophagitis?
nodes.note: Her thickened basal layer and long papillae are the reactive changes of reflux; neutrophils join in more severe injury. Fifteen or more eosinophils per high-power field points to eosinophilic esophagitis instead. **No goblet cells** keeps this out of the next stage of the disease.

nodes.q: In a well-growing 6-week-old who spits up small amounts of milk, which developmental feature explains the same problem?
nodes.note: Normal growth, no bilious or projectile vomiting and a normal examination make this a physiologic problem that clears by about a year of age; the treatment is reassurance.

nodes.q: Which findings would call for an upper endoscopy before a drug trial?
nodes.a: Alarm features (trouble swallowing, weight loss, vomiting blood, black stools or anemia)
nodes.note: She has none of these, so a trial of treatment would be reasonable.

nodes.q: Which complication replaces the squamous lining with intestinal-type lining after years of acid injury?
nodes.note: Metaplasia: the squamous lining turns into columnar lining with goblet cells, seen as salmon-colored mucosa above the Z line. It raises the risk of cancer.

nodes.q: Which cancer can follow?
nodes.note: Metaplasia leads to dysplasia and then cancer in the lower third of the esophagus.

nodes.q: Which narrowing can scar the lower esophagus after years of reflux?
nodes.note: Presents as trouble swallowing solids that gets steadily worse; treated by dilation plus acid suppression.

nodes.q: Which wheezing airway disease can reflux worsen, especially at night?
nodes.note: Microaspiration and a vagal reflex narrow the airways. Other extra-esophageal effects: chronic cough, hoarseness (laryngitis) and erosion of the back teeth.

nodes.q: Which measures come first for her?
nodes.a: Lifestyle changes: raising the head of the bed, smaller meals, no alcohol or fatty food, and no lying down after eating
nodes.note: Weight loss helps if overweight. If symptoms persist, drug therapy follows.

nodes.q: Which drug class is the most effective at relieving symptoms and healing erosions when lifestyle change fails?
nodes.note: Better than histamine-2 blockers for healing esophagitis; taken 30 minutes before a meal. Long-term use is linked to low magnesium, low vitamin B12, fractures and Clostridioides difficile infection.

nodes.q: Omeprazole acts on which target on the parietal cell?
nodes.a: The H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump), irreversibly inhibited
nodes.note: It blocks the final common step of acid secretion, whether the signal came from histamine, gastrin or acetylcholine.

nodes.q: Blocking the histamine-2 receptor with ranitidine or famotidine lowers which second messenger in the parietal cell?
nodes.note: The histamine-2 receptor is coupled to Gs, which raises cAMP and activates the proton pump. Gastrin (CCK-B receptor) and acetylcholine (M3 receptor) raise calcium instead. Ranitidine was withdrawn in 2020 (NDMA contamination); famotidine remains.

nodes.q: Her years of heartburn could point to Barrett esophagus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Biopsy with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia)** and salmon-colored mucosa extending above the Z line
**Squamous lining intact with basal zone hyperplasia and long papillae, no goblet cells**

nodes.note: The trap: Barrett esophagus comes from reflux, so the symptoms are identical; only the biopsy separates them.

nodes.q: Her regurgitation could suggest achalasia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Trouble swallowing both solids and liquids from the start + bird's-beak narrowing on barium swallow + failure of the lower sphincter to relax**; regurgitates undigested food
**Burning after large meals, normal swallowing, sour fluid**

nodes.q: Erosions of the esophagus could be esophageal candidiasis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Painful swallowing + white plaques that scrape off, in someone with HIV, on steroids or otherwise immunosuppressed**
**Burning, painless swallowing, no white plaques, normal immunity**

nodes.q: Her endoscopy could suggest an early esophageal cancer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Progressive trouble swallowing + weight loss + heavy smoking and alcohol; atypical squamous cells on biopsy**
**No atypical cells, painless swallowing, no weight loss**

nodes.q: Other causes of chest burning were also possible. How do you tell them apart?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from her case
rows: **Epigastric pain that changes with meals + Helicobacter pylori or NSAID use; ulcer crater on endoscopy**
**Young atopic patient with food getting stuck + rings and furrows + 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field**
**Chest pain on swallowing + corkscrew esophagus on barium swallow**
**Pain on swallowing after taking pills such as doxycycline or bisphosphonates without enough water**
**Nausea, early fullness and bloating, often with diabetes; slow gastric emptying on scan**

image_prompts.root: A pastel cross-section of the lower esophagus with a squamous lining showing redness and shallow erosions just above the gastroesophageal junction, with stomach acid washing upward through a relaxed lower sphincter.

root.stem: A 39-year-old man has had constipation for years and sees bright red spots on the toilet paper after bowel movements, with no pain during the passage. Yesterday after straining he had sudden severe anal pain without bleeding, and today a single tender, bluish, grape-sized lump sits at the anal verge. Anoscopy shows large, nontender swollen veins high inside the anal canal. There is no tear in the skin, no warty growth, no change in stool caliber, no weight loss, no diarrhea and no family history of colon cancer.
root.oneliner: 39M + years of constipation + bright red spots on paper, painless + sudden severe anal pain after straining, no bleeding + single tender bluish lump at the anal verge + large nontender veins high in the anal canal + no skin tear, no warty growth, no weight loss, no diarrhea, no family history of colon cancer
highlight: bright red spots on the toilet paper
sudden severe anal pain without bleeding
large, nontender swollen veins high inside the anal canal
no family history of colon cancer

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Swollen vascular cushions of the anal canal. The clincher: **painless bright red blood on the paper with large swollen veins high in the anal canal, and a sudden tender bluish lump at the verge when a clot forms**.

nodes.q: Which habit is the main predisposing cause?
nodes.note: Straining raises the pressure in the rectal venous plexus. Pregnancy, obesity and a low-fiber diet add to it.

nodes.q: Which landmark separates painless from painful hemorrhoids?
nodes.note: Above it the hemorrhoids are internal, covered by mucosa with visceral nerves, and do not hurt; below it they are external, covered by skin with somatic nerves (inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve), and hurt. Above the line: superior rectal artery and lymph to the internal iliac nodes; below: inferior rectal artery and lymph to the superficial inguinal nodes.

nodes.q: Which type is the tender bluish lump at the anal verge?
nodes.note: A clot in the veins under the anal skin gives sudden severe pain without bleeding; pain peaks in about 2 days and then settles.

nodes.q: Into which venous system do the veins above the line drain?
nodes.a: The portal system, through the superior rectal vein
nodes.note: The superior rectal vein drains to the inferior mesenteric vein and on to the portal vein. Below the line the inferior rectal vein drains through the internal iliac vein to the inferior vena cava. This portosystemic link is why portal hypertension can cause anorectal varices (a separate entity from hemorrhoids).

nodes.q: Which office procedure treats a prolapsing internal hemorrhoid?
nodes.note: The band cuts off the blood supply so the tissue shrinks and falls off.

nodes.q: Why must the band be placed above the dentate line?
nodes.a: Below the line the skin has somatic pain nerves, so a band there causes severe pain
nodes.note: A man in severe pain hours after a band was placed was most likely banded below the line.

nodes.q: Which procedure relieves a thrombosed lump seen within 72 hours?
nodes.a: Excision of the clot under local anesthetic
nodes.note: Later, sitz baths, stool softeners and pain control are enough.

nodes.q: Which measures treat uncomplicated internal hemorrhoids first?
nodes.note: Avoid straining and prolonged sitting on the toilet.

nodes.q: Which result can chronic slow bleeding cause?
nodes.note: Fatigue and microcytic red cells.

nodes.q: Which test excludes colorectal cancer when rectal bleeding comes with age over 45 or alarm features?
nodes.note: He is 39 with none of these, so hemorrhoids can be treated first.

nodes.q: His bleeding could come from an anal fissure. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Tearing pain during and after bowel movements + bright red streak + a tear in the posterior midline**
**Painless bright red blood with large swollen veins, or a sudden tender lump unrelated to the passage; no skin tear**

nodes.note: The trap: both bleed bright red after straining on hard stools.

nodes.q: His lump could be a condyloma from human papillomavirus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Several soft, warty, cauliflower-like growths, painless, in a sexually active patient**
**Single smooth, tender, bluish lump that appears suddenly after straining**

nodes.q: His lump could be an anal cancer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hard, ulcerated mass with itching or bleeding, linked to human papillomavirus type 16, anal intercourse or HIV**
**Smooth bluish lump with sudden severe pain that improves within days**

nodes.q: Other causes of anal or rectal bleeding or a lump were possible. How do you tell them apart?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: **Soft, painless flap of skin, often left after a thrombosed hemorrhoid heals**
**Change in stool caliber, weight loss, iron deficiency or occult blood, usually after age 45**
Weight loss and change in stool
**Bloody diarrhea with abdominal pain over weeks**
**Abdominal pain relieved by a bowel movement with altered stool habit; no bleeding**

root.stem: A 62-year-old woman has been in the hospital for 5 days for pyelonephritis and has received ciprofloxacin since admission. Her fever and flank pain improved, but today she has sudden watery diarrhea and lower abdominal cramps. Her temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), the lower abdomen is moderately tender, bowel sounds are increased, and the stool is brown with no blood. Her white blood cell count is 15,000/mm3. She has not traveled and has not eaten outside the hospital, and no one else on the ward has diarrhea.
root.oneliner: 62F + hospital day 5 on ciprofloxacin for pyelonephritis + sudden watery diarrhea and lower abdominal cramps + fever 38.3°C + lower abdominal tenderness, brisk bowel sounds + brown stool, no blood + white blood cells 15,000 + no travel, no outside food, no sick contacts
highlight: no one else on the ward

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Overgrowth of a toxin-making bacterium after antibiotics wipe out the normal gut bacteria. The clincher: **watery diarrhea with cramps and fever that starts days into antibiotics (or up to weeks after), often in the hospital**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.a: Pseudomembranous colitis (the organism was formerly called Clostridium difficile)
nodes.note: Also called antibiotic-associated colitis; the older genus name still appears on exams.

nodes.q: Which kind of organism is it?
nodes.note: The spores survive alcohol hand gel and dry surfaces, so wash hands with soap and water and use contact precautions.

nodes.q: Which antibiotics most often trigger it?
nodes.note: They kill the normal bowel flora, which lets the spores germinate. Other risks: proton pump inhibitors, age over 65, long hospital stay.

nodes.q: Which toxins cause the damage?
nodes.a: Toxin A (an enterotoxin) and toxin B (a cytotoxin)
nodes.note: They glucosylate and inactivate Rho GTPases, break down the actin cytoskeleton and kill the colon cells; neutrophils, fibrin and dead cells form a pseudomembrane.

nodes.q: What does the colon lining look like if it is scoped?
nodes.a: Raised yellow-white plaques (pseudomembranes) on inflamed mucosa
nodes.note: Scoping is rarely needed once the stool toxin is positive.

nodes.q: Which test is the most appropriate next step?
nodes.a: A stool test for Clostridioides difficile toxin (or its toxin gene)
nodes.note: Not stool culture or an ova and parasite test; waiting to see if diarrhea stops after the antibiotic is withdrawn only delays treatment.

nodes.q: Which treatment is first-line for an initial episode, together with stopping the triggering antibiotic?
nodes.note: Oral metronidazole used to be first-line and is now reserved for when neither is available; oral drugs work because they act inside the bowel. Fulminant disease adds intravenous metronidazole.

nodes.q: Which treatment helps after several recurrences?
nodes.note: It restores the normal gut flora. Bezlotoxumab, a monoclonal antibody against toxin B, also lowers the chance of recurrence.

nodes.q: Which severe complication dilates the colon?
nodes.note: Suspect it with a swollen, tender abdomen, high white count or shock.

nodes.q: Which event kills?
nodes.a: Colonic perforation with peritonitis and sepsis
nodes.note: Treatment is intravenous antibiotics and colectomy.

nodes.q: Her illness could be food-borne gastroenteritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Short illness after a shared meal or travel with sick contacts, no recent antibiotics**; often vomiting
**Onset in hospital days into ciprofloxacin, with no sick contacts or food exposure**

nodes.note: The trap: both give acute watery diarrhea with cramps and fever.

nodes.q: Her diarrhea could be giardiasis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Camping or untreated water, then weeks of foul-smelling greasy diarrhea with gas; cysts or trophozoites in stool**
**Sudden watery diarrhea on antibiotics with fever and a high white count; no ova or parasites**

nodes.q: Other causes of diarrhea were possible. How do you tell them apart?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from her case
rows: **Greasy, bulky, foul stools for months with weight loss and high stool fat**
**Recurrent bloody diarrhea over weeks with abdominal pain, often in a young adult**
Blood in the stool and a chronic course

image_prompts.root: A pastel colon lumen with yellow-white raised pseudomembranes on inflamed red mucosa, beside a spore-forming rod bacterium.

root.stem: A 45-year-old woman has felt tired for 3 months. She injected drugs for a year when she was 20. Her examination is normal and the liver is not palpable. Alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase have been mildly raised on three tests over 8 months, albumin is 3.3 g/dL, alkaline phosphatase is normal and bilirubin is 1.4 mg/dL. Tests for hepatitis A and hepatitis B are negative, anti-nuclear and anti-smooth muscle antibodies are negative, and antimitochondrial antibody is negative. A polymerase chain reaction test detects viral RNA in her blood. A liver biopsy shows lymphocytes in the portal tracts with focal hepatocyte death and early fibrosis.
root.oneliner: 45F + 3 months of fatigue + injected drugs for a year at 20 + normal examination, no palpable liver + mildly raised aminotransferases for 8 months + albumin 3.3 + normal alkaline phosphatase + negative hepatitis A and B tests, negative autoantibodies and antimitochondrial antibody + viral RNA in the blood + portal lymphocytes, focal hepatocyte death, early fibrosis
highlight: mildly raised on three tests over 8 months
Tests for hepatitis A and hepatitis B are negative
detects viral RNA in her blood
lymphocytes in the portal tracts with focal hepatocyte death and early fibrosis

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Chronic hepatitis C (hepatitis C virus, HCV)
nodes.note: Persistent infection of the liver with an RNA virus. The clincher: **blood exposure (injection drug use or a transfusion before 1992) + raised liver enzymes for more than 6 months + viral RNA in the blood**.

nodes.q: Which virus family does it belong to?
nodes.note: An enveloped, single-stranded positive-sense RNA virus. Its RNA polymerase has no proofreading, so the envelope proteins keep mutating; that explains chronic infection and the lack of a vaccine.

nodes.q: Which exposure is the main route?
nodes.note: Transfusion before 1992 screening, needle-stick and (rarely) sexual or birth transmission are others.

nodes.q: About how many people with acute infection develop chronic infection?
nodes.note: Acute infection is usually silent, which is why many learn of it only years later.

nodes.q: Which immune mechanism injures the hepatocytes?
nodes.a: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells recognizing foreign (viral) peptides on major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I
nodes.note: Class I molecules are on every nucleated cell and present internal (viral) peptides; helper CD4+ T cells recognize class II molecules, found on antigen-presenting cells. The virus itself is not directly cytopathic.

nodes.q: Besides the portal lymphocytes, which change inside the hepatocytes is characteristic of hepatitis C on biopsy?
nodes.note: Dense lymphoid aggregates in the portal tracts and bile duct injury are the other typical features. Fibrosis progresses over decades. Ground-glass hepatocytes belong to hepatitis B.

nodes.q: Which blood tests confirm it?
nodes.a: Anti-HCV antibody screen, then HCV RNA to prove active infection
nodes.note: Screening is advised once for all adults and in every pregnancy.

nodes.q: Which treatment cures it?
nodes.a: Direct-acting antivirals (for example sofosbuvir with velpatasvir)
nodes.note: Taken for 8 to 12 weeks; cure means no RNA 12 weeks after treatment (sustained virologic response).

nodes.q: Sofosbuvir inhibits which viral enzyme?
nodes.note: Other direct-acting antivirals block the NS3/4A protease or the NS5A protein.

nodes.q: Which complication follows after decades of fibrosis?
nodes.note: Link: portal hypertension and liver failure.

nodes.q: Which liver cancer can follow?
nodes.note: Surveillance with ultrasound every 6 months in cirrhosis.

nodes.q: Which immune-complex disease with purpura and joint pain can accompany it?
nodes.note: Immune complexes of IgM rheumatoid factor and IgG precipitate in the cold. Hepatitis C is also linked to membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, porphyria cutanea tarda and lichen planus.

nodes.q: Her chronic hepatitis could be hepatitis B. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hepatitis B surface antigen and DNA in the blood; DNA virus with ground-glass hepatocytes**; vaccine exists
**Hepatitis B tests negative, HCV RNA positive; RNA virus with no vaccine**

nodes.note: The trap: both are blood-borne viruses causing years of raised enzymes and fibrosis.

nodes.q: Her biopsy could suggest autoimmune hepatitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Young or middle-aged woman with other autoimmune disease, anti-nuclear or anti-smooth muscle antibodies, high immunoglobulin G, plasma cells at the interface**
**Negative autoantibodies, injection drug exposure, viral RNA in blood, lymphocytes in portal tracts**

nodes.q: Her fatigue in middle age could be primary biliary cholangitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Itching + high alkaline phosphatase + antimitochondrial antibody; granulomatous destruction of small bile ducts**
**Raised aminotransferases with a normal alkaline phosphatase and a negative antimitochondrial antibody**

image_prompts.root: A pastel liver lobule with portal tract lymphocytes attacking hepatocytes bearing viral peptides, a fine thread of early fibrosis, and an RNA virus particle beside it.

root.stem: A 31-year-old man, a doctoral student writing his thesis under heavy pressure, has had gnawing upper abdominal pain for 4 months with a feeling of fullness after small meals. An over-the-counter histamine-2 blocker helped only partly. He has not vomited, lost weight, had trouble swallowing or passed black stools, takes no anti-inflammatory drugs, and his mood and sleep are normal. Vital signs and examination are normal. An upper endoscopy shows no ulcer or mass, and a biopsy of the stomach shows no Helicobacter pylori.
root.oneliner: 31M + doctoral student under heavy stress + 4 months of gnawing epigastric pain + fullness after small meals + partial relief with histamine-2 blocker + no vomiting, weight loss, dysphagia or black stools + no anti-inflammatory drugs + normal mood and sleep + normal examination + normal endoscopy, biopsy without Helicobacter pylori
highlight: gnawing upper abdominal pain for 4 months
not vomited, lost weight, had trouble swallowing or passed black stools

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Chronic upper abdominal symptoms with no structural cause. The clincher: **months of epigastric pain or early fullness with a normal endoscopy and no alarm features**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names mean dyspepsia with no ulcer or other lesion found.

nodes.q: Which finding is required before calling it functional?
nodes.a: A normal upper endoscopy (no structural disease)
nodes.note: Rome IV criteria: bothersome epigastric pain or burning, or early satiety or postprandial fullness, for at least 3 months, with onset at least 6 months ago.

nodes.q: Which sensory abnormality makes normal stretch of his stomach feel painful?
nodes.note: Impaired relaxation of the stomach after a meal (poor accommodation) and slow emptying add to it, and stress acts through the brain-gut axis. There is no acid hypersecretion, so acid blockers help only partly.

nodes.q: In a patient under 60 without alarm features, which test comes first?
nodes.a: Test for Helicobacter pylori (stool antigen or urea breath test) and treat if positive
nodes.note: Endoscopy is for age 60 or older or alarm features such as weight loss, vomiting, bleeding or trouble swallowing.

nodes.q: If the test is negative, which drug class is tried?
nodes.a: A proton pump inhibitor for 4 to 8 weeks
nodes.note: A low-dose tricyclic antidepressant is next if symptoms persist.

nodes.q: His pain could be from peptic ulcer disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Ulcer crater on endoscopy + Helicobacter pylori or anti-inflammatory drug use**; duodenal pain relieved by meals
**Normal endoscopy, no Helicobacter pylori, no anti-inflammatory drugs**

nodes.note: The trap: both give epigastric pain with partial response to acid blockers.

nodes.q: His early fullness could suggest gastric lymphoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Weight loss + mass or thickened folds + Helicobacter pylori with dense lymphoid infiltrate on biopsy**
**No weight loss, no mass, no organism, normal biopsy**

nodes.q: His pain could be irritable bowel syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Lower abdominal pain relieved by a bowel movement, with altered stool frequency or form**
**Upper abdominal pain or fullness related to meals, with normal stools**

nodes.q: Stress could point to a psychiatric disorder. How do you tell them apart?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: **Two weeks of low mood or loss of interest with sleep, appetite and energy change**
**Excessive worry on most days for 6 months with restlessness and muscle tension**

image_prompts.root: A pastel stomach with a smooth normal lining on endoscopy and a thought cloud of stress above it, with no ulcer visible.

root.stem: A 28-year-old man has had 6 hours of severe cramping pain in the left middle of the abdomen that comes in waves, with one episode of vomiting. He has no fever, no diarrhea and no blood in the stool, and he has never had abdominal surgery. A firm mass is felt in the middle of the abdomen, and there is no rebound tenderness. A CT scan with contrast shows, in the left mid abdomen, a loop of small bowel lying inside the loop beyond it, with concentric rings of bowel wall in cross-section.
root.oneliner: 28M + 6 hours of cramping, wave-like left mid-abdominal pain + one vomit + no fever, diarrhea or blood in stool + no prior abdominal surgery + firm midabdominal mass, no rebound + CT: small bowel inside small bowel in the left mid abdomen, concentric rings
highlight: 6 hours of severe cramping pain in the left middle of the abdomen
no fever, no diarrhea and no blood in the stool
firm mass is felt in the middle of the abdomen
a loop of small bowel lying inside the loop beyond it

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A segment of bowel (intussusceptum) telescopes into the segment beyond it. The clincher: **colicky abdominal pain with vomiting, a palpable abdominal mass, and a target-like bowel-within-bowel on imaging**.

nodes.q: Given where his pain, mass and CT finding lie, which part of the bowel has telescoped?
nodes.note: The jejunum lies in the left upper and mid abdomen; the ileum lies mostly in the right lower abdomen, and the duodenum is fixed and retroperitoneal on the right. In adults most intussusceptions are small bowel into small bowel (enteroenteric); a colonic one suggests cancer.

nodes.q: Which finding starts it in an adult?
nodes.a: A lead point such as a tumor, polyp, lipoma or Meckel diverticulum
nodes.note: Peristalsis drags the lead point into the bowel beyond it.

nodes.q: What is the name of this concentric-ring appearance on CT?
nodes.note: In children the ultrasound shows the same target (or a pseudokidney on long view); a contrast enema shows a coiled-spring appearance.

nodes.q: In a 6-month-old with the same problem, which segment is involved?
nodes.a: Ileocolic (ileum into the cecum and colon)
nodes.note: Usually no lead point: enlarged Peyer patches (lymphoid hyperplasia) after a viral infection; a small risk follows rotavirus vaccination. When a child does have a lead point, think of Meckel diverticulum, IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) or cystic fibrosis.

nodes.q: Which stool appearance accompanies it in infants?
nodes.note: Blood and mucus; also drawing up legs, vomiting and a sausage-shaped mass in the right upper abdomen.

nodes.q: Which procedure both diagnoses and treats it in a stable child?
nodes.note: Surgery if peritonitis or perforation.

nodes.q: Which treatment does the man need?
nodes.a: Surgical resection of the involved bowel
nodes.note: Adults have a lead point in most cases and a possible cancer, so reduction by enema is not used.

nodes.q: Which complication kills?
nodes.a: Bowel ischemia and necrosis with perforation and peritonitis
nodes.note: Blood supply of the telescoped segment is squeezed in the fold.

nodes.q: His vomiting and cramps could be adhesive small bowel obstruction. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Previous abdominal surgery + distension + air-fluid levels with a transition point**; no mass
**Palpable mass + target sign, no previous surgery**

nodes.note: The trap: both give crampy pain and vomiting.

nodes.q: His pain could be appendicitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Periumbilical pain moving to the right lower quadrant + fever + tenderness at McBurney point**
**Colicky left mid-abdominal pain with a mass and a target on CT**

nodes.q: His wave-like pain could suggest volvulus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Marked distension with constipation in an older, often bedbound patient; coffee-bean loop (sigmoid) or bird's-beak on imaging**
**Target sign and mass; no coffee-bean loop**

image_prompts.root: A pastel loop of small bowel with one segment telescoped into the next like a collapsing telescope, with a cross-section showing concentric rings like a target.

root.stem: A 24-year-old man has passed hard, pebble-like stools that hurt, and his last bowel movement was 5 days ago. He sees streaks of bright red blood on the toilet paper. His diet has little fiber and he drinks little water. His abdomen is distended with quiet bowel sounds, and a pink ring of mucosa protrudes from the anus when he strains. He has not traveled to the tropics, has no diarrhea and no weight loss, and takes no medicines.
root.oneliner: 24M + hard pebble-like painful stools + last bowel movement 5 days ago + bright red streaks on paper + low fiber, little water + distended abdomen, quiet bowel sounds + pink mucosa protruding on straining + no tropical travel, no diarrhea, no weight loss, no medicines
highlight: last bowel movement was 5 days ago
has not traveled to the tropics
no diarrhea and no weight loss

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Infrequent (fewer than 3 per week), hard stools with straining. The clincher: **hard pebble-like stools and long gaps between bowel movements, with straining that leads to blood on the paper and a ring of mucosa at the anus**.

nodes.q: Which habit most likely caused it in this young man?
nodes.a: Low fiber and low fluid intake
nodes.note: Secondary causes to think of: hypothyroidism, hypercalcemia, diabetes, drugs (opioids, anticholinergics, verapamil, iron), and Hirschsprung disease in children.

nodes.q: Why does straining cause the complications?
nodes.a: It raises pressure inside the abdomen and the rectal veins
nodes.note: The repeated pressure pushes the lining out and swells the veins.

nodes.q: Which finding is the protruding pink ring of mucosa?
nodes.note: Treated by correcting the constipation; surgery if full-thickness and persistent.

nodes.q: Which swollen venous cushions can bleed bright red?
nodes.note: Painless bright red blood on the paper.

nodes.q: Which painful tear can hard stool cause?
nodes.note: Tearing pain during bowel movements; the pain leads to stool withholding and worse constipation.

nodes.q: Which complication follows days of retained hard stool?
nodes.note: Overflow diarrhea may leak around it; removed by manual disimpaction.

nodes.q: Which measures treat it first?
nodes.a: Fiber, fluids, exercise and an osmotic laxative such as polyethylene glycol
nodes.note: Lactulose or magnesium salts draw water into the bowel; stimulants such as bisacodyl are added if needed.

nodes.q: Which findings call for a colonoscopy?
nodes.a: Alarm features (age 45 or older, weight loss, iron deficiency anemia, blood mixed into the stool, or a family history of colon cancer)
nodes.note: His streaks of bright red blood on the paper fit the hard stools and straining, and he has none of the others; bleeding that persists after the stools soften still needs a look.

nodes.q: His rectal prolapse could be from whipworm infection. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Rectal prolapse in a malnourished child from the tropics, with bloody diarrhea, anemia and barrel-shaped eggs in stool**
**Hard stools and straining in a person with no tropical exposure or diarrhea**

nodes.note: The trap: both can end with rectal prolapse.

nodes.q: His blood on the paper could be from hemorrhoids alone. How do you tell them apart?

**Hard pebble stools, 5 days without a bowel movement and a distended abdomen**; the hemorrhoids and prolapse are consequences

root.stem: A 6-year-old girl was given aspirin for fever and aches 5 days after the rash of chickenpox began. Over 24 hours she has had repeated vomiting and become sleepy, and she then had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. She has an enlarged liver, no jaundice and no stiff neck. Aspartate and alanine aminotransferases are raised, ammonia is raised, glucose is low, bilirubin is normal, and cerebrospinal fluid is normal. She has had no earlier episodes and has developed normally.
root.oneliner: 6F + aspirin for fever 5 days into chickenpox + 24 hours of vomiting then drowsiness + generalized seizure + enlarged liver, no jaundice, no stiff neck + raised aminotransferases and ammonia + low glucose + normal bilirubin + normal cerebrospinal fluid + no earlier episodes, normal development
highlight: 5 days after the rash of chickenpox
enlarged liver, no jaundice and no stiff neck
no earlier episodes and has developed normally

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Acute liver injury with encephalopathy in a child given aspirin during a viral illness. The clincher: **aspirin during influenza or chickenpox + vomiting then drowsiness or seizure + enlarged liver without jaundice + high ammonia and normal bilirubin**.

nodes.q: Besides chickenpox, which viral infection classically precedes it?
nodes.note: Giving aspirin during either illness is the trigger; the syndrome became rare once aspirin was no longer given to children.

nodes.q: Dysfunction of which organelle explains the disease?
nodes.note: Salicylate injures liver mitochondria (swelling, uncoupling), so the processes that run inside them fail.

nodes.q: Which mitochondrial pathway fails, letting ammonia rise?
nodes.note: Its first steps (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and ornithine transcarbamylase) sit in the mitochondrial matrix. Ammonia is not converted to urea and rises, adding to the brain swelling.

nodes.q: Which mitochondrial process that powers gluconeogenesis during fasting fails, so her glucose falls?
nodes.note: Without it the liver lacks the acetyl-CoA and energy for gluconeogenesis, and the unburned fat builds up as tiny droplets in the hepatocytes.

nodes.q: What does a liver biopsy show?
nodes.a: Microvesicular fatty change without inflammation (swollen mitochondria on electron microscopy)
nodes.note: Hepatocytes are filled with tiny fat droplets; the nucleus stays central.

nodes.q: Which brain complication follows?
nodes.note: The high ammonia and mitochondrial failure make the brain swell.

nodes.q: Which event kills?
nodes.a: Brain herniation from raised intracranial pressure
nodes.note: Treat in intensive care, give glucose, lower the ammonia and the pressure.

nodes.q: Which fever drug is used instead in children with viral illness?
nodes.note: Aspirin is avoided in children, with Kawasaki disease as the exception.

nodes.q: How does aspirin work in its usual role?
nodes.a: It irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2)
nodes.note: It acetylates the enzyme, blocking thromboxane A2 and prostaglandin production.

nodes.q: Her high ammonia could suggest a urea cycle disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Recurrent episodes after a protein load or in the newborn period; high orotic acid with ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency; no aspirin trigger**
**Single episode after aspirin during a viral illness, normal development, low glucose**

nodes.note: The trap: both give high ammonia with vomiting and confusion.

nodes.q: Her low glucose could suggest a fatty acid oxidation defect. How do you tell them apart?

split.a: Fatty acid oxidation defect (for example medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency)
split.note: **Fasting hypoglycemia with low ketones, earlier episodes and a family history; no aspirin trigger**
**First episode ever, triggered by aspirin during a viral infection, normal development**

nodes.q: Her seizure and drowsiness could suggest viral encephalitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever, headache and neck stiffness with cerebrospinal fluid lymphocytes; normal liver tests**
**Normal cerebrospinal fluid, enlarged liver and high aminotransferases and ammonia**

nodes.q: Her liver enzymes could suggest acute liver failure from another cause. How do you tell them apart?

split.a: Acute liver failure (for example viral hepatitis)
split.note: **Jaundice, high bilirubin and prolonged prothrombin time**
**No jaundice, normal bilirubin and low glucose after aspirin use**

root.stem: A 66-year-old woman has felt tired again for the past month. One year ago she had surgery to remove the right side of her colon, followed by chemotherapy, for a stage III malignant tumor found there. Before that operation she had 3 months of fatigue, a hemoglobin of 9.1 g/dL and a mean corpuscular volume of 70 fL, but no abdominal pain, no visible blood in her stool and no change in bowel habits. Her mother and brother were both treated for the same kind of tumor, and her 40-year-old daughter asks whether a stool test for hidden blood would be enough to screen her. She has never smoked, has no liver disease, and eats a balanced diet without diarrhea or travel abroad. A computed tomography (CT) scan now shows five new 2- to 3-cm masses in the liver and in both lungs.
root.oneliner: 66F + fatigue + right colectomy and chemotherapy for a stage III tumor 1 year ago + earlier hemoglobin 9.1 and mean corpuscular volume 70 with no change in bowel habits, no visible blood + mother and brother with the same tumor + never smoker, no liver disease, balanced diet, no diarrhea or travel + five new 2-3 cm masses in liver and both lungs
highlight: surgery to remove the right side of her colon
no visible blood in her stool
Her mother and brother were both treated for the same kind of tumor
five new 2- to 3-cm masses in the liver and in both lungs

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A malignant tumor of the colon lining that spreads first to the liver. The clincher: **iron deficiency anemia with no bowel symptoms in an older adult (a right-sided tumor), then new masses in the liver and lungs after surgery**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The same disease; nearly all colorectal cancers are adenocarcinomas, which is how the exam often lists it.

nodes.q: Which type of anemia did her earlier blood count show?
nodes.note: Slow, hidden bleeding from the tumor drains her iron stores. New iron deficiency in an older adult is colon cancer until proven otherwise.

nodes.q: Why did her tumor bleed silently without changing her bowel habits?
nodes.a: It sat in the right colon, where the lumen is wide and the stool is liquid, so it grew large without blocking the bowel
nodes.note: A tumor in the cecum or ascending colon is bulky and exophytic and oozes blood that is not seen in the stool. Left-sided tumors narrow the smaller lumen and change bowel habits early.

nodes.q: Which sequence of gene changes turns a polyp into this cancer?
nodes.a: The adenoma-carcinoma sequence: loss of the APC gene, then a KRAS mutation, then loss of p53
nodes.note: Normal lining, then adenoma, then carcinoma over years. A second route, the microsatellite instability pathway, follows mismatch repair defects.

nodes.q: Which enzyme lets the cancer cells break through the basement membrane?
nodes.note: Type IV collagen is the main collagen of the basement membrane. Crossing it is what separates invasive carcinoma from dysplasia.

nodes.q: Which finding made her colon cancer stage III?
nodes.note: Stage depends on depth of invasion, lymph nodes and distant metastases; stage IV means distant spread, as now in her liver and lungs.

nodes.q: Suppose her tumor had been in the sigmoid colon instead. Which named group of nodes would it reach first, after the small nodes along the bowel wall?
nodes.note: Her cecal tumor drained along the ileocolic vessels to the superior mesenteric nodes. The sigmoid is supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery, so its lymph follows that artery.

nodes.q: Which organ is the most common first site of distant spread?
nodes.note: Veins from the colon and upper rectum drain by the portal vein into the liver, which filters the blood first. Rectal cancers also seed the liver this way, and a large firm rectal mass with weight loss and anemia carries the same risk.

nodes.q: Through which vein did tumor cells from the cecum reach the portal vein?
nodes.a: Superior mesenteric vein (receiving the ileocolic vein)
nodes.note: Ileocolic vein, then superior mesenteric vein, then portal vein, then the right hepatic branch to the right lobe. The inferior mesenteric vein drains the left colon and joins the splenic vein instead.

nodes.q: Through which large vessel did the liver deposits reach her lungs?
nodes.note: Hepatic veins empty into the inferior vena cava, then the right heart and the pulmonary arteries. The liver is the first filter and the lung the second; the pulmonary veins carry blood away from the lungs. Low rectal tumors drain through the middle and inferior rectal veins into the inferior vena cava and can reach the lungs first.

nodes.q: Which streptococcus found in the blood, often with endocarditis, should prompt a colonoscopy to look for a tumor like hers?
nodes.a: Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly Streptococcus bovis biotype I)
nodes.note: A group D, gamma-hemolytic streptococcus that grows in bile and salt; colonic tumors let it enter the blood. Clostridium septicum is the other bowel-tumor clue, causing spontaneous gas gangrene.

nodes.q: Her daughter asks for only a stool test for hidden blood. What is its main weakness given the family history?
nodes.note: It misses many cancers and advanced polyps, so a negative result cannot rule out disease in a high-risk person; a highly sensitive test is needed to rule a disease out. Management (Step 2): with a first-degree relative affected, colonoscopy starts at age 40 or 10 years before the relative's age at diagnosis, whichever is earlier, and is repeated every 5 years; average-risk screening starts at 45.

nodes.q: Which blood marker is followed after surgery to detect a recurrence?
nodes.note: A rising level after resection suggests recurrence. It is not a screening test.

nodes.q: Which chemotherapy lowers the risk of recurrence after surgery for stage III colon cancer?
nodes.note: Given for about 3 to 6 months after resection. Metastatic disease adds targeted antibodies, for example bevacizumab.

nodes.q: Which enzyme does fluorouracil block?
nodes.note: It cannot make thymidine, so DNA synthesis stops in dividing cells. Leucovorin stabilizes the drug-enzyme complex.

nodes.q: Which tumor test decides whether the anti-epidermal growth factor receptor antibody cetuximab can be used in metastatic disease?
nodes.note: Tumors with a RAS mutation do not respond, because the signal runs on without the receptor.

nodes.q: Her liver masses could suggest hepatocellular carcinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B or C + raised alpha-fetoprotein**; usually one mass that lights up in the arterial phase and washes out
**Several round masses in both lobes + a known colon cancer + raised carcinoembryonic antigen**; no cirrhosis

nodes.note: The trap: both give liver masses in an older adult, but she has no liver disease.

nodes.q: Her lung masses could suggest a primary lung cancer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Smoker + one spiculated mass or hilar mass** with cough or coughing blood
**Several round 'cannonball' nodules in both lungs + liver masses + a known colon cancer**

nodes.q: Her liver masses could also come from gastric cancer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Epigastric pain, early satiety, a left supraclavicular (Virchow) node, ovarian (Krukenberg) deposits**
**Prior right colon resection with iron deficiency and a family history of colon cancer**; no upper-abdominal symptoms

nodes.q: Other causes of her earlier iron deficiency were possible. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: In an older adult, occult bleeding from the bowel comes first.

head: Cause
Clincher
Why it does not fit
rows: She has a balanced diet and is postmenopausal
**Diarrhea, weight loss, anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies, duodenal villous atrophy**
**Travel or barefoot contact with tropical soil + eosinophilia**

nodes.q: Her family history could suggest familial adenomatous polyposis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hundreds to thousands of polyps from the teens + germline APC mutation**; colon cancer by about age 40 if untreated
**One large right-sided tumor in her sixties without polyposis**

nodes.q: Other common causes of hidden bowel blood loss were possible. How do you tell them apart?

head: Cause
Clincher
Why it does not fit
rows: **Bright red blood on the paper or stool, painless, rarely causes anemia**
She saw no blood in her stool
**Painless bleeding from small vessels in the right colon of an older adult**
It does not form masses in the liver and lungs
**Sudden painless bright red bleeding, or left lower quadrant pain with fever**
No pain, no fever and no metastases

root.stem: A 66-year-old woman has had fever, chills and pain in the left lower abdomen for 1 day. For 5 years she has had worsening constipation and eats little fiber. Two years ago a barium enema showed three separate, poorly outlined regions of narrowing in the distal sigmoid colon. Her temperature is 38.7°C, the left lower abdomen is tender, and the leukocyte count is 22,000/mm3 with 8% bands. She has no weight loss and has never seen blood in her stool. A computed tomography (CT) scan shows a thick-walled sigmoid colon with small outpouchings and a 5-cm abscess beside it.
root.oneliner: 66F + fever, chills, left lower abdominal pain for 1 day + 5 years of worsening constipation, low fiber diet + barium enema 2 years ago with three poorly outlined narrowed regions of the distal sigmoid + leukocytosis with bands + no weight loss, no visible blood + 5-cm abscess beside a thick-walled sigmoid with outpouchings
highlight: fever, chills and pain in the left lower abdomen
three separate, poorly outlined regions of narrowing in the distal sigmoid colon
never seen blood in her stool

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Inflammation and infection of outpouchings of the sigmoid colon wall. The clincher: **fever with left lower quadrant pain in an older adult with chronic constipation and a pericolic abscess on CT**.

nodes.q: Which layers of the colon wall make up the outpouchings?
nodes.a: Mucosa and submucosa only (a false diverticulum)
nodes.note: They herniate through weak points in the muscle where the vasa recta pierce it, pushed out by high pressure in the sigmoid from a low-fiber diet and straining (a pulsion diverticulum). A true diverticulum, such as Meckel, has all layers.

nodes.q: Which event starts the inflammation?
nodes.a: A hardened stool plug (fecalith) blocks the neck of a diverticulum
nodes.note: Bacteria overgrow behind the blockage, the thin wall inflames and a small perforation forms, which becomes a pericolic abscess.

nodes.q: Which family of receptors on her neutrophils binds bacterial lipopolysaccharide from the gut and helps activate them?
nodes.note: Pattern-recognition receptors of innate immunity; their signaling through nuclear factor kappa B makes neutrophils release cytokines and kill bacteria. The bands in her blood count are young neutrophils pushed out by the infection.

nodes.q: What explains the regions of narrowing seen on the barium enema years earlier?
nodes.a: Scarring (fibrosis) from repeated bouts of inflammation
nodes.note: The wall thickens and the lumen narrows over long segments, which can mimic cancer and explains her constipation.

nodes.q: If the abscess ruptures into the peritoneal cavity, which protein forms most of the exudate that coats the surface of the liver?
nodes.note: Fibrinous (then suppurative) peritonitis from leaked plasma proteins clotting on the peritoneal surface; generalized peritonitis with sepsis is what kills. Fibrin is later replaced by collagen if the patient survives.

nodes.q: If the inflamed sigmoid tracks into a nearby organ and causes air in the urine, which organ is most often involved?
nodes.note: A colovesical fistula; it is the most common fistula in diverticular disease and causes pneumaturia and recurrent urinary infection.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis during an attack?
nodes.a: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast
nodes.note: Shows wall thickening, fat stranding, outpouchings and any abscess. Avoid colonoscopy and barium enema during the attack because of perforation risk; colonoscopy 6 to 8 weeks later excludes cancer.

nodes.q: Which treatment does a 5-cm abscess need in addition to antibiotics?
nodes.note: Abscesses over about 3 to 4 cm are drained; peritonitis or failed drainage needs surgery (sigmoid resection with end colostomy, the Hartmann procedure).

nodes.q: Which drug is added to a cephalosporin or fluoroquinolone to cover anaerobes such as Bacteroides fragilis?
nodes.note: Inside anaerobes it is reduced to free radicals that break DNA. A disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol is the classic side effect.

nodes.q: Her narrowed sigmoid could suggest colon cancer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Weeks of bowel-habit change, narrow stools, iron deficiency anemia, a short abrupt 'apple-core' narrowing with overhanging edges**
**Acute fever and left lower quadrant pain + pericolic abscess + long smooth narrowed segments with outpouchings**

nodes.note: The trap: both narrow the sigmoid, and colonoscopy is still needed afterward.

nodes.q: Other causes of left lower quadrant pain with colitis were possible. How do you tell them apart?

head: Cause
Clincher
Why it does not fit
rows: **Sudden crampy pain then bloody diarrhea at the splenic flexure watershed in an older adult with vascular disease**
She has no bloody diarrhea and has an abscess
**Young adult, bloody diarrhea, continuous disease from the rectum**
Constipation with abscess, not bloody diarrhea
**Skip lesions, transmural inflammation, noncaseating granulomas, fistulas**
Disease is limited to the sigmoid with outpouchings
**Painless bleeding from the right colon in an older adult**
She has fever and pain but no bleeding

root.stem: A newborn boy, 1 day old, has bilious (green) vomiting and does not want to feed. He was born at term after a normal pregnancy and has no features of Down syndrome. He is dehydrated and his abdomen is mildly distended. An abdominal x-ray shows gas in the stomach, and gas is seen in the lower abdomen, not just two large bubbles in the upper abdomen. He has passed meconium.
root.oneliner: Newborn boy, 1 day old + bilious vomiting + poor feeding + dehydration + mild distension + no Down syndrome features + gas in the lower abdomen on x-ray, not just two bubbles + has passed meconium
highlight: gas is seen in the lower abdomen

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The gut did not rotate normally in the embryo, so the midgut hangs on a narrow stalk and twists. The clincher: **bilious vomiting in a newborn, which is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise**.

nodes.q: Which embryonic step failed?
nodes.a: Incomplete 270-degree counterclockwise rotation of the midgut around the superior mesenteric artery
nodes.note: This leaves the cecum in the upper abdomen and the duodenojejunal junction on the right.

nodes.q: Why does the bowel twist?
nodes.a: The midgut is attached by a short, narrow mesenteric base carrying the superior mesenteric artery and vein
nodes.note: The loops can wind around this stalk, usually clockwise.

nodes.q: Which artery is squeezed by the twist?
nodes.note: It supplies the gut from the distal duodenum to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon, not the celiac or inferior mesenteric territory.

nodes.q: Which event follows if the twist is not undone?
nodes.a: Midgut infarction (dead bowel), then peritonitis and shock
nodes.note: Hours matter; bloody stools and a tender, discolored abdomen are late signs.

nodes.q: Which bands can obstruct the duodenum even without a twist?
nodes.note: Peritoneal bands that run from the misplaced cecum across the duodenum to the right abdominal wall.

nodes.q: Which test shows the twist in a stable infant?
nodes.note: Shows the duodenojejunal junction to the right of the midline and a corkscrew duodenum; ultrasound may show the superior mesenteric vein wrapped around the artery (whirlpool sign). An unstable infant goes straight to surgery. Most cases appear in the first month, but the same anomaly can first show itself in an adult with sudden severe abdominal pain, found on the same contrast study.

nodes.q: Which operation treats it?
nodes.note: Untwist the bowel counterclockwise, cut the Ladd bands, widen the mesentery, remove the appendix and place the bowel in non-rotation, after fluid resuscitation.

nodes.q: His vomiting could suggest duodenal atresia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **'Double bubble' with no gas beyond it + Down syndrome + polyhydramnios**; bilious vomiting from the first feed
**Bilious vomiting with gas in the lower abdomen and meconium passed**; normal pregnancy

nodes.note: The trap: both give bilious vomiting in the first days, but he has gas beyond the duodenum and no Down syndrome features.

nodes.q: Other developmental anomalies of the gut were possible. How do you tell them apart?

head: Cause
Clincher
Why it does not fit
rows: **Nonbilious projectile vomiting at 3 to 6 weeks + olive-shaped mass + hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis**
He is 1 day old with bilious vomiting
**Failure to pass meconium in 48 hours + empty rectum + absent ganglion cells**
**Bowel outside the abdomen through a wall defect, with no covering sac**
**Mirror-image organs, sometimes with primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome)**
Organs are placed normally; the gut is twisted

root.stem: A 5-year-old boy has had intermittent bright red blood on his stools for 2 weeks. He is otherwise well, with normal vital signs and a normal physical examination. His hemoglobin is mildly low with a normal mean corpuscular volume, and a stool test for hidden blood is positive. Colonoscopy shows one smooth, round, red polyp about 1.5 cm wide on a stalk in the rectosigmoid colon. Biopsy shows widened, inflamed connective tissue with cystically dilated, mucus-filled glands. His parents and siblings have no polyps.
root.oneliner: 5M + 2 weeks of painless intermittent bright red blood on stools + otherwise well, normal exam + mild anemia with normal mean corpuscular volume + positive hidden blood + single smooth stalked rectosigmoid polyp + inflamed stroma with cystic mucus-filled glands + no family polyps
highlight: intermittent bright red blood on his stools for 2 weeks

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A benign polyp of early childhood. The clincher: **painless rectal bleeding in a child aged 2 to 5 with a single smooth stalked rectosigmoid polyp**.

nodes.q: Into which class of polyp does it fall, judged by its tissue?
nodes.note: A hamartoma is a disorganized overgrowth of tissue native to the site: here cystically dilated, mucus-filled glands in abundant inflamed lamina propria, with no dysplasia (also called a retention polyp). Unlike Peutz-Jeghers polyps, there is no branching smooth-muscle core.

nodes.q: Why is his anemia mild and normocytic rather than microcytic?
nodes.a: The bleeding has lasted only 2 weeks, so iron stores are not yet used up
nodes.note: Prolonged blood loss gives microcytic iron deficiency anemia.

nodes.q: What is the cancer risk of a single polyp like his?
nodes.note: A solitary juvenile polyp is not premalignant; it often shrinks or falls off by itself, which can end the bleeding.

nodes.q: Which condition is suspected when a child has five or more of these polyps or a family history?
nodes.note: Autosomal dominant, from SMAD4 or BMPR1A mutations, with a raised lifetime risk of colorectal cancer; needs lifelong colonoscopic surveillance.

nodes.q: Which procedure both confirms the diagnosis and treats it?
nodes.note: Removal also stops the bleeding; send the polyp for histology.

nodes.q: His polyp could suggest a tubular adenoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Adult, crowded dysplastic tubular glands**; premalignant, and rare in children except in familial adenomatous polyposis
**Child of 2 to 5, cystic mucus-filled glands in inflamed stroma, no dysplasia**

nodes.note: The trap: both are stalked colonic polyps that can bleed, but his biopsy shows cystic glands without dysplasia.

nodes.q: Other causes of a polyp or bleeding mass were possible. How do you tell them apart?

head: Cause
Clincher
Why it does not fit
rows: **Small rectosigmoid polyp in an adult with sawtooth (serrated) glands**
He is a child and the glands are cystic, not serrated
**Pseudopolyps of regenerating mucosa in ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease**
He has no diarrhea or colitis
**Small yellow submucosal nodule of neuroendocrine cells, usually in appendix or small bowel**
His polyp is a mucosal stalked polyp with mucus glands
**Invasive irregular glands in an older adult**
Rare at age 5 and the biopsy has no invasion

nodes.q: His polyp could suggest Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Dark spots on the lips and buccal mucosa + many small bowel polyps with branching smooth muscle + STK11 mutation**
**Solitary rectal polyp with cystic glands and no skin spots**

root.stem: A 75-year-old man has had 3 months of weight loss and a dull upper abdominal pain that goes through to his back. Over the past 2 weeks he has become jaundiced with dark urine and pale stools, and he has had no fever. He smokes one pack a day and was diagnosed with diabetes 4 months ago. His gallbladder is palpable and not tender, and both legs are swollen. Last month a tender red cord appeared along a vein of his left arm and faded, and then a new one appeared on his right thigh. A computed tomography (CT) scan shows an 8-cm mass in the head of the pancreas that surrounds and markedly narrows the inferior vena cava.
root.oneliner: 75M + 3 months of weight loss + dull epigastric pain through to the back + 2 weeks of jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, no fever + smoker + new diabetes 4 months ago + palpable non-tender gallbladder + swollen legs + tender red venous cords that move from arm to thigh + 8-cm pancreatic head mass encasing the inferior vena cava
highlight: a new one appeared on his right thigh
8-cm mass in the head of the pancreas

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A cancer of the pancreatic duct cells (ductal adenocarcinoma), usually in the head. The clincher: **jaundice without colic or fever, a palpable non-tender gallbladder and weight loss in an older smoker with new diabetes**.

nodes.q: Which sign names the palpable, non-tender gallbladder with jaundice?
nodes.note: A tumor blocks the common bile duct, so the gallbladder swells; in gallstone disease the gallbladder is usually scarred and small.

nodes.q: Which modifiable risk factor is the strongest?
nodes.note: Others: chronic pancreatitis, obesity, and new-onset diabetes in an older person, which can be an early sign of the cancer.

nodes.q: Which oncogene is mutated in most of these cancers?
nodes.note: Found in about 90 percent, with loss of the tumor suppressors CDKN2A, TP53 and SMAD4 later.

nodes.q: Which serum tumor marker is typically raised?
nodes.note: Useful to follow treatment, not to screen. Carcinoembryonic antigen can also be raised but is less specific.

nodes.q: With his inferior vena cava narrowed, through which veins does blood from his legs return to the superior vena cava?
nodes.a: The ascending lumbar, azygos and hemiazygos veins
nodes.note: The inferior vena cava lies directly behind the pancreatic head. The azygos system links the lumbar veins below to the superior vena cava above, forming the main collateral route.

nodes.q: What is the name of the tender red venous cords that appear in one limb, fade and reappear in another?
nodes.note: Mucin and tissue factor from the tumor make the blood hypercoagulable; it can be the first sign of the cancer.

nodes.q: Which imaging study is first for a suspected mass?
nodes.note: Shows the mass and a dilated bile and pancreatic duct (double-duct sign); endoscopic ultrasound with biopsy gives tissue.

nodes.q: Which operation is the only potential cure, for resectable disease?
nodes.note: Few patients qualify: most have vessel encasement or metastases at diagnosis, as here with the inferior vena cava. Palliation uses FOLFIRINOX (fluorouracil, leucovorin, irinotecan, oxaliplatin) or gemcitabine with nab-paclitaxel.

nodes.q: Which class of drug is gemcitabine?
nodes.note: It blocks DNA synthesis in dividing cells by inhibiting DNA polymerase and ribonucleotide reductase.

nodes.q: His pancreatic mass could suggest chronic pancreatitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Years of alcohol use, steatorrhea, diabetes and calcifications on CT**; pain that is long-standing, mass is inflammatory
**Recent weight loss and painless jaundice, a growing mass that encases vessels**; smoker, diabetes of recent onset

nodes.note: The trap: chronic pancreatitis raises the risk of pancreatic cancer and can mimic it.

nodes.q: His mass could suggest a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hypervascular mass with a hormone syndrome (insulinoma, gastrinoma) and chromogranin positivity**; slower growth and better survival
**Jaundice, weight loss and vessel encasement in an older smoker**, with no hormone syndrome

nodes.q: His jaundice could suggest a gallstone in the common bile duct. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Colicky right upper quadrant pain, often fever (cholangitis), and a small scarred gallbladder that cannot be felt**
**Jaundice without colic, with weight loss, no fever and a palpable non-tender gallbladder**

nodes.note: The Courvoisier sign points away from stones, because a chronically inflamed gallbladder cannot distend.

root.stem: A 30-year-old man with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection who takes no antiretroviral medication has had 10 days of nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps and watery diarrhea without blood, and has lost 2.3 kg. He swims at a public pool most weekends. He has no fever, no recent antibiotics, and no night sweats or enlarged liver and spleen. His CD4+ T-cell count is 80/mm3. A special stain of his stool shows round 4- to 6-micrometer oocysts that stain red.
root.oneliner: 30M + HIV, no antiretrovirals + 10 days of watery nonbloody diarrhea, cramps, nausea, vomiting + 2.3 kg weight loss + public pool + no fever, no antibiotics, no night sweats, no hepatosplenomegaly + CD4+ count 80 + special stain shows small round red-staining oocysts
highlight: no night sweats or enlarged liver and spleen
round 4- to 6-micrometer oocysts that stain red

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A protozoal intestinal infection. The clincher: **watery nonbloody diarrhea in a patient with advanced HIV and acid-fast oocysts in the stool**.

nodes.q: Which organism causes it?
nodes.a: Cryptosporidium (a protozoan; Cryptosporidium parvum or hominis)
nodes.note: The oocysts are passed in stool and survive chlorine, so public pools cause outbreaks.

nodes.q: Which stain shows the oocysts?
nodes.note: The oocysts stain red against the background; stool microscopy is the usual diagnosis.

nodes.q: How does it cause diarrhea?
nodes.a: It damages the brush border of the small intestine, causing villous blunting and a secretory-malabsorptive loss of fluid
nodes.note: Watery stool, no blood and no fever because the organism does not invade.

nodes.q: Which CD4+ T-cell level predicts severe, prolonged disease?
nodes.note: In healthy people the illness is self-limited; in advanced HIV it can last for months.

nodes.q: Which treatment restores his ability to clear the infection?
nodes.a: Antiretroviral therapy to raise the CD4+ count
nodes.note: Fluids and electrolytes are key. Nitazoxanide shortens the illness in immunocompetent patients but works poorly until immune recovery in HIV.

nodes.q: His red-staining stool organisms could suggest Mycobacterium avium complex infection. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **CD4+ count below 50 + fever, night sweats, weight loss and enlarged liver and spleen**; acid-fast bacilli on blood culture or biopsy
**Watery diarrhea, no fever or hepatosplenomegaly + round 4- to 6-micrometer oocysts on modified acid-fast stain**

nodes.note: The trap: both are acid-fast and both occur in advanced HIV.

nodes.q: Other causes of diarrhea in HIV or after swimming were possible. How do you tell them apart?

head: Cause
Clincher
Why it does not fit
rows: **Larger oval acid-fast oocysts (20 to 30 micrometers) + eosinophilia; treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole**
His oocysts are small and round
**Foul, fatty stools and gas after drinking stream water; pear-shaped trophozoites with two nuclei**
The stain shows round acid-fast oocysts
**Bloody mucoid stool with fever and tenesmus**
His stool has no blood and he has no fever

root.stem: A 40-year-old man has had 6 months of constipation and weakness. His hemoglobin is 10 g/dL and his mean corpuscular volume is 73 fL. His father and two uncles had colon cancer, one of them before age 50, and his paternal grandmother had endometrial cancer, over three generations. Colonoscopy found a mass in the right colon, with only two small polyps and no carpet of polyps. He has no unusual skin lesions or sun sensitivity, no brown skin spots, and no history of sarcoma in the family. After colectomy the tumor is mucinous with many lymphocytes.
root.oneliner: 40M + 6 months of constipation and weakness + hemoglobin 10, mean corpuscular volume 73 + father and two uncles with colon cancer, one before 50, grandmother with endometrial cancer, three generations + right colon mass, two small polyps, no polyposis + no skin lesions, sun sensitivity, brown spots or sarcoma in family + mucinous tumor with many lymphocytes
highlight: father and two uncles had colon cancer
only two small polyps and no carpet of polyps
no unusual skin lesions or sun sensitivity
no history of sarcoma in the family

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An inherited cancer syndrome from a defect in DNA mismatch repair. The clincher: **colorectal and endometrial cancers over several generations, one before age 50, and no polyposis**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease; 'nonpolyposis' separates it from familial adenomatous polyposis.

nodes.q: Which named family-history criteria does his pedigree meet?
nodes.note: Three relatives with a Lynch-type cancer, in at least two generations, with one diagnosed before age 50 and familial adenomatous polyposis excluded.

nodes.q: Which family of genes carries the inherited defect?
nodes.a: DNA mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2)
nodes.note: Autosomal dominant germline mutation; MLH1 and MSH2 are the most common. The second copy is lost in the tumor.

nodes.q: Which change in the tumor DNA results from this defect?
nodes.note: Copy errors in short repeated DNA sequences go unrepaired. Mutations pile up, so the few polyps progress fast to cancer at a young age, typically right-sided, mucinous and full of lymphocytes, as in his tumor.

nodes.q: Which cancer outside the colon is most common in affected women?
nodes.note: Also ovarian, stomach, small bowel, ureter and renal pelvis; sebaceous tumors in the Muir-Torre variant.

nodes.q: How are carriers screened?
nodes.a: Colonoscopy every 1 to 2 years starting at age 20 to 25
nodes.note: Or 2 to 5 years before the youngest relative's diagnosis. Tumors can be tested for loss of mismatch repair proteins.

nodes.q: Which drug class works especially well in metastatic tumors with mismatch repair deficiency?
nodes.a: Programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) inhibitors such as pembrolizumab
nodes.note: Many mutations make neoantigens that the immune system can attack once the checkpoint is blocked.

nodes.q: His colon cancer could suggest familial adenomatous polyposis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hundreds to thousands of colonic polyps from the teens + germline APC mutation**; retinal pigment lesions
**Few polyps + cancer at young age in many relatives + mismatch repair defect**

nodes.note: The trap: both give early-onset colon cancer in families.

nodes.q: Other inherited cancer syndromes were possible. How do you tell them apart?

head: Cause
Clincher
Why it does not fit
rows: **TP53 mutation; sarcoma, breast, brain, adrenal and leukemia before age 45**
No sarcoma in the family and colon cancers dominate
**Defective nucleotide excision repair; severe sunburn and skin cancers in childhood**
No sun sensitivity or skin lesions
