root.stem: A 52-year-old woman has had 8 months of itching and fatigue, with dry eyes and a dry mouth. She drinks no alcohol and takes no new drugs. She has yellow fatty plaques around her eyelids, and her liver is mildly enlarged. Alkaline phosphatase is 4 times the upper limit, aminotransferases are only mildly raised, and anti-mitochondrial antibodies are positive. She has no inflammatory bowel disease, and her ultrasound shows normal bile ducts. Years later she develops cirrhosis and needs a liver transplant.
root.oneliner: 52F + 8 months of itching and fatigue + dry eyes and mouth + no alcohol, no new drugs + xanthelasma + mild hepatomegaly + alkaline phosphatase 4x normal, mild aminotransferases + anti-mitochondrial antibodies + no inflammatory bowel disease, normal bile ducts on ultrasound + later cirrhosis and liver transplant
highlight: dry eyes and a dry mouth
yellow fatty plaques around her eyelids

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An autoimmune destruction of small bile ducts in the liver, mainly in middle-aged women. The clincher: **itching and raised alkaline phosphatase with anti-mitochondrial antibodies**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The older name, changed because cirrhosis occurs only late.

nodes.q: Which antigen do anti-mitochondrial antibodies target?
nodes.a: The E2 subunit of pyruvate dehydrogenase
nodes.note: Found in about 95 percent; IgM is also raised.

nodes.q: What does the liver biopsy show?
nodes.a: Lymphocytic destruction of interlobular bile ducts with granulomas (florid duct lesion)
nodes.note: T cells attack the bile duct cells.

nodes.q: Which other autoimmune condition explains her dry eyes and mouth?
nodes.note: Others: autoimmune thyroiditis and limited systemic sclerosis.

nodes.q: Which sign shows her high blood cholesterol?
nodes.note: Fatty plaques around the eyelids from cholestasis.

nodes.q: Which fat-soluble vitamins can she lack?
nodes.a: Vitamins A, D, E and K
nodes.note: Bile acids are needed to absorb fat. Lack of vitamin D causes osteomalacia (and the disease itself adds osteoporosis); lack of vitamin K causes bleeding.

nodes.q: Which drug slows progression?
nodes.note: It dilutes toxic bile acids; add obeticholic acid or a fibrate if the response is poor. Cholestyramine treats itching.

nodes.q: Which treatment is the only cure of end-stage disease?
nodes.note: The disease can recur in the graft.

nodes.q: Which enzyme do tacrolimus and cyclosporine inhibit in T cells to prevent rejection?
nodes.note: Blocking calcineurin keeps the nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT) from entering the nucleus, so interleukin-2 is not made and T cells do not activate.

nodes.q: Her cholestasis could suggest primary sclerosing cholangitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Man with ulcerative colitis, perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (p-ANCA), beaded bile ducts on cholangiography**
**Middle-aged woman, anti-mitochondrial antibodies, normal large bile ducts**

nodes.note: The trap: both are cholestatic liver diseases that end in cirrhosis.

nodes.q: Her tiredness could suggest autoimmune hepatitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Very high aminotransferases, anti-smooth muscle or antinuclear antibodies, plasma cells at the portal interface**
**Alkaline phosphatase high, aminotransferases only mildly up, anti-mitochondrial antibodies**

image_prompts.root: Pastel teaching picture: a small liver bile duct surrounded by lymphocytes with a granuloma, and yellow plaques on an eyelid; no text

root.stem: A 52-year-old man has had 2 months of burning epigastric pain that starts 2 to 3 hours after meals and wakes him at night; eating relieves it. He takes ibuprofen 600 mg daily for knee arthritis and has noticed black tarry stools for 2 days. He has no diarrhea, no pain radiating to the back, and his weight is stable. Endoscopy shows a single 1.5-cm ulcer with smooth, regular edges in the first part of the duodenum. A biopsy dropped into urea broth with a pH indicator turns the medium from yellow to pink within an hour, and a silver stain of the adjacent mucosa shows curved rods.
root.oneliner: 52M + burning epigastric pain 2-3 h after meals and at night, relieved by eating + daily ibuprofen + black tarry stools + single smooth-edged duodenal ulcer + biopsy turns urea medium pink, curved rods
highlight: no pain radiating to the back
single 1.5-cm ulcer with smooth, regular edges

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A break in the lining of the duodenum or stomach caused by acid and pepsin; his is a duodenal ulcer. The clincher: **burning epigastric pain 2 to 3 hours after meals and at night, relieved by eating, with an ulcer seen at endoscopy**.

nodes.q: Which bacterial infection causes most of these ulcers?
nodes.note: A curved, flagellated Gram-negative rod that lives in the mucus layer of the stomach; a silver stain (Steiner or Warthin-Starry) shows the curved rods. Antral infection lowers somatostatin, which raises gastrin and acid output, so most duodenal ulcers and many gastric ulcers follow. It is also catalase- and oxidase-positive, but urease is the enzyme that changes the pH.

nodes.q: Which enzyme of the organism splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, so that his biopsy turned the medium pink?
nodes.note: The ammonia neutralizes stomach acid around the bacterium so it survives, and the rise in pH turns the indicator (phenol red or phenolphthalein) from yellow to pink or red: the rapid urease test. The same reaction is the basis of the urea breath test.

nodes.q: Besides neutralizing acid, how does the organism injure the mucosa?
nodes.a: It releases proteases and other enzymes that break down the protective mucus and cause local tissue destruction
nodes.note: Proteases and phospholipases break down mucus; toxins such as the vacuolating cytotoxin (VacA) and the cag pathogenicity island protein (CagA) add to the damage and the inflammation. Urease-made ammonia is itself toxic to the epithelium.

nodes.q: Which noninvasive test, in which he swallows labeled urea, confirms the infection and later confirms cure?
nodes.note: The stool antigen test is the other noninvasive choice. Stop proton pump inhibitors 2 weeks before testing or the result can be falsely negative. Antibody tests stay positive after cure, so they cannot confirm eradication.

nodes.q: Which regimen eradicates the organism?
nodes.a: Triple therapy: a proton pump inhibitor plus clarithromycin plus amoxicillin (metronidazole if penicillin-allergic)
nodes.note: Where clarithromycin resistance is common, bismuth quadruple therapy (proton pump inhibitor, bismuth, metronidazole and tetracycline) is preferred. Eradication heals the ulcer and prevents recurrence.

nodes.q: Which drug in his history is the second cause of his ulcer?
nodes.note: Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID); NSAIDs and Helicobacter pylori are the two main causes of peptic ulcers. Without the infection, NSAID use is the strongest predisposing factor; smoking, alcohol, diet and psychological stress are weaker, and smoking mainly slows healing.

nodes.q: Which enzyme do these drugs inhibit?
nodes.note: Phospholipase A2 first frees arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids; cyclooxygenase then converts arachidonic acid into prostaglandin G2 and H2, the parents of the prostaglandins, prostacyclin and thromboxane. Aspirin blocks it irreversibly (acetylation); ibuprofen and naproxen block it reversibly.

nodes.q: Which product of this pathway normally protects the stomach lining?
nodes.note: Made through cyclooxygenase-1, it raises mucus and bicarbonate secretion, increases mucosal blood flow and lowers acid secretion by parietal cells; prostacyclin also helps. Without them, acid injures the mucosa. Selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors such as celecoxib spare much of this protection.

nodes.q: Which drug replaces the lost protective prostaglandin?
nodes.note: A prostaglandin E1 analogue that lowers the risk of NSAID ulcers in a patient who must keep taking the NSAID. Side effects are diarrhea and uterine contractions, so it must not be given in pregnancy. Sucralfate coats the ulcer base but does not prevent NSAID ulcers; a proton pump inhibitor is the usual alternative. Antibiotics such as ampicillin or metronidazole do not protect against NSAID injury.

nodes.q: Which other drugs carry the same ulcer risk as his ibuprofen?
nodes.a: Other non-selective NSAIDs, such as naproxen and aspirin
nodes.note: Other drugs used for rheumatoid arthritis, such as gold, penicillamine, chloroquine and cyclophosphamide, and acetaminophen (no peripheral cyclooxygenase effect) do not injure the stomach lining through prostaglandins.

nodes.q: Which complication explains his black tarry stools?
nodes.a: Bleeding from the ulcer (upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage)
nodes.note: Digested blood turns the stool black and tarry (melena). Bleeding is the most common complication of peptic ulcer disease.

nodes.q: Which artery is eroded by a deep ulcer on the back wall of the first part of the duodenum?
nodes.note: It runs behind the first part of the duodenum, so a posterior ulcer can bleed massively.

nodes.q: What is the first-line management of the bleeding?
nodes.a: Resuscitation with fluids, a proton pump inhibitor, then upper endoscopy with endoscopic treatment of the ulcer
nodes.note: Proton pump inhibitors block the hydrogen-potassium ATPase of the parietal cell. Test for Helicobacter pylori and treat it afterwards.

nodes.q: Which complication causes sudden severe abdominal pain, pain in the shoulder and a board-like abdomen?
nodes.a: Perforation of the ulcer into the peritoneal cavity (a perforated viscus)
nodes.note: Gas and gastric contents escape and cause chemical peritonitis. Irritation of the diaphragm refers pain to the shoulder.

nodes.q: Which wall of the first part of the duodenum usually perforates?
nodes.note: Anterior ulcers perforate into the peritoneal cavity; posterior ulcers erode into the gastroduodenal artery and bleed. The duodenum is the most common site of a perforated ulcer in a young man; a perforated stomach ulcer is the next most common source.

nodes.q: Which finding on an upright chest x-ray shows the perforation?
nodes.note: Free air under the diaphragm means a perforated hollow organ. A CT scan is more sensitive when the film is normal.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Emergency surgical repair (for example an omental patch) with intravenous fluids, antibiotics and a proton pump inhibitor
nodes.note: The patient is made nil by mouth. Nasogastric decompression is used; delay raises the risk of sepsis.

nodes.q: Which late complication, from scarring of a chronically inflamed duodenum, makes patients vomit undigested food after meals?
nodes.note: Vomiting of acid causes a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis; a succussion splash may be heard.

nodes.q: His ulcer is in the duodenum. How does a gastric ulcer differ?

split.note: Pain **worse soon after eating**, weight loss, usually in the antrum or lesser curvature; always biopsy because it can be malignant
Pain **2 to 3 hours after meals and at night, relieved by eating**, weight stable or gained; almost never malignant and Brunner glands enlarge

nodes.note: Both are linked to Helicobacter pylori and NSAIDs, and both are called peptic ulcers.

nodes.q: His smooth, regular ulcer edges point to a benign ulcer. How do you tell gastric adenocarcinoma apart?

split.note: **Irregular, heaped-up edges + weight loss + biopsy showing malignant glands**; linked to Helicobacter pylori, nitrosamines and a smoked-food diet
**Smooth, regular edges + a biopsy showing only inflammation with curved rods + stable weight**

nodes.note: Both give epigastric pain and a bleeding ulcer.

nodes.q: He has no diarrhea. How do you tell Zollinger-Ellison syndrome apart?

split.note: **Multiple ulcers beyond the first part of the duodenum + watery diarrhea + very high gastrin** from a pancreatic or duodenal gastrinoma; ulcers do not heal on standard treatment
**A single ulcer in the first part of the duodenum + no diarrhea** + Helicobacter pylori or NSAID exposure

nodes.note: Both cause severe ulcer pain and bleeding.

nodes.q: His pain does not go to the back. How do you tell acute pancreatitis apart?

split.note: **Constant epigastric pain radiating to the back + high lipase**, often after gallstones or heavy alcohol; no relief with food
**Burning pain 2 to 3 hours after meals, relieved by eating, no radiation to the back**

image_prompts.root: A pastel cross-section of the stomach and first part of the duodenum with a small round ulcer in the duodenal wall, curved bacteria in the mucus nearby and a bleeding vessel at its base.

root.stem: A 68-year-old woman has had 9 months of cramping upper abdominal pain that starts about 30 minutes after meals and lasts about 1 hour. She avoids eating and has lost 11 kg (24 lb). She smoked for 40 years, had coronary artery bypass grafting 6 years ago, and takes aspirin, atenolol and simvastatin. She does not drink alcohol, does not vomit, and has no jaundice. Her blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg and her pulse is irregularly irregular. At the apex there is an opening snap followed by a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble. An abdominal bruit is heard; the abdomen is soft and not tender, and her pedal pulses are weak. A CT scan shows a 3-cm ectatic aorta below the renal arteries, and the stool is negative for blood.
root.oneliner: 68F + cramping pain 30 min after meals + fear of eating + 11 kg weight loss + prior bypass surgery + irregularly irregular pulse with opening snap + abdominal bruit + soft nontender abdomen + weak pedal pulses + ectatic infrarenal aorta + stool negative for blood
highlight: coronary artery bypass grafting 6 years ago
3-cm ectatic aorta below the renal arteries

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Narrowed arteries cannot meet the extra blood flow the gut needs after a meal. The clincher: **cramping pain 30 to 60 minutes after eating, fear of eating and weight loss in a patient with widespread atherosclerosis**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Also called abdominal angina. It is called angina because pain comes when demand outstrips supply, like exertional chest pain.

nodes.q: Why does the pain begin shortly after she eats?
nodes.a: Digestion raises the gut's blood demand, which a fixed narrowed supply cannot meet
nodes.note: The pain stops as demand falls, usually within about an hour.

nodes.q: Which behavior caused her weight loss?
nodes.note: She eats less to avoid the pain; malabsorption from the chronic gut ischemia adds to the loss.

nodes.q: Which disease process narrows the arteries?
nodes.note: It narrows the origins of the arteries from the aorta. Her coronary bypass, smoking, high blood pressure and weak pedal pulses show the same disease elsewhere.

nodes.q: Which artery to the small bowel is the key vessel narrowed?
nodes.note: It supplies the small bowel and the right colon, so its stenosis causes the pain after meals. A bruit may be heard over the upper abdomen.

nodes.q: Her ectatic aorta lies below the renal arteries. Which second gut artery, arising from that segment, is the one most likely narrowed along with the superior mesenteric artery?
nodes.note: Symptoms usually need at least two of the three main gut arteries (celiac trunk, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric) to be narrowed, because collaterals protect against one: the pancreaticoduodenal arcades link celiac and superior mesenteric, and the marginal artery and arc of Riolan link superior and inferior mesenteric. The celiac trunk and superior mesenteric artery arise above the renal arteries; the inferior mesenteric arises from the infrarenal aorta, where her disease is. Hepatic and phrenic arteries are branches, not main gut trunks.

nodes.q: Low flow in this system injures the colon first at which watershed area between the superior and inferior mesenteric territories?
nodes.note: The splenic flexure (Griffith point) lies between the superior and inferior mesenteric supplies; the rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck point) is the other watershed. Ischemia there causes ischemic colitis: pain followed by bloody diarrhea.

nodes.q: Which test shows the narrowed arteries?
nodes.note: Duplex ultrasound is a first screening test; conventional angiography is used when treating.

nodes.q: What is the definitive treatment?
nodes.note: Treat risk factors with aspirin, a statin and smoking cessation. Untreated disease can end in bowel infarction.

nodes.q: If she suddenly developed severe abdominal pain with a soft abdomen, which mechanism would most likely have blocked her superior mesenteric artery?
nodes.a: Embolism from a clot in the left atrium
nodes.note: Atrial fibrillation with mitral stenosis forms clots in the left atrium that travel down the aorta; the superior mesenteric artery is the most common site because it leaves the aorta at a narrow angle. Abdominal x-ray may show distended small bowel and right colon, the territory of that artery.

nodes.q: Which exam finding marks the early phase of the attack?
nodes.a: Pain out of proportion to the abdominal examination
nodes.note: The abdomen stays soft until the bowel wall dies.

nodes.q: Which event follows if the blood supply is not restored?
nodes.note: Lactate rises, the bowel wall may bleed and the patient becomes septic. Small bowel infarction is hemorrhagic (red) because of the dual and collateral blood supply.

nodes.q: Which urgent treatment is given?
nodes.a: Intravenous heparin, CT angiography and emergency revascularization or resection of dead bowel
nodes.note: Embolectomy or stenting restores flow; a second-look operation checks the bowel.

nodes.q: Her plaques could also block the artery in a sudden attack. How do you tell thrombosis from embolism?

split.note: **Weeks to months of pain after meals and weight loss before the sudden attack**; no atrial fibrillation needed
**Sudden onset with no earlier symptoms + atrial fibrillation or valve disease**

nodes.note: The trap: both occlude the superior mesenteric artery in a patient with atherosclerosis.

nodes.q: Her pain comes after meals, as in peptic ulcer disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Burning epigastric pain relieved by eating or antacids + stool positive for blood**; no bruit, and weight stable
**Cramping pain 30 to 60 minutes after meals + fear of eating + abdominal bruit + atherosclerosis**

nodes.q: Her weight loss could suggest pancreatic cancer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Painless jaundice, pain radiating to the back, a palpable gallbladder or a mass** in an older smoker
**Pain that follows each meal and fades, abdominal bruit, no jaundice or mass**

nodes.q: Her pain after eating could suggest chronic pancreatitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Long alcohol use, pain radiating to the back, fatty stools, pancreatic calcifications on imaging**
**Pain after meals in a patient with atherosclerosis and an abdominal bruit, with no alcohol use or fatty stools**

nodes.q: Her fear of eating could suggest gastroparesis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Early fullness, nausea and vomiting, usually with long-standing diabetes**; delayed gastric emptying on scintigraphy
**Cramping pain 30 to 60 minutes after eating without vomiting + abdominal bruit**

root.stem: A 59-year-old man has had 3 months of progressive trouble swallowing, first with meat and bread and now with soft foods, and has lost 6.8 kg (15 lb). He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years and drinks four to six beers a day. He has no heartburn, has never had acid reflux, and does not regurgitate undigested food. His voice is hoarse and his serum calcium is 12.4 mg/dL. Barium swallow shows an irregular narrowing in the middle of the esophagus, and endoscopy shows a 6-cm mass that is centrally ulcerated with a raised rim of surrounding mucosa. A chest x-ray shows enlarged paratracheal and hilar lymph nodes.
root.oneliner: 59M + progressive dysphagia for solids then soft food + 6.8 kg weight loss + 40 pack-year smoking + daily heavy alcohol + no reflux + hoarse voice + high calcium + irregular mid-esophageal narrowing with ulcerated mass + mediastinal nodes
highlight: one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years
four to six beers a day
irregular narrowing in the middle of the esophagus
centrally ulcerated with a raised rim
enlarged paratracheal and hilar lymph nodes

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A cancer of the squamous lining of the upper and middle esophagus. The clincher: **progressive dysphagia (solids, then soft food) with weight loss in a heavy smoker and drinker, and an ulcerated mid-esophageal mass**.

nodes.q: Why does his trouble swallowing start with solids rather than liquids?
nodes.a: A fixed mechanical narrowing of the lumen by the tumor
nodes.note: Mechanical obstruction blocks solids first and liquids only later; a motility disorder such as achalasia troubles solids and liquids from the start. Weight loss and cachexia are alarm features.

nodes.q: Which two exposures in his history act together as the main risk factors?
nodes.a: Cigarette smoking and heavy alcohol use
nodes.note: Other risks: very hot drinks, nitrosamines, achalasia, lye strictures, Plummer-Vinson syndrome, human papillomavirus and tylosis. Worldwide this is the most common esophageal cancer; in the United States adenocarcinoma is now more common.

nodes.q: What would a biopsy show?
nodes.a: Squamous cells with foci of keratinization (keratin pearls and intercellular bridges)
nodes.note: Adenocarcinoma shows glands (acinar formation) instead.

nodes.q: Which part of the esophagus is typical for this cancer type?
nodes.note: Adenocarcinoma arises in the lower third. His barium swallow shows a mid-esophageal narrowing.

nodes.q: An esophagectomy at the level of his tumor ligates arterial branches of which vessel?
nodes.note: The middle esophagus gets branches directly from the thoracic aorta. The upper esophagus is supplied by the inferior thyroid artery from the thyrocervical trunk, and the lower esophagus by the left gastric and inferior phrenic arteries.

nodes.q: Which lymph node group drains the middle third of the esophagus?
nodes.a: The mediastinal nodes (tracheobronchial and posterior mediastinal)
nodes.note: This explains his enlarged paratracheal and hilar nodes. The upper third drains to the deep cervical nodes and the lower third to the celiac and left gastric nodes.

nodes.q: Which nerve does the tumor invade to make his voice hoarse?
nodes.note: It loops under the aortic arch next to the esophagus.

nodes.q: Which hormone from the tumor explains his high calcium?
nodes.note: Squamous cell carcinomas, like those of the lung, secrete it and cause hypercalcemia of malignancy.

nodes.q: Which complication links the esophagus to the airway and causes coughing with swallowing and pneumonia?
nodes.note: Tumor invasion also spreads to the aorta and pericardium.

nodes.q: Which test makes the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Endoscopic ultrasound stages the depth and the nodes; CT and PET scans look for distant spread.

nodes.q: Which treatment is used for a locally advanced squamous tumor?
nodes.a: Chemoradiation (surgery for selected early or resectable tumors)
nodes.note: Squamous cell carcinoma is more radiosensitive than adenocarcinoma. Prognosis is poor because the esophagus has no serosa and spread is early.

nodes.q: He has no heartburn. How do you tell esophageal adenocarcinoma apart?

split.note: **Lower third + long-standing reflux and Barrett esophagus + obesity**; biopsy shows glands (acinar formation)
**Middle third + smoking and alcohol + keratinization on biopsy + no reflux**

nodes.note: The trap: both give progressive dysphagia, weight loss and an ulcerated mass.

nodes.q: His difficulty began with solids. How do you tell achalasia apart?

split.note: **Dysphagia for solids and liquids from the start + regurgitation of undigested food + bird's beak on barium swallow**; no mass
**Solids first, then liquids, over months + weight loss + an irregular mid-esophageal narrowing with an ulcerated mass**

nodes.q: His mass is ulcerated with a raised rim. How does an esophageal leiomyoma differ?

split.note: **Smooth bulge covered by normal mucosa** that is mostly silent; biopsy shows smooth muscle differentiation
**Ulcerated mass with a raised mucosal rim + weight loss**; biopsy shows keratinization

nodes.q: His enlarged hilar nodes in a heavy smoker could suggest small cell lung carcinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Central lung mass + cells with neuroendocrine (dense-core) granules, positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin**; paraneoplastic inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, Cushing syndrome or Lambert-Eaton syndrome rather than high calcium
**Keratinization on biopsy + ulcerated esophageal mass + high calcium**

nodes.q: Rarely, an ulcerated esophageal mass is a melanoma. How do you tell it apart from his tumor?

split.note: **Rare tumor with intracytoplasmic melanin pigment** on the biopsy, often a dark polypoid mass
**Keratinization and intercellular bridges with no pigment**

root.stem: A 31-year-old woman has had 10 years of fewer than three bowel movements a week with diffuse cramping lower abdominal pain that eases after she passes stool. Every few months she has 2 to 6 days of loose, watery stools. She passed meconium on her first day of life, her mood, sleep, appetite and energy are normal, and she has never lost weight, seen blood in her stool, or been woken at night by symptoms. The abdomen is mildly tender all over with normal bowel sounds. Blood count, metabolic panel, thyroid function and tissue transglutaminase antibody tests are normal.
root.oneliner: 31F + 10 years of fewer than 3 stools a week + cramping pain eased by defecation + episodes of loose stools + normal mood, sleep, appetite + no weight loss, blood or night symptoms + normal tests
highlight: fewer than three bowel movements a week
2 to 6 days of loose, watery stools
passed meconium on her first day of life
mood, sleep, appetite and energy are normal
mildly tender all over with normal bowel sounds
tissue transglutaminase antibody tests are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A functional bowel disorder with recurrent abdominal pain tied to defecation and a change in stool habit, with normal tests. The clincher: **cramping pain relieved by passing stool + altered stool frequency, with no alarm features and normal tests**.

nodes.q: Which feature of her pain best points to the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The Rome IV criteria need pain at least 1 day a week for 3 months, linked to defecation or to a change in stool frequency or form.

nodes.q: Which type of finding is absent that makes a functional diagnosis safe?
nodes.a: Alarm features (blood in the stool, weight loss, anemia, night symptoms, fever or onset after age 50)
nodes.note: Their presence calls for colonoscopy and further workup.

nodes.q: Which basic abnormality is thought to cause the symptoms?
nodes.a: Visceral hypersensitivity with altered gut motility (a disorder of the gut-brain axis)
nodes.note: There is no structural or inflammatory lesion; serotonin signaling in the gut is involved. It is more common in women, may start after a bout of infectious gastroenteritis, and often coexists with anxiety, depression and fibromyalgia.

nodes.q: Which limited tests exclude the main look-alikes?
nodes.a: Blood count, an inflammatory marker (C-reactive protein or fecal calprotectin) and celiac serology
nodes.note: Colonoscopy is reserved for alarm features or age over 45 to 50 for screening.

nodes.q: Which measures come first in management?
nodes.a: Reassurance, a fiber supplement and dietary changes (for example a low-FODMAP diet)
nodes.note: Antispasmodics such as dicyclomine ease cramping; low-dose tricyclic antidepressants help persistent pain.

nodes.q: Which receptor action would slow her episodes of loose stool?
nodes.a: Agonism at mu-opioid receptors of the myenteric plexus (loperamide)
nodes.note: Loperamide is an opioid that does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so it slows motility and raises water absorption without central effects. Avoid it in bloody or infectious diarrhea and in colitis. Inhibiting colonic water absorption, blocking 5-hydroxytryptamine 1 receptors (the triptan target is agonism) or blocking tumor necrosis factor would not help her.

nodes.q: Which receptor does alosetron block for severe diarrhea-predominant disease in women?
nodes.note: It can cause ischemic colitis and severe constipation, so its use is restricted. Bile acid binders such as cholestyramine help when bile acid diarrhea is the cause; they reduce bile acid reabsorption rather than increase it.

nodes.q: Which drug group is added when constipation dominates and fiber fails?
nodes.a: Secretagogues such as linaclotide (guanylate cyclase C agonist) or lubiprostone (chloride channel activator)
nodes.note: They increase intestinal fluid secretion.

nodes.q: Her stools are sometimes loose. How do you tell celiac disease apart?

split.note: **Positive tissue transglutaminase antibodies + iron deficiency anemia or weight loss**; villous atrophy on duodenal biopsy
**Negative celiac serology + normal blood count + stable weight**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause chronic bloating and altered stools in a young woman.

nodes.q: Her constipation has lasted 10 years. How do you tell Hirschsprung disease apart?

split.note: **Delayed passage of meconium after birth + constipation from infancy + aganglionic rectum**
**Passed meconium on day one + intermittent loose-stool episodes + pain eased by defecation**

nodes.q: Constipation can accompany depression. How do you tell major depressive disorder apart?

split.note: **Low mood, loss of interest, poor sleep, appetite and energy for at least 2 weeks**; constipation is a side symptom
**Normal mood, sleep, appetite and energy + recurrent pain relieved by defecation**

nodes.q: Constipation with mild pain could suggest colon polyps. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Usually silent, found at screening or by blood in the stool or iron deficiency anemia**
**Pain eased by defecation with alternating stool habit, normal blood count and no blood in the stool**

nodes.q: Her symptoms could be feigned. How do you tell factitious disorder apart?

split.note: **Deliberate falsification or induction of symptoms (for example secret laxative use) to take the sick role**; findings are inconsistent with the story
**Consistent symptoms that follow bowel habit, with no evidence of deception**

nodes.q: Her loose stools could suggest ulcerative colitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bloody diarrhea with urgency, night stools and raised inflammatory markers**; continuous rectal inflammation on colonoscopy
**Never any blood, no night symptoms and a normal inflammatory marker**

nodes.q: Her pain could follow dairy. How do you tell lactose intolerance apart?

split.note: **Bloating and watery diarrhea within hours of dairy that stop when dairy is stopped; positive hydrogen breath test**
**Pain relieved by defecation with no clear link to dairy and constipation between episodes**

root.stem: A 5-year-old boy has had 2 years of itching, yellow skin and eyes, pale greasy stools and dark urine. He bruises easily, walks with a wide-based unsteady gait and has absent ankle reflexes. The liver edge is felt 4 cm below the right costal margin. Serum alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyltransferase are markedly raised, bilirubin is high and mostly conjugated, and alanine and aspartate aminotransferases are only mildly raised. His blood count and reticulocyte count are normal. Ultrasound shows no dilated bile ducts.
root.oneliner: 5M + 2 years of itching, jaundice, pale greasy stools, dark urine + easy bruising + wide-based gait and absent ankle reflexes + hepatomegaly + high alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyltransferase, conjugated bilirubin, mildly raised aminotransferases + normal reticulocytes + no dilated ducts
highlight: 4 cm below the right costal margin

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Impaired bile formation or flow. The clincher: **itching, pale stools and dark urine with jaundice, and markedly raised alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) with mildly raised aminotransferases**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Cholestatic jaundice is used too. The terms describe the same pattern of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with raised ALP and GGT.

nodes.q: Why do ALP and GGT detect defects in bile flow?
nodes.a: They are found in the bile ductules (bile duct and canalicular membranes)
nodes.note: When bile flow is blocked, bile acids increase their production and release them into the blood. ALP also comes from bone and placenta; a raised GGT shows the ALP is from the liver. They are not on the basal surface of hepatocytes, and they are not needed for bile salt synthesis or bilirubin conjugation.

nodes.q: Why are his stools pale and his urine dark?
nodes.a: Conjugated bilirubin cannot reach the gut, so stools lack stercobilin, and it spills into the blood and urine
nodes.note: Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble so it appears in urine; unconjugated bilirubin does not.

nodes.q: Which substance builds up in the skin and causes the itching?
nodes.note: Cholestyramine binds bile acids in the gut to relieve itching.

nodes.q: Which step of fat absorption fails when bile salts are missing?
nodes.note: Bile salts emulsify fat and form micelles that carry fats and fat-soluble vitamins to the intestinal cells; without them stools are fatty.

nodes.q: Which group of vitamins is therefore deficient?
nodes.a: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K)
nodes.note: Vitamin E deficiency causes ataxia and absent reflexes (spinocerebellar and dorsal column damage), as in this boy; vitamin K deficiency causes bruising with a prolonged prothrombin time; vitamin D deficiency causes rickets; vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness.

nodes.q: Which test separates an intrahepatic cause from an obstruction outside the liver?
nodes.a: Ultrasound of the liver and bile ducts
nodes.note: Dilated ducts mean obstruction (stones, tumor); normal ducts mean an intrahepatic cause (primary biliary cholangitis, drugs, sepsis, genetic cholestasis such as Alagille syndrome). Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) or endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) follows.

nodes.q: Which drug improves bile flow in many chronic cholestatic diseases?
nodes.note: A hydrophilic bile acid that protects bile duct cells; also replace fat-soluble vitamins and, for obstruction, relieve the block.

nodes.q: Which long-term liver complication follows untreated chronic cholestasis?
nodes.note: Bile acids injure the liver and fibrosis follows. Cholesterol also builds up and can form skin xanthomas.

nodes.q: His aminotransferases are only mildly raised. How do you tell hepatocellular injury apart?

split.note: **Aminotransferases in the hundreds to thousands + only mildly raised ALP**
**Markedly raised ALP and GGT + itching + pale stools**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause jaundice.

nodes.q: His jaundice could suggest Gilbert syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia during fasting or illness, with normal ALP and no dark urine**
**Conjugated bilirubin with dark urine, raised ALP and itching**

nodes.q: His jaundice could suggest hemolysis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Unconjugated bilirubin + high reticulocyte count + low haptoglobin**; urine is not dark and ALP is normal
**Conjugated bilirubin with dark urine and raised ALP and GGT**

nodes.q: His disease started in early childhood. How do you tell biliary atresia apart?

split.note: **Newborn with persistent jaundice and acholic stools in the first weeks of life + fibrosed extrahepatic ducts**; needs a Kasai operation by about 2 months
**Jaundice and itching from age 3 + fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies + ducts that are not dilated**

root.stem: A 27-year-old woman develops severe vomiting and abdominal cramps 3 hours after eating a custard pie at a picnic. The custard sat at room temperature for 8 hours before the pie was thoroughly baked and then refrigerated. Six other guests have the same illness. She has no fever, only mild loose stools without blood, and no one ate seafood, poultry, ground beef or deli meats.
root.oneliner: 27F + severe vomiting 3 h after custard pie left 8 h at room temperature then baked + six others sick + no fever, no bloody stool + no seafood, poultry, beef or deli meat
highlight: 3 hours after eating a custard pie
sat at room temperature for 8 hours
Six other guests have the same illness
no one ate seafood, poultry, ground beef or deli meats

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Illness from a preformed toxin in food, not from an infection. The clincher: **severe vomiting 1 to 6 hours after eating food left at room temperature (custard, cream, ham, potato salad), with no fever and many people sick at once**.

nodes.q: The pie was thoroughly baked afterward. Why did that not prevent the illness?
nodes.a: The enterotoxin was already formed in the custard and is heat-stable
nodes.note: Cooking kills the bacteria but not the toxin. This is why the incubation period is so short: the toxin is eaten, not made in the gut.

nodes.q: Which source usually contaminates the food?
nodes.a: A food handler carrying Staphylococcus aureus in the nose or on the skin
nodes.note: Hands with infected cuts or boils contaminate the food, and high-sugar or high-salt foods left out let the organism grow.

nodes.q: Where does the eaten toxin act to cause vomiting?
nodes.a: On the gut wall, where it stimulates vagal nerve signals to the vomiting center in the brainstem
nodes.note: Diarrhea is minor because the bowel lining is not invaded. Staphylococcal enterotoxins are also superantigens, like toxic shock syndrome toxin: they bind major histocompatibility complex class II and the T-cell receptor outside the antigen groove.

nodes.q: Which enzyme test separates this organism from other staphylococci?
nodes.note: It is a Gram-positive coccus in clusters, catalase-positive, forms golden colonies on blood agar and ferments mannitol on high-salt mannitol salt agar.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Oral or intravenous fluids and supportive care only
nodes.note: Symptoms stop within 24 hours; antibiotics are not needed because the toxin, not live bacteria, causes the illness.

nodes.q: Fried rice can cause the same short-incubation vomiting. How do you tell Bacillus cereus apart?

split.note: **Vomiting 1 to 6 hours after reheated fried rice**; also a heat-stable preformed toxin
**Vomiting 1 to 6 hours after custard, cream, ham or potato salad left out + a food handler**

nodes.note: The trap: both are preformed toxins with the same incubation period, so the food is the clue.

nodes.q: Custard or eggs can carry Salmonella. How do you tell Salmonella enteritidis apart?

split.note: **Onset 6 to 48 hours after poultry or eggs + fever + diarrhea, sometimes bloody**
**Vomiting within hours + no fever + short illness**

nodes.q: Group illness after a picnic could be Campylobacter jejuni. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **2 to 5 days after undercooked poultry + fever + bloody diarrhea**; can lead to Guillain-Barre syndrome
**Severe vomiting 2 to 4 hours after the pie + no fever + no blood in the stool**

nodes.q: Vomiting and cramps could suggest Vibrio parahaemolyticus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Watery diarrhea 12 to 24 hours after raw or undercooked seafood**
**Vomiting within hours of an unrefrigerated custard pie + no seafood eaten**

nodes.q: Her group illness could be Escherichia coli. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bloody diarrhea 3 to 4 days after undercooked ground beef; hemolytic uremic syndrome in children**
**Vomiting within hours + no blood in the stool + no beef eaten**

nodes.q: Illness after a shared meal could be Listeria monocytogenes. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever with mild diarrhea after unpasteurized dairy or deli meats; severe in pregnancy and the newborn; grows in the refrigerator**
**Vomiting 2 to 4 hours after custard with no fever, in a healthy adult**

nodes.q: Her abdominal cramps could suggest Yersinia enterocolitica. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever and right lower quadrant pain mimicking appendicitis 4 to 7 days after undercooked pork or raw milk**
**Brief violent vomiting within hours + no fever + no right lower quadrant pain**

image_prompts.root: A pastel picnic scene with a custard pie sitting out in the sun, a clock showing hours passing, and a few guests holding their stomachs.

root.stem: A 46-year-old woman has had a temperature of 39°C (102.2°F) and malaise for 2 days. She has chronic alcohol dependence. There are several spider angiomas on the face, chest and back, and she is not jaundiced. The abdomen is protuberant and nontender with shifting dullness, there is no right upper quadrant tenderness, her pelvic examination is normal, and a firm liver edge is felt 3 cm below the right costal margin. Her albumin is low, and antinuclear and anti-smooth-muscle antibody tests were negative last year. Peritoneal aspiration yields serous fluid with 1100 leukocytes/mm3 (80% neutrophils) and 100 erythrocytes/mm3.
root.oneliner: 46F + fever 39°C + chronic alcohol use + spider angiomas + ascites, nontender abdomen + normal pelvic exam + negative autoantibodies + ascitic fluid with 1100 leukocytes (80% neutrophils)

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Infection of ascitic fluid with no surgical abdominal source, in a patient with cirrhosis. The clincher: **fever in a patient with cirrhosis and ascites, with ascitic fluid neutrophils of 250 per mm3 or more**.

nodes.q: Which ascitic fluid count makes the diagnosis?
nodes.a: A neutrophil count of at least 250 per mm3
nodes.note: Her fluid has 1100 leukocytes per mm3, 80% neutrophils, so about 880 neutrophils. A positive culture is not needed to treat.

nodes.q: Which group of organisms most often causes it?
nodes.a: Gram-negative enteric bacilli (Escherichia coli and Klebsiella)
nodes.note: Streptococcus pneumoniae and other streptococci also occur. Gut bacteria cross the wall in portal hypertension and seed the fluid.

nodes.q: Which feature of cirrhotic ascites lets bacteria grow?
nodes.a: Low ascitic fluid protein, which means low opsonic and complement activity
nodes.note: Portal hypertension, gut bacterial translocation and impaired reticuloendothelial clearance add to the risk.

nodes.q: Which test is done at once in a febrile patient with ascites?
nodes.a: Diagnostic paracentesis with cell count and culture (inoculated into blood culture bottles)
nodes.note: The serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) is 1.1 g/dL or more in portal hypertension. Blood cultures are drawn too.

nodes.q: Which treatment is started without waiting for culture?
nodes.a: An intravenous third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime or ceftriaxone) with intravenous albumin
nodes.note: Albumin lowers the risk of hepatorenal syndrome. Do not delay antibiotics.

nodes.q: Which antibiotic class is given long-term to prevent recurrence after one episode?
nodes.note: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the alternative. Recurrence is common without prophylaxis; liver transplant evaluation is considered.

nodes.q: Which kidney complication most often makes an episode fatal?
nodes.note: It develops in about a third of patients: infection worsens the splanchnic vasodilation of cirrhosis, the kidneys are underperfused and creatinine rises. Intravenous albumin lowers this risk.

nodes.q: Her abdomen is nontender. How do you tell secondary bacterial peritonitis (for example a perforation) apart?

split.note: **Polymicrobial fluid with very high neutrophils, glucose below 50 mg/dL, protein above 1 g/dL and high lactate dehydrogenase; free air; peritonitis signs**
**One organism, neutrophils at 250 per mm3 or more, nontender abdomen, no free air**

nodes.note: The trap: both have ascitic neutrophils over 250 and fever.

nodes.q: Her fever could suggest acute cholecystitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Right upper quadrant pain + positive Murphy sign + gallstones on ultrasound**; no infected ascitic fluid
**No right upper quadrant tenderness + ascitic fluid with 880 neutrophils per mm3**

nodes.q: Her alcohol history could suggest chronic pancreatitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Pain radiating to the back + fatty stools + pancreatic calcifications**; fever is not typical
**Fever with ascites and neutrophils in the fluid, with no back pain**

nodes.q: Her liver disease could be an autoimmune hepatitis flare. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **High aminotransferases + antinuclear and anti-smooth-muscle antibodies + high immunoglobulin G**; fever is uncommon
**Fever with ascitic fluid neutrophils; negative autoimmune antibodies**

nodes.q: Fever with abdominal findings in a woman could suggest pelvic inflammatory disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Lower abdominal pain + cervical motion tenderness + cervical discharge**
**Normal pelvic examination + ascites with neutrophils in the fluid**

image_prompts.root: A pastel cross-section of an abdomen with cloudy ascitic fluid around a small cirrhotic liver and a few bacteria crossing the gut wall.

root.stem: A 55-year-old man who drinks about eight beers every day has a swollen abdomen and swelling of both legs up to the hips. His eyes are yellow. He has red spider-like marks on his chest, red palms, and dilated veins radiating from the navel. The abdomen has shifting dullness and a fluid wave, and the liver edge is hard and nodular. His neck veins are flat, no pericardial knock is heard, and a chest x-ray shows bilateral pleural effusions with a normal heart size. Echocardiography shows a normal left ventricular ejection fraction. Serum albumin is low and the international normalized ratio is 1.9. Urine dipstick shows no protein, and Doppler ultrasound shows open hepatic veins. Endoscopy shows large esophageal varices, and he had 3 days of bleeding from internal hemorrhoids.
root.oneliner: 55M + about 8 beers daily + swollen abdomen with shifting dullness and fluid wave + leg swelling to the hips + jaundice + spider marks, red palms, veins radiating from the navel + hard nodular liver + flat neck veins, no pericardial knock + bilateral pleural effusions, normal ejection fraction + low albumin, international normalized ratio 1.9 + no urine protein + open hepatic veins + esophageal varices + bleeding internal hemorrhoids
highlight: drinks about eight beers every day
swelling of both legs up to the hips
dilated veins radiating from the navel
shifting dullness and a fluid wave
bilateral pleural effusions with a normal heart size

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Scarring of the liver that raises the pressure in the portal vein. The clincher: **a heavy drinker with spider angiomata, palmar erythema, a hard nodular liver, ascites and caput medusae**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The older name for alcohol-related cirrhosis.

nodes.q: What does long-term destruction of liver cells do to the structure of the liver?
nodes.a: Fibrous bands replace the lost cells and the lobule architecture collapses into regenerating nodules
nodes.note: Stellate cells lay down collagen around the sinusoids. Alcohol typically gives a small, shrunken, micronodular liver. The scarring raises the pressure in the portal vein; hepatic venous and central venous pressures stay normal.

nodes.q: At which level of the liver circulation is blood flow blocked in his disease?
nodes.note: Fibrosis in the space of Disse and around the sinusoids resists flow, so pressure backs up into the portal vein. Schistosomiasis blocks before the sinusoids (presinusoidal); Budd-Chiari syndrome and right heart failure block after them (post-hepatic).

nodes.q: Raised portal pressure also reaches the tributaries of the portal vein. Which veins draining the gastric fundus into the splenic vein can form gastric varices in him?
nodes.note: The splenic, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric, left gastric and short gastric veins all belong to the portal system. The hepatic, renal, suprarenal and inferior phrenic veins drain into the inferior vena cava and are not affected.

nodes.q: When portal pressure stays high, blood opens collateral channels to the systemic veins. Which channel produced the dilated veins around his navel?
nodes.a: Paraumbilical veins linking to the superficial epigastric veins of the abdominal wall
nodes.note: The dilated navel veins are called caput medusae. The other main collaterals are at the lower esophagus and the rectum.

nodes.q: Which portal vein branch links to the esophageal veins and formed the varices seen on endoscopy?
nodes.note: It joins the esophageal veins that drain to the azygos system.

nodes.q: Which event from these varices is the leading cause of death in him?
nodes.note: Painless vomiting of large amounts of blood with shock. Acute care: IV octreotide, endoscopic band ligation and antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone).

nodes.q: Which drug class lowers portal pressure to prevent a first bleed from large varices?
nodes.note: Beta-1 block lowers cardiac output; beta-2 block leaves alpha-1 vasoconstriction unopposed in the splanchnic vessels, so less blood reaches the portal vein. Band ligation is the alternative.

nodes.q: His bleeding hemorrhoids come from raised pressure in which vein?
nodes.note: It drains to the inferior mesenteric vein and so to the portal system, and it connects with the middle and inferior rectal veins that drain to the inferior vena cava. Veins of the internal hemorrhoidal plexus swell when pressure backs up.

nodes.q: Which procedure lowers portal pressure in a patient who keeps bleeding from varices?
nodes.note: A catheter goes through the internal jugular vein and the inferior vena cava into a hepatic vein, then a stent is placed through the liver tissue to a portal vein branch. Because portal blood now bypasses the liver, it can worsen hepatic encephalopathy.

nodes.q: The stent joins a branch of the portal vein to which other vein?
nodes.note: This makes a portocaval shunt that sends portal blood straight to the inferior vena cava, bypassing the scarred liver.

nodes.q: Which breast finding would you expect on further examination?
nodes.note: The damaged liver cannot break down estrogen, so the estrogen to androgen ratio rises; testicular atrophy and loss of body hair go with it. Spider angiomata and palmar erythema have the same cause.

nodes.q: Why does he need to cut down on dietary salt?
nodes.a: Secondary hyperaldosteronism makes the kidneys hold on to sodium and water
nodes.note: Portal hypertension and splanchnic vasodilation lower the effective circulating volume, which activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. The result is ascites and edema.

nodes.q: Which drug is added to a loop diuretic for his massive ascites?
nodes.note: An aldosterone antagonist, which targets the cause. Side effects are hyperkalemia and gynecomastia. Large-volume paracentesis is used when ascites is tense.

nodes.q: Why does he have edema to the hips and pleural effusions when his heart pumps normally?
nodes.a: Low plasma oncotic pressure from low albumin
nodes.note: The liver makes albumin, and with fewer working liver cells less is made. Fluid leaks out of the capillaries into tissues and pleural spaces.

nodes.q: Why is his international normalized ratio raised?
nodes.a: The liver makes fewer clotting factors
nodes.note: Factor VII has the shortest half-life, so the prothrombin time rises early.

nodes.q: Which tumor is the long-term cancer risk in cirrhosis?
nodes.note: Screening is liver ultrasound with serum alpha-fetoprotein every 6 months.

nodes.q: If he becomes confused and drowsy with a flapping tremor of the hands, which gut-derived toxin that his liver fails to clear is the main cause?
nodes.note: Hepatic encephalopathy. Triggers: variceal bleeding (protein load in the gut), infection, constipation, low potassium, sedatives and a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt. Lactulose traps ammonia as ammonium in the acidified colon; rifaximin kills ammonia-producing bacteria.

nodes.q: Which infection of the ascitic fluid is he at risk of?
nodes.note: Diagnosed by an ascitic fluid neutrophil count of 250/mm3 or more; treat with cefotaxime or ceftriaxone.

nodes.q: His swollen abdomen and legs could suggest congestive heart failure. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Distended neck veins + low ejection fraction + pulmonary crackles and a third heart sound**; the liver is congested and tender, not nodular
**Flat neck veins + normal ejection fraction + spider angiomata, palmar erythema and a hard nodular liver**

nodes.note: The trap: both give ascites, leg edema and pleural effusions; the neck veins and the ejection fraction settle it.

nodes.q: His ascites and leg edema could suggest constrictive pericarditis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Distended neck veins that rise on inspiration (Kussmaul sign) + pericardial knock** and a calcified pericardium; liver stigmata are absent
**Flat neck veins + no pericardial knock + stigmata of chronic liver disease**

nodes.note: Constriction causes liver congestion that looks like cirrhosis.

nodes.q: His ascites and portal hypertension could suggest Budd-Chiari syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hepatic vein thrombosis on Doppler + painful enlarged liver + sudden ascites**, often in a clotting disorder or with a liver tumor
**Open hepatic veins + shrunken hard nodular liver + years of alcohol use**

nodes.note: Both raise portal pressure, but Budd-Chiari blocks the hepatic veins after the liver.

nodes.q: His low albumin and edema could suggest nephrotic syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Heavy proteinuria (more than 3.5 g per day) + hyperlipidemia + fatty casts**; normal liver tests and no stigmata
**No protein in the urine + low albumin from poor synthesis + raised international normalized ratio + liver stigmata**

nodes.note: Both give low albumin, but only cirrhosis loses the liver's synthetic work.

root.stem: A 17-year-old boy has had abdominal pain for 2 days. It began around the navel with nausea and loss of appetite, then moved to the right lower abdomen and became severe. This morning the pain spread across the whole abdomen. His temperature is 39.0°C. The right lower quadrant is exquisitely tender, and there is guarding with rebound tenderness over the whole abdomen. The white blood cell count is 16,000/mm3. He has no diarrhea, no weight loss, no prior episodes of cramping, no recent sore throat, and no painless rectal bleeding. CT shows a swollen, blind-ending tube arising from the cecum with a calcified stone in its lumen, a break in its wall, and a collection of fluid beside it.

pain spread across the whole abdomen
guarding with rebound tenderness over the whole abdomen
no diarrhea, no weight loss, no prior episodes of cramping
a break in its wall, and a collection of fluid beside it

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Inflammation of the appendix, most often in teenagers and young adults. The clincher: **pain that starts around the navel and moves to the right lower quadrant, with fever, anorexia and rebound tenderness**.

nodes.q: Which event most often starts the inflammation?
nodes.note: A fecalith (the calcified stone on his CT) in adults, or lymphoid hyperplasia in children. Mucus builds up, pressure rises, bacteria grow and the wall becomes ischemic.

nodes.q: Why does the pain start at the navel and then move to the right lower abdomen?
nodes.a: Visceral pain from the gut (midgut, T10 level) turns into somatic pain when the inflamed appendix touches the parietal peritoneum
nodes.note: The midgut sends pain fibres to the T10 level, felt at the navel. Peritoneal irritation then gives sharp, localized pain at McBurney point.

nodes.q: Pressing on his left lower quadrant causes pain in his right lower quadrant. What is this sign called?
nodes.note: Related signs: pain on hip extension (psoas sign, retrocecal appendix) and on internal rotation of the flexed hip (obturator sign). Maximal tenderness is at McBurney point, one third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the navel.

nodes.q: Which white cell type makes up most of his raised white cell count?
nodes.note: Acute bacterial inflammation: cytokines (interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor) release neutrophils from marrow and demarginate them. Lymphocytosis fits viral illness, and eosinophilia fits allergy or parasites. A swollen appendix with tan exudate on the serosa is acute suppurative inflammation.

nodes.q: Which complication has happened by the time of the CT?
nodes.a: Perforation with peritonitis and an abscess
nodes.note: Risk is highest after 48 hours of symptoms. Pain that suddenly spreads across the abdomen with fever marks rupture.

nodes.q: Which kind of bacteria fills the peritoneal fluid after perforation?
nodes.a: Mixed aerobic and anaerobic colonic bacteria (polymicrobial infection)
nodes.note: Escherichia coli is the commonest aerobe, and anaerobes outnumber aerobes about 1000 to 1 in the colon. Not a fungus: Candida albicans is unusual without prior surgery, long antibiotic courses or immunosuppression.

nodes.q: In a foul-smelling abscess the Gram stain shows gram-negative rods, but the aerobic culture grows only enterococci. Which organism is the likely gram-negative rod?
nodes.note: A strict anaerobe: it does not grow on aerobic culture plates, so it is missed. Foul-smelling pus suggests anaerobes. Escherichia coli is the commonest aerobic gram-negative rod, but it would have grown on MacConkey agar.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis when the picture is unclear?
nodes.a: CT of the abdomen with contrast
nodes.note: Ultrasound is the first choice in children and pregnant women. Appendicitis in a typical case is a clinical diagnosis.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Appendectomy with IV antibiotics that cover gram-negative rods and anaerobes
nodes.note: A perforated case with an abscess may be drained first, with interval appendectomy later. Typical pairs are ceftriaxone plus metronidazole.

nodes.q: Which drug covers the anaerobes, and how does it kill them?
nodes.a: Metronidazole; it forms free radicals that damage bacterial DNA
nodes.note: Active only in anaerobic conditions, where the nitro group is reduced. Avoid alcohol (disulfiram-like reaction).

nodes.q: Which late problem can arise when infected material enters the portal veins?
nodes.a: Pylephlebitis (infected portal vein thrombus) with liver abscesses
nodes.note: Look for fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain days after the appendix has been removed or has ruptured.

nodes.q: His fever and right lower quadrant pain could suggest mesenteric adenitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Child after a **sore throat or viral illness**; diffuse tenderness that **shifts when the patient changes position**; no peritonitis
**Pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant + guarding and rebound + raised white cell count**

nodes.note: The trap: both give fever and right lower quadrant tenderness in a child or teen.

nodes.q: His right lower quadrant pain could suggest Crohn disease of the terminal ileum. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Weeks of diarrhea, weight loss and cramping** with earlier episodes; fistulas, aphthous ulcers; skip lesions and a thick-walled ileum on CT
**Acute onset over 2 days, no diarrhea or weight loss, migrating pain**

nodes.q: His pain and peritonitis could suggest Meckel diverticulitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Usually **under 5 years or with painless rectal bleeding** from acid-secreting gastric tissue; pain around the navel and a normal appendix at surgery
**No rectal bleeding + pain moving to McBurney point**

nodes.note: Both give right-sided pain that can look the same before surgery.

nodes.q: The same picture in an older adult could suggest diverticulitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Age over 50, **left lower quadrant pain** with constipation or a low-fiber diet; CT shows sigmoid wall thickening and fat stranding

has no blood in her stool
small amount of gas beyond them

nodes.q: Which x-ray sign shows the blockage?

nodes.q: If the ring is only partly obstructing, when might it first show?

nodes.q: What is the surgical treatment?
nodes.note: The ring is not cut out because that risks a pancreatic leak or fistula. First: nasogastric decompression and IV fluids.

nodes.q: Her double bubble and Down syndrome features could suggest duodenal atresia. How do you tell them apart?

nodes.note: The trap: both give bilious vomiting from the first days, polyhydramnios, a double bubble and a link to Down syndrome.

nodes.note: Both give vomiting after every feed and weight loss, but pyloric stenosis vomit has no bile.

nodes.q: Her vomiting with every feed could suggest esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Coughing, choking and cyanosis with the first feed**; a feeding tube coils in the upper esophagus on x-ray; gas in the stomach with a distal fistula
**No choking with feeds; bile-stained vomiting; double bubble**

nodes.q: Her weight loss in the first week could suggest biliary atresia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Conjugated jaundice after 2 weeks + pale chalky stools + dark urine**; no vomiting of bile
**Bile-stained vomit + yellow-brown stools without jaundice**

nodes.q: A congenital gut anomaly in an infant could suggest Meckel diverticulum. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Child about 2 years old with **painless rectal bleeding** from acid-secreting gastric tissue; no bile-stained vomiting

root.stem: A 58-year-old man comes for a routine visit and his stool is positive for occult blood. Colonoscopy shows a 1.4-cm pedunculated, coarsely lobulated polyp in the transverse colon. The excised polyp is covered by colonic epithelium and has branching glands lined by tall, dark-staining cells with mildly abnormal nuclei, and the stalk is not invaded. highlight: branching glands lined by tall, dark-staining cells with mildly abnormal nuclei
no dark spots on his lips or hands
no history of inflammatory bowel disease
no relatives with polyps or colon cancer

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A benign epithelial polyp with dysplasia that can turn into cancer. The clincher: **a pedunculated polyp with branching glands lined by tall hyperchromatic (dysplastic) cells and no invasion of the stalk**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Colorectal adenoma and adenomatous polyp are the same lesion.

nodes.q: Which adenoma type carries the highest risk of cancer?
nodes.note: Tubular is the commonest and least risky; tubulovillous is in between. Villous lesions are broad and sessile and can cause watery diarrhea with low potassium.

nodes.q: Besides villous architecture, which size threshold raises an adenoma's cancer risk?
nodes.note: His 1.4-cm polyp crosses it. High-grade dysplasia also raises the risk. Invasive cancer is defined by spread through the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa.

nodes.q: In the adenoma-carcinoma sequence, which gene is lost first?
nodes.note: APC loss lets beta-catenin drive growth (Wnt pathway). Next come K-ras mutation, then loss of p53.

nodes.q: Which oncogene is activated in the adenoma stage?
nodes.note: A mutated GTPase stays switched on and drives the RAF-MEK growth pathway.

nodes.q: Which anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) antibody will not work if K-ras is mutated?
nodes.note: Panitumumab fails the same way. The pathway is switched on below the receptor, so blocking the receptor does nothing.

nodes.q: After the polyp is removed, how is he followed up?
nodes.a: Surveillance colonoscopy at an interval set by the number, size and histology of polyps
nodes.note: Average-risk screening starts at age 45; fecal immunochemical testing is one noninvasive option.

nodes.q: Which cancer can this polyp become if left in place?
nodes.note: Most colorectal cancers arise from adenomas over about 10 years, which is why removing them prevents cancer.

nodes.q: In an older man, which blood count finding should prompt colonoscopy to look for this cancer, especially on the right side?
nodes.note: Right-sided cancers bleed slowly and silently; left-sided cancers cause obstruction and a change in bowel habit.

nodes.q: Which bacterium causing endocarditis should prompt a colonoscopy for this cancer?

split.note: Small, **rectosigmoid**, sessile; **serrated (sawtooth) glands without dysplasia**; almost no cancer risk
**Pedunculated, branching glands with tall hyperchromatic dysplastic cells**; may be anywhere in the colon

nodes.note: The trap: both are common colon polyps in older adults.

nodes.q: An adenoma in a man in his fifties could suggest familial adenomatous polyposis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hundreds to thousands of adenomas + germline mutation of the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene (autosomal dominant)**; family history; cancer by about age 40 without colectomy

nodes.q: His pedunculated polyp could suggest a juvenile polyp. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Child aged 2 to 5 years with **painless rectal bleeding**; **cystic mucus-filled glands in inflamed stroma**; a hamartoma
Adult; **dysplastic branching glands**

nodes.q: His polyp could suggest a Peutz-Jeghers polyp. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Dark spots on lips and hands + family history**; arborizing smooth muscle core; hamartoma, mainly small bowel
**No pigmentation, single polyp, dysplastic glands without a muscle core**

nodes.q: His polyp could suggest an inflammatory pseudopolyp. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Long-standing ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease**; islands of regenerating mucosa between ulcers; no dysplasia
**No bowel disease; dysplastic epithelium**

root.stem: A 42-year-old woman has had 6 hours of sudden severe upper abdominal pain that goes through to her back, with nausea and repeated vomiting. She has known gallstones and is slightly obese. The pain eases a little when she leans forward. Her pulse is 115/min and her temperature is 37.5°C. There is no jaundice or yellow eyes, and her pregnancy test is negative. The abdomen is tender in the epigastrium without a pulsatile mass, and both flanks are bluish. Serum lipase is five times the upper limit of normal. eases a little when she leans forward
lipase is five times the upper limit of normal
fluid around the pancreas and no free air

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Acute inflammation of the pancreas from autodigestion. The clincher: **sudden epigastric pain boring through to the back, eased by leaning forward, in a woman with gallstones, with fluid around the pancreas on CT**.

nodes.q: Gallstones are the likely trigger. Which structure do they block?
nodes.note: The common channel of the bile duct and main pancreatic duct. Blockage lets pancreatic juice back up into the gland. Alcohol is the other leading cause; the mnemonic I GET SMASHED also lists hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia, drugs and scorpion sting.

nodes.q: Which enzyme change starts the autodigestion?
nodes.a: Trypsinogen is activated to trypsin inside the gland
nodes.note: Active trypsin turns on the other enzymes (lipase, elastase, phospholipase), which digest the pancreas and the fat around it.

nodes.q: Which type of necrosis do the released enzymes cause in the fat around the pancreas?
nodes.note: Lipase splits fat into fatty acids that bind calcium and form chalky white deposits (saponification). Severe disease adds hemorrhagic necrosis of the gland.

nodes.q: Which sign describes the bluish discoloration of the flanks?
nodes.note: Blood from retroperitoneal hemorrhage tracks into the flank. The periumbilical version is the Cullen sign. Both mark severe necrotizing disease.

nodes.q: Which blood test is the most specific for confirming it?
nodes.a: Serum lipase (more than 3 times the upper limit of normal)
nodes.note: Amylase also rises but is less specific and normalizes sooner.

nodes.q: What is the initial treatment?
nodes.a: Early goal-directed IV fluids (lactated Ringer), pain control and early oral feeding
nodes.note: Fluids prevent hypovolemia and necrosis; overly aggressive fluids cause overload. Gallstone pancreatitis needs cholecystectomy in the same admission; ERCP (endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography) is added for cholangitis or persistent duct blockage.

nodes.q: Why can her blood calcium fall?
nodes.a: Calcium is used up in the calcium soaps formed in the areas of fat necrosis
nodes.note: Hypocalcemia is a poor prognostic sign.

nodes.q: Which lung complication can follow severe pancreatitis?
nodes.note: Inflammatory mediators and phospholipase injure the alveolar capillaries and surfactant. Shock and kidney failure are the other causes of early death.

nodes.q: Four weeks later she develops a walled-off fluid collection. What is it called?
nodes.note: It has no epithelial lining, only granulation tissue and fibrosis. Persistent pain and early satiety suggest it.

nodes.q: Her gallstones and fast pulse could suggest acute cholangitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Charcot triad: fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain** with raised alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin; Reynolds pentad adds shock and confusion
**Epigastric pain to the back + lipase more than 3 times normal + no jaundice**

nodes.note: The trap: both follow gallstones and both can cause a fast pulse and upper abdominal pain.

nodes.q: Her back pain and bluish flanks could suggest a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Older man with hypertension and smoking, **pulsatile abdominal mass + hypotension**; CT shows retroperitoneal blood around the aorta
**Peripancreatic fluid, high lipase and gallstones, no pulsatile mass**

nodes.note: Both can cause back pain and Grey Turner sign.

nodes.q: Her sudden abdominal pain and bluish flanks could suggest a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Positive pregnancy test + missed period + pelvic pain and vaginal bleeding**; free fluid in the pelvis
**Negative pregnancy test + epigastric pain to the back + lipase 5 times normal**

nodes.q: Her gallstones and upper abdominal pain could suggest acute cholecystitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Right upper quadrant pain + Murphy sign** after a fatty meal; gallbladder wall thickening on ultrasound; lipase normal
**Epigastric pain to the back, relieved leaning forward + lipase 5 times normal**

nodes.q: Her sudden severe epigastric pain could suggest a perforated peptic ulcer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sudden board-like rigid abdomen + free air under the diaphragm** on an upright chest film; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug or ulcer history
**No free air + peripancreatic fluid + high lipase**

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A rare multisystem infection with malabsorption. The clincher: **foamy macrophages in the small bowel lamina propria that are PAS-positive and diastase-resistant, with rod-shaped bacilli**, in a middle-aged man with diarrhea, weight loss and arthritis.

nodes.q: Which organism causes it?

nodes.q: Why does he have greasy diarrhea and weight loss?

nodes.q: His joint aches began years ago. When does the arthritis typically appear relative to the bowel symptoms?

nodes.q: His double vision shows the infection has spread to which organ system?

nodes.q: His diarrhea, weight loss and arthritis could suggest Crohn disease. How do you tell them apart?

nodes.q: His fatty diarrhea could suggest celiac disease. How do you tell them apart?

nodes.q: His fat malabsorption could suggest intestinal lymphangiectasia. How do you tell them apart?

**Macrophages with rod-shaped bacilli + arthritis + eye findings**

nodes.q: His malabsorption in middle age could suggest amyloidosis of the bowel. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Congo red staining with apple-green birefringence**; deposits in the wall, with an underlying chronic disease or plasma cell disorder
**PAS-positive macrophages with bacilli**; Congo red negative

nodes.q: His chronic diarrhea could suggest hypogammaglobulinemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Recurrent sinopulmonary infections + absent plasma cells + Giardia**
**No recurrent infections + PAS-positive macrophages**

nodes.q: Which growth requirement lets the organism live in seawater and shellfish?

root.stem: A 54-year-old woman with chronic hepatitis C has had 6 months of vague upper abdominal discomfort, nausea and a 5-kg weight loss. She bruises easily on her forearms after minor bumps. Prothrombin time is prolonged at 19 seconds (international normalized ratio 1.8), the platelet count is normal, and the activated partial thromboplastin time is only mildly raised. Factor V activity is low and prothrombin time stays prolonged after vitamin K injection for 3 days. She has no diet problem or antibiotic use, and D-dimer and fibrinogen levels are normal.
root.oneliner: 54F + chronic hepatitis C + 6 months of upper abdominal discomfort, nausea + 5-kg weight loss + easy bruising + prothrombin time 19 seconds, international normalized ratio 1.8 + normal platelets + mildly raised activated partial thromboplastin time + low factor V + no correction with vitamin K + no poor diet or antibiotics + normal D-dimer and fibrinogen
highlight: stays prolonged after vitamin K injection
no diet problem or antibiotic use
D-dimer and fibrinogen levels are normal

nodes.q: What is causing her easy bruising?
nodes.note: Bleeding tendency from failing synthesis of clotting factors. The clincher: **prolonged prothrombin time with low factor V that does not correct with vitamin K**.

nodes.q: Damage to which cells causes the raised prothrombin time?
nodes.note: They make most clotting factors (II, V, VII, IX, X, XI) and fibrinogen, so synthesis falls. Factor VIII is also made by endothelial cells and stays normal or high.

nodes.q: Which clotting factor has the shortest half-life, so the prothrombin time rises first?
nodes.note: About 6 hours. It belongs to the extrinsic pathway, which the prothrombin time measures; the activated partial thromboplastin time rises later.

nodes.q: Why does factor V help separate this from vitamin K deficiency?
nodes.a: Factor V is made in the liver but does not need vitamin K
nodes.note: In liver disease factor V falls; in vitamin K deficiency it stays normal.

nodes.q: If her hepatitis progresses to cirrhosis with an enlarged spleen, which blood count falls and adds to the bleeding?
nodes.note: Portal hypertension enlarges the spleen, which sequesters platelets, and the liver makes less thrombopoietin. Her count is normal, so this is not yet present.

nodes.q: Despite a raised prothrombin time, why are these patients still at risk of clots such as portal vein thrombosis?
nodes.a: The liver also makes less of the natural anticoagulants protein C, protein S and antithrombin
nodes.note: Hemostasis is rebalanced, not simply weakened, so a high international normalized ratio does not protect against thrombosis.

nodes.q: How is bleeding or a planned procedure managed?
nodes.a: Fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate, with a vitamin K trial
nodes.note: Reserve for active bleeding or high-risk procedures, not to correct numbers. Vitamin K is given to exclude deficiency.

nodes.q: Her raised prothrombin time and bruising could suggest vitamin K deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Poor diet, malabsorption or long antibiotic use**; prolonged prothrombin time that **corrects with vitamin K**; factor V normal
**Chronic hepatitis, low factor V and no correction with vitamin K**

nodes.note: The trap: both prolong the prothrombin time and cause bruising.

nodes.q: Her bruising with a prolonged prothrombin time could suggest disseminated intravascular coagulation. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low platelets + low fibrinogen + high D-dimer** after sepsis, obstetric or cancer trigger; factor VIII low
**Normal platelets, fibrinogen and D-dimer in a stable patient + factor VIII normal or high**
