root.stem: A 51-year-old man has had 6 months of constant upper abdominal pain that goes through to his back and is not relieved by antacids. He has lost 11 kg and passes three or four large, pale, foul-smelling stools a day with oil droplets in the toilet. He has drunk a bottle of wine daily for 15 years. His fasting glucose is 148 mg/dL, his vitamin D level is low and he has diffuse bone aches. A stool test shows a very low fecal elastase. An abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan shows a shrunken pancreas with scattered calcifications and no mass. He has no jaundice or fever and his stools contain no blood. He has never had repeated chest infections, and nobody in his family has gluten sensitivity.
root.oneliner: 51M + 6 months of constant upper abdominal pain through to the back, not relieved by antacids + 11 kg weight loss + large pale foul stools with oil droplets + wine daily for 15 years + fasting glucose 148 + low vitamin D with bone aches + very low fecal elastase + CT: shrunken pancreas with calcifications, no mass + no jaundice, fever or bloody stool + no chest infections, no gluten sensitivity in family
highlight: constant upper abdominal pain that goes through to his back
a bottle of wine daily for 15 years
shrunken pancreas with scattered calcifications and no mass
nobody in his family has gluten sensitivity

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Long-lasting inflammation that replaces pancreatic tissue with scar. The clincher: **pancreatic calcifications on imaging in a heavy drinker with fatty stools, weight loss and pain through to the back**.

nodes.q: Which imaging finding is most specific for it?
nodes.note: They show as flecks in the mid-upper abdomen on x-ray or CT. The gland is often shrunken, with a dilated duct.

nodes.q: Which exposure is the most common cause in adults?
nodes.note: Other causes: cystic fibrosis and other gene mutations, pancreas divisum, high triglycerides, autoimmune disease. Gallstones are a leading cause of acute pancreatitis, not of the chronic form.

nodes.q: What happens to the gland over the years?
nodes.a: Repeated inflammation destroys the acinar cells and replaces them with fibrosis
nodes.note: Protein plugs and calcium block the small ducts. Pain comes first; fatty stools appear only after about 90% of the enzyme-making tissue is lost.

nodes.q: Why does the pain go through to his back?
nodes.a: The pancreas lies in the retroperitoneum, against the spine
nodes.note: Pain from the gland is felt in the upper abdomen and back; it is often constant and may be worse after meals.

nodes.q: Which mechanism causes his large, pale, foul-smelling stools?
nodes.a: Fat maldigestion from loss of pancreatic lipase, a generalized malabsorption
nodes.note: Undigested fat stays in the stool as oil droplets. It is not a motility problem or an osmotic diarrhea, and portal hypertension plays no part.

nodes.q: Which pancreatic protein lets lipase work on fat droplets coated with bile salts?
nodes.note: Colipase binds the droplet and anchors lipase to it. Without it, triglycerides cannot be split into monoglycerides and fatty acids.

nodes.q: Why does the lipase that remains work poorly in his duodenum?
nodes.a: The duodenal pH is low because pancreatic bicarbonate is lost
nodes.note: Duct cells normally secrete bicarbonate that neutralizes gastric acid. In an acid duodenum lipase is inactivated and bile acids precipitate, so fat digestion fails even further.

nodes.q: Which stool test is the simple screen for pancreatic exocrine failure?
nodes.note: Elastase passes through the gut intact, so a low level shows lost enzyme output. The 72-hour fecal fat collection is the older quantitative test.

nodes.q: Which vitamins are poorly absorbed when fat is not absorbed?
nodes.a: The fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K
nodes.note: They travel inside fat micelles. Low vitamin K can prolong the prothrombin time.

nodes.q: Which bone change follows poor vitamin D absorption?
nodes.a: Impaired mineralization of the bone matrix (osteomalacia)
nodes.note: Low vitamin D means less calcium and phosphate absorption, so new osteoid does not mineralize; bones ache and soften.

nodes.q: Which complication explains his raised blood glucose?
nodes.a: Diabetes from loss of islet cells (pancreatogenic, or type 3c, diabetes)
nodes.note: Both insulin and glucagon are lost, so blood glucose swings widely and hypoglycemia is common.

nodes.q: Which walled-off fluid collection with no epithelial lining can form after flares?
nodes.note: A collection of enzyme-rich fluid walled off by granulation tissue and fibrosis, with no true epithelial lining.

nodes.q: Which vein next to the inflamed pancreas can clot and cause isolated gastric varices?
nodes.note: Splenic vein thrombosis gives left-sided (sinistral) portal hypertension: gastric varices in the fundus with a normal liver.

nodes.q: Which cancer becomes more likely after years of inflammation?
nodes.note: Chronic pancreatitis raises the risk; new weight loss or jaundice in a known case should prompt imaging.

nodes.q: Which drug replaces the missing digestive enzymes?
nodes.note: Pancrelipase is a mix of lipase, protease and amylase, taken with each meal. A proton pump inhibitor is often added so that stomach acid does not destroy the enzymes.

nodes.q: Which supplements does he also need?
nodes.a: The fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K
nodes.note: Given alongside the enzymes; check vitamin D and bone density.

nodes.q: Which change in his habits slows the disease?
nodes.note: Also needed: pain control, starting with simple analgesics, and small low-fat meals.

nodes.q: His fatty stools could suggest celiac disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies + villous atrophy on duodenal biopsy**; improves off gluten; normal pancreas and normal fecal elastase
**Pancreatic calcifications + very low fecal elastase + heavy alcohol use**; stools do not improve off gluten

nodes.note: The trap: both cause fatty stools, weight loss and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.

nodes.q: His weight loss and back pain could suggest pancreatic cancer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **A mass in the pancreatic head on CT, often with painless jaundice**, raised cancer antigen 19-9, and no diffuse calcification
**Diffuse calcifications and a shrunken gland with no mass or jaundice**

nodes.note: Both give weight loss and pain through to the back; the two can coexist.

nodes.q: His diarrhea and weight loss could suggest Crohn disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Skip lesions of the terminal ileum + oral ulcers, fistulas**; stool may contain blood and mucus; fecal elastase is normal
**Calcified, shrunken pancreas + low fecal elastase**; no blood in the stool

nodes.q: His upper abdominal pain could suggest peptic ulcer disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Burning epigastric pain linked to meals and relieved by antacids or acid suppression**; Helicobacter pylori; no fatty stools
**Constant pain through to the back, not relieved by antacids, with fatty stools**

nodes.q: His pancreatic findings could suggest a pancreatic islet cell tumor. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **A discrete mass on CT with hormone excess** (gastrin: ulcers and diarrhea; vasoactive intestinal peptide: watery diarrhea); the gland is not diffusely calcified
**Diffuse calcification and atrophy with no mass; the stool is fatty, not watery**

nodes.q: His enzyme loss could suggest cystic fibrosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Begins in childhood with repeated chest infections + high sweat chloride + mutation of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene**; pancreatic insufficiency from thick secretions
**Adult with 15 years of heavy alcohol use and no lung disease**

nodes.note: Cystic fibrosis is also a cause of chronic pancreatitis, so a young patient with it needs a sweat test.

nodes.q: His fatty diarrhea could suggest small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bloating and gas, positive hydrogen breath test, improves with rifaximin**; fecal elastase is normal; low B12 with high folate
**Calcified pancreas + very low fecal elastase; improves with pancrelipase**

root.stem: A 3-year-old girl has had 5 months of a swollen belly and large, pale, foul-smelling stools that began a few weeks after wheat cereal was added to her diet. She is at the 3rd percentile for weight and height. Stool testing shows excess fat, and her serum anti-tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies are raised. Her symptoms improve when bread and pasta are removed. She has no repeated chest infections and a normal sweat chloride test, her stool is not acidic, no parasites are seen in her stool, and her blood eosinophil count is normal. She has no joint pain. Her aunt has gluten sensitivity.
root.oneliner: 3F + swollen belly + large pale foul stools after wheat cereal started + 3rd percentile weight and height + excess stool fat + raised anti-tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies + better off bread and pasta + no chest infections, normal sweat chloride + non-acidic stool + no parasites + normal eosinophils + no joint pain + aunt with gluten sensitivity
highlight: a few weeks after wheat cereal was added
anti-tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies are raised
improve when bread and pasta are removed
no parasites are seen in her stool

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An immune reaction to gluten that flattens the lining of the small intestine. The clincher: **malabsorption that starts after wheat is introduced, with anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies and improvement on a gluten-free diet**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.a: Celiac sprue (also called gluten-sensitive enteropathy or nontropical sprue)
nodes.note: All of these describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which dietary protein triggers the reaction?
nodes.a: Gliadin, the part of gluten found in wheat, barley and rye
nodes.note: Rice and corn are safe; oats are safe only if not contaminated with wheat.

nodes.q: Which human leukocyte antigen (HLA) types carry the risk?
nodes.note: Tissue transglutaminase deamidates gliadin so it binds HLA-DQ2/DQ8 tightly, and CD4 T cells attack the lining (a type IV hypersensitivity reaction). Nearly all patients carry one of these types, but so do many healthy people: a negative result rules the disease out and a positive one proves nothing.

nodes.q: Which cells fail to absorb nutrients in this disease?
nodes.a: Enterocytes, the absorptive cells covering the villi
nodes.note: The villi flatten and the microvilli are lost, so brush-border enzymes and absorptive surface disappear.

nodes.q: Which part of the small bowel is hit hardest?
nodes.note: Gluten contact is highest here, and iron, folate and calcium are absorbed here. The ileum is usually spared, so vitamin B12 absorption is often normal.

nodes.q: Which absorption test is low here because the mucosa is damaged, but normal when the problem is only pancreatic enzyme loss?
nodes.note: D-xylose needs no digestion, only an intact mucosa. Low urine and blood D-xylose points to mucosal disease (celiac, giardiasis); a normal result with fatty stools points to the pancreas.

nodes.q: Which biopsy finding underlies the disease?
nodes.a: Villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia and more intraepithelial lymphocytes
nodes.note: The mucosa looks flat. The biopsy must be taken while the patient is still eating gluten.

nodes.q: Which blood test is the best first screen?
nodes.a: Immunoglobulin A (IgA) anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody, with a total IgA level
nodes.note: Anti-endomysial antibodies are very specific. Selective IgA deficiency can give a false-negative result, which is why total IgA is checked; if IgA is low, IgG-based tests are used.

nodes.q: Which antibody deficiency is more common in celiac patients and can make the screening test falsely negative?
nodes.note: Other associations: type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease and Down syndrome.

nodes.q: Which nutrients are lost when the proximal bowel is damaged?
nodes.a: Iron, folate, calcium and the fat-soluble vitamins
nodes.note: In adults, iron deficiency anemia that does not respond to iron pills and low bone density are often the presenting findings.

nodes.q: Which itchy blistering skin disease is linked?
nodes.note: Grouped vesicles on the elbows, knees and buttocks, with IgA deposits at the tips of the dermal papillae. It responds to dapsone and to a gluten-free diet.

nodes.q: Which cancer becomes more likely after years of untreated disease?
nodes.note: Small-bowel adenocarcinoma is also increased.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.note: Remove wheat, barley and rye. Symptoms and antibody levels fall within weeks to months; persistent symptoms usually mean hidden gluten intake.

nodes.q: Her fatty stools and poor growth could suggest cystic fibrosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Repeated chest infections + high sweat chloride**; stool fat improves with pancreatic enzymes, not with diet changes
**Normal sweat chloride + anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies + villous atrophy**; improves off gluten

nodes.note: The trap: both cause pale fatty stools and failure to thrive in a young child.

nodes.q: Her bloating and loose stools could suggest lactose intolerance. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Gas and watery acidic stool after milk, with normal villi** and no excess fat or weight loss
**Fatty stool that is not acidic + antibodies + flattened villi**; celiac damage can cause a secondary lactase deficiency too

nodes.q: Her foul stools could suggest giardiasis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Contaminated water or day-care exposure + pear-shaped trophozoites or cysts in stool**; responds to metronidazole
**No parasites in stool + raised antibodies + improvement off gluten**

nodes.q: Her weight loss and fatty stools could suggest Whipple disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Middle-aged man with arthritis and weight loss; periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positive foamy macrophages in the lamina propria** (Tropheryma whipplei)
**Young child with antibodies, flattened villi and no joint pain**

nodes.q: Her small-bowel symptoms could suggest eosinophilic gastroenteritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Eosinophils infiltrating the bowel wall**, often with blood eosinophilia and allergic disease; antibodies are negative
**Normal blood eosinophil count; antibodies raised; lymphocytes rather than eosinophils on biopsy**

root.stem: A 56-year-old overweight man has had 12 years of heartburn that is worse at night, with regurgitation of sour fluid. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes a day for 30 years. For 3 months he has had trouble swallowing solid food. He is not immunocompromised, has no history of asthma or eczema, and swallows liquids normally. Endoscopy shows salmon-pink tongues of mucosa extending up from the stomach into the lower esophagus. A biopsy of the lower esophagus shows columnar epithelium with goblet cells, with no tumor cells.
root.oneliner: 56M + overweight + 12 years of nocturnal heartburn and regurgitation + 30 pack-years of smoking + 3 months of trouble swallowing solids + normal with liquids + no immunocompromise, asthma or eczema + endoscopy: salmon-pink tongues of mucosa in the lower esophagus + biopsy: columnar epithelium with goblet cells, no tumor
highlight: 12 years of heartburn that is worse at night
two packs of cigarettes a day for 30 years
no history of asthma or eczema

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Replacement of the normal lining of the lower esophagus by intestinal-type columnar cells after long-term acid reflux. The clincher: **goblet cells on biopsy of the lower esophagus in a patient with long-standing heartburn**.

nodes.q: Which long-standing condition drives the change?
nodes.note: Acid and bile damage the squamous lining, and it is repaired with a more acid-resistant lining. Risk factors: age over 50, male sex, white race, obesity, smoking.

nodes.q: What kind of tissue change is it?
nodes.a: Metaplasia: squamous epithelium replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium
nodes.note: The change is reversible in principle and is not yet cancer. Goblet cells are the marker of intestinal differentiation.

nodes.q: Which structure normally keeps stomach acid out of the esophagus?
nodes.note: Reflux follows transient sphincter relaxations, low sphincter tone (smoking, obesity, fatty meals) and hiatal hernia.

nodes.q: Which cancer is the main risk?
nodes.note: It arises in the lower third of the esophagus near the gastroesophageal junction, whereas squamous cell carcinoma is usually in the middle third. It is now the commonest esophageal cancer in the US.

nodes.q: Which sequence of changes leads to it?
nodes.a: Metaplasia, then low-grade dysplasia, then high-grade dysplasia, then invasive cancer
nodes.note: The cancer risk in nondysplastic Barrett is small (about 0.3% a year) and rises with dysplasia.

nodes.q: His biopsy shows no tumor. Which benign narrowing from long-term acid injury best explains his trouble swallowing solids?
nodes.note: Scarring of the lower esophagus gives slowly progressive dysphagia to solids. Dysphagia with weight loss that spreads to liquids should raise concern for cancer.

nodes.q: Which test finds the disease and monitors it?
nodes.note: Surveillance endoscopy every 3 to 5 years if there is no dysplasia; sooner if dysplasia is found. Screening is considered in men with chronic reflux and other risk factors.

nodes.q: Which drug class controls the underlying reflux?
nodes.note: They irreversibly block the H+/K+ ATPase of gastric parietal cells and are used long-term.

nodes.q: How is high-grade dysplasia treated?
nodes.a: Endoscopic eradication (for example radiofrequency ablation) with endoscopic resection of visible lesions
nodes.note: Esophagectomy is kept for invasive cancer not suitable for endoscopic therapy.

nodes.q: His smoking and trouble swallowing could suggest esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Upper or middle esophagus; **heavy alcohol and tobacco use**; squamous cells with keratin pearls on biopsy; no metaplasia
Lower esophagus; **long reflux history + goblet cells**; leads to adenocarcinoma

nodes.note: The trap: smoking and dysphagia point to cancer, but the cell type and site follow the underlying cause.

nodes.q: His heartburn could suggest simple reflux esophagitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Squamous mucosa with basal zone hyperplasia, elongated papillae and scattered eosinophils and neutrophils**; no goblet cells
**Intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells**

nodes.q: His trouble swallowing could suggest eosinophilic esophagitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Young atopic patient (asthma, eczema); **rings and furrows with more than 15 eosinophils per high-power field**
Older man with long reflux and **goblet cells**; no allergic history

nodes.q: His trouble swallowing could suggest esophageal candidiasis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Immunocompromised patient with painful swallowing and white plaques**; yeast and pseudohyphae on biopsy
**Not immunocompromised; salmon-pink mucosa with goblet cells**

nodes.q: His trouble swallowing could suggest achalasia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Difficulty with solids and liquids from the start; bird-beak narrowing on barium swallow**; loss of myenteric neurons
**Reflux history, solids only, salmon-pink mucosa with goblet cells**

root.stem: A 3-year-old girl has had 2 days of fever to 39.4°C, crampy abdominal pain and frequent small stools with blood and mucus. She cries and strains after each stool. Several children at her day-care center have had the same illness. She has taken no antibiotics recently, has not eaten undercooked beef, poultry or eggs, and has no pet reptile. A stool smear stained with methylene blue shows many neutrophils. Stool culture on MacConkey agar grows colorless colonies of a nonmotile gram-negative rod that makes no hydrogen sulfide.
root.oneliner: 3F + fever to 39.4°C + crampy pain + frequent small bloody mucoid stools + straining after each stool + day-care outbreak + no recent antibiotics, undercooked meat or eggs, no reptile + many fecal neutrophils + colorless colonies on MacConkey agar, nonmotile gram-negative rod, no hydrogen sulfide

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An invasive bacterial infection of the colon. The clincher: **fever with small bloody mucoid stools and straining (tenesmus) in a day-care outbreak, with fecal neutrophils**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Dysentery means bloody diarrhea with fever and cramps.

nodes.q: Why does it pass so easily from child to child?
nodes.a: A very low infectious dose (10 to 100 organisms)
nodes.note: It resists stomach acid, so a few organisms on hands are enough. Spread is fecal-oral: person to person, food, water and flies.

nodes.q: Which species causes most infections in US day-care outbreaks?
nodes.note: Usually the mildest species.

nodes.q: Which species is the commonest cause in low-income countries?
nodes.note: Shigella dysenteriae type 1 is the most severe and makes Shiga toxin.

nodes.q: Which sugar does it fail to ferment, so its colonies are colorless on MacConkey agar?
nodes.note: Shigella is a lactose-nonfermenting, nonmotile gram-negative rod that makes no hydrogen sulfide. Salmonella also ferments no lactose but is motile and makes hydrogen sulfide; this separates the two.

nodes.q: How does it cause bloody stool?
nodes.a: It invades the colonic epithelium through M cells and spreads from cell to cell by actin polymerization
nodes.note: Mucosal destruction brings neutrophils and blood into the stool. Shiga toxin cleaves an adenine from the 28S ribosomal RNA of the 60S subunit and halts protein synthesis in epithelial cells.

nodes.q: Which kidney and blood complication follows Shiga toxin?
nodes.note: Anemia with schistocytes, low platelets and acute kidney injury. It is mostly linked to Shiga toxin from the dysentery species and enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli.

nodes.q: Which joint complication can follow weeks later?
nodes.note: Arthritis, urethritis and conjunctivitis, associated with human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B27.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Oral or intravenous rehydration; an antibiotic (azithromycin, or a fluoroquinolone in adults) for moderate to severe disease
nodes.note: Antibiotics shorten illness and shedding. Avoid antimotility drugs, which can prolong the illness.

nodes.q: Her bloody diarrhea could suggest Clostridioides difficile colitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Recent antibiotic or hospital exposure**; watery diarrhea; toxins A and B in stool; pseudomembranes on colonoscopy
**No antibiotic use; day-care outbreak; invasive bloody stool with fever**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause colitis with neutrophils in the stool.

nodes.q: Her bloody stool could suggest enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli infection. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Undercooked beef; little or no fever; no fecal neutrophils**; does not ferment sorbitol on culture
**Fever + many fecal neutrophils + colorless colonies that make no hydrogen sulfide + day-care outbreak**

nodes.q: Her fever and bloody stool could suggest nontyphoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Poultry, eggs or reptile exposure**; motile rod that makes hydrogen sulfide
**Person-to-person spread in day-care; nonmotile rod with no hydrogen sulfide**

nodes.q: Her cramps and diarrhea could suggest Clostridium perfringens food poisoning. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Watery diarrhea 8 to 16 hours after reheated meat or gravy**; no fever or blood; resolves within a day; no person-to-person spread
**Fever, blood and mucus for days, with spread among day-care children**

nodes.q: Her fever and bloody stool could suggest Campylobacter jejuni enteritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Undercooked poultry or unpasteurized milk; comma- or S-shaped rod that grows at 42°C**; later Guillain-Barré syndrome
**No poultry exposure; day-care spread; straight nonmotile rod**

image_prompts.root: Pastel teaching picture of a toddler with abdominal cramps in a day-care room next to an inflamed colon with small bleeding ulcers, no text

root.stem: A 52-year-old man of northern European descent has had 8 months of tiredness, aching hands and knees, and loss of sexual desire. His skin has turned bronze-gray, and he was recently found to have diabetes. He is short of breath on exertion, and his older brother died of cirrhosis at 49. He drinks little alcohol, has never been transfused, and hepatitis B and C tests are negative. Examination shows an enlarged liver, swelling of the second and third knuckles of both hands, small testes, and an enlarged heart with crackles at both lung bases. Serum transferrin saturation is 82% and ferritin is 2,400 ng/mL. Ceruloplasmin is normal and there are no Kayser-Fleischer rings. A liver biopsy shows iron in the hepatocytes and cirrhosis.
root.oneliner: 52M + northern European + fatigue, aching hands and knees, low libido + bronze-gray skin + new diabetes + exertional dyspnea + brother died of cirrhosis + little alcohol, never transfused, negative hepatitis B and C tests + hepatomegaly, swollen 2nd and 3rd knuckles, small testes, big heart, basal crackles + transferrin saturation 82%, ferritin 2,400 + normal ceruloplasmin, no Kayser-Fleischer rings + iron in hepatocytes, cirrhosis
highlight: hepatitis B and C tests are negative
swelling of the second and third knuckles
iron in the hepatocytes and cirrhosis

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A genetic disease of too much iron absorption with iron deposits in organs. The clincher: **transferrin saturation above 45% with very high ferritin, bronze skin, diabetes, cirrhosis and heart disease**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The classic trio is cirrhosis, diabetes and bronze skin.

nodes.q: Which gene is mutated?
nodes.note: Autosomal recessive. The gene lies on chromosome 6 near the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) genes. Hepcidin is too low, so the gut absorbs too much iron and ferroportin releases iron freely.

nodes.q: What happens to body iron over the years?
nodes.a: Iron is absorbed in excess and cannot be excreted, so it builds up in parenchymal cells
nodes.note: Iron is toxic because it generates free radicals. Symptoms usually appear after age 40 in men; women are protected until menopause by menstrual blood loss.

nodes.q: Why is his skin bronze-gray?
nodes.a: Hemosiderin and extra melanin in the skin
nodes.note: The extra iron pigment sits in the dermis.

nodes.q: Why does he have diabetes?
nodes.a: Iron destroys the pancreatic islet cells
nodes.note: Combined with liver disease, this causes insulin deficiency.

nodes.q: Why has his sexual desire fallen and his testes shrunk?
nodes.a: Iron damages the pituitary, causing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism
nodes.note: Low luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone.

nodes.q: Which joint disease explains his swollen second and third knuckles?
nodes.a: Calcium pyrophosphate arthropathy of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints
nodes.note: Hook-like osteophytes on radiographs.

nodes.q: His heart is enlarged with a weak ventricle. Which type of cardiomyopathy is this?
nodes.note: Iron in the myocytes weakens the ventricle (it can also behave as a restrictive cardiomyopathy early), and arrhythmias are common. Heart failure is a main cause of death if untreated, and it can improve with iron removal.

nodes.q: Which cancer is he at greatest risk of?
nodes.note: Once cirrhosis is present, the risk is many times higher (often quoted as up to 200-fold) and persists even after iron is removed, so he needs ultrasound surveillance.

nodes.q: Which two tests should be done first in him and his relatives?
nodes.note: Then confirm with HFE gene testing; liver biopsy with Prussian blue stain shows iron, and magnetic resonance imaging can estimate liver iron. First-degree relatives should be screened.

nodes.q: What is the first-line treatment?
nodes.note: Remove blood until ferritin falls to about 50 ng/mL. It prevents progression but cannot reverse cirrhosis or hypogonadism.

nodes.q: Which drug removes iron if phlebotomy cannot be used?
nodes.a: An iron chelator such as deferoxamine or deferasirox
nodes.note: Deferoxamine is given parenterally; deferasirox is oral.

nodes.q: Which marine bacterium is a special danger to him?
nodes.note: Iron overload and liver disease predispose to severe infection after eating raw shellfish or wound exposure to seawater. Iron-loving Yersinia enterocolitica and Listeria are also more dangerous.

nodes.q: His cirrhosis and abnormal liver tests could suggest Wilson disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Teens to young adults; **low serum ceruloplasmin, Kayser-Fleischer rings, psychiatric or movement symptoms**; copper in liver
**Transferrin saturation 82%, normal ceruloplasmin, no corneal rings, iron on liver biopsy**

nodes.q: His high ferritin and iron-laden liver could suggest secondary hemosiderosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Repeated transfusions or ineffective erythropoiesis (for example thalassemia)**; iron mainly in macrophages (Kupffer cells)
**Never transfused; iron in hepatocytes with high transferrin saturation**

nodes.note: The trap: both give high ferritin and iron on liver biopsy.

nodes.q: His cirrhosis could suggest alcoholic liver disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Heavy long-term drinking; aspartate aminotransferase (AST) higher than alanine aminotransferase (ALT) by 2:1; Mallory-Denk bodies**; transferrin saturation usually normal
**Drinks little; transferrin saturation 82%; diabetes, bronze skin and cardiomyopathy**

nodes.q: His cirrhosis could suggest chronic viral hepatitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Positive hepatitis B or C serology or viral RNA/DNA**; no iron overload
**Negative hepatitis tests; very high ferritin and transferrin saturation**

root.stem: A 71-year-old woman develops sudden severe pain in her lower chest and upper abdomen. She retches repeatedly but brings up nothing, and a nasogastric tube cannot be passed beyond the lower esophagus. Her pulse is 120/min and blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg. Her upper abdomen is tender and distended, and her lower abdomen is soft. Serum lipase is normal, she has no fever or jaundice, and she has no history of ulcers or weight loss. An upright chest x-ray shows a gas-filled structure with an air-fluid level behind the heart.
root.oneliner: 71F + sudden severe lower chest and upper abdominal pain + retching without vomiting + nasogastric tube will not pass + pulse 120, BP 82/50 + tender distended upper abdomen, soft lower abdomen + normal lipase + no fever or jaundice + no ulcers or weight loss + chest x-ray: gas-filled structure with air-fluid level behind the heart
highlight: sudden severe pain in her lower chest and upper abdomen
retches repeatedly but brings up nothing
cannot be passed beyond the lower esophagus
upper abdomen is tender and distended
no history of ulcers or weight loss
gas-filled structure with an air-fluid level behind the heart

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The stomach twists on itself and closes both ends. The clincher: **Borchardt triad: severe epigastric or chest pain, retching without vomiting, and inability to pass a nasogastric tube**.

nodes.q: Which underlying condition most often allows the stomach to twist?
nodes.note: Part of the stomach slides through a defect beside the esophagus into the chest, and the hernia sac lets it rotate. The gas-filled structure behind the heart on the chest x-ray is the herniated stomach.

nodes.q: Her hernia must be told apart from the commoner sliding hiatal hernia. How do they differ?

split.note: **The gastroesophageal junction slides up into the chest** (hourglass stomach); causes reflux; rarely strangulates
**The gastroesophageal junction stays in place and the fundus rolls up beside the esophagus**; little reflux; can twist and strangulate

nodes.q: Which type of twist is most common?
nodes.note: The stomach rotates around its long axis, from the cardia to the pylorus; it is the type linked to paraesophageal hernia and tends to cause acute strangulation. The mesenteroaxial type, around the short axis, is often chronic and incomplete.

nodes.q: Why is she hypotensive?
nodes.a: Fluid sequestration and ischemia of the twisted stomach
nodes.note: Venous outflow is blocked first, then arterial flow.

nodes.q: If the twist is not reversed, which event in the stomach wall leads to death?
nodes.a: Strangulation with gastric necrosis and perforation
nodes.note: Perforation leads to peritonitis and septic shock. This is why acute volvulus is a surgical emergency, with high mortality once ischemia is present.

nodes.q: Which imaging study confirms the diagnosis and shows the anatomy?
nodes.a: Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and chest
nodes.note: Upper gastrointestinal contrast study can show an upside-down stomach, but CT is preferred in an unstable patient.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Emergency surgery: untwist the stomach, repair the hernia and fix the stomach to the abdominal wall (gastropexy)
nodes.note: Decompress with a tube if one can be passed and resuscitate with fluids first; resect any necrotic stomach.

nodes.q: Her upper abdominal pain and retching could suggest acute pancreatitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Raised lipase**, pain through to the back, and a nasogastric tube passes easily
**Normal lipase + retching without vomiting + nasogastric tube will not pass**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause severe upper abdominal pain with shock.

nodes.q: Her sudden pain and shock could suggest a perforated duodenal ulcer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Known ulcer disease or use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; free air under the diaphragm; rigid abdomen**
**No ulcer history; gas-filled structure behind the heart; abdomen soft below**

nodes.q: Her upper abdominal pain and retching could suggest gastric cancer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Weeks of weight loss, early satiety or anemia**; thickened stomach wall or mass
**Sudden onset with no weight loss; retching without vomiting**

nodes.q: Her upper abdominal pain could suggest acute cholecystitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Right upper quadrant pain after a fatty meal with fever and Murphy sign**; gallstones on ultrasound
**No fever or jaundice; tube will not pass; gas bubble behind the heart**

root.stem: A 24-year-old man has had 3 weeks of foul-smelling, greasy diarrhea with bloating and a lot of gas, and has lost 5 kg. He returned a month ago from a hiking trip on which he drank untreated stream water. He has no fever and has not seen blood in his stool. A stool sample contains no white blood cells, a modified acid-fast stain is negative, and anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies are negative. Microscopy shows pear-shaped organisms with two nuclei that move like a falling leaf. Milk now worsens his bloating.
root.oneliner: 24M + 3 weeks of foul greasy diarrhea with bloating and gas + 5 kg weight loss + hiking, drank untreated stream water + no fever, no blood + no fecal white cells + negative modified acid-fast stain + negative anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies + pear-shaped binucleate organisms that move like a falling leaf + milk worsens bloating
highlight: foul-smelling, greasy diarrhea with bloating and a lot of gas
not seen blood in his stool
pear-shaped organisms with two nuclei that move like a falling leaf

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A protozoal infection of the proximal small bowel. The clincher: **greasy, foul diarrhea with gas after drinking untreated water, with pear-shaped binucleate trophozoites in stool**.

nodes.q: The exam may name the organism. What is it?
nodes.a: Giardia lamblia (also called Giardia intestinalis or Giardia duodenalis)
nodes.note: These are names for the same protozoan.

nodes.q: Which form of the organism did he swallow?
nodes.note: Cysts in fecally contaminated water infect campers who drink stream water, day-care children and travelers. Cysts resist chlorination, so water must be filtered or boiled.

nodes.q: Why does his stool contain no blood or white cells?
nodes.a: The trophozoites attach to the duodenal lining with a ventral sucking disc and do not invade
nodes.note: They blunt the villi and interfere with absorption, which causes fat malabsorption and gas without inflammation.

nodes.q: Which sugar intolerance explains why milk worsens his bloating?
nodes.note: Damaged brush border loses lactase; it recovers weeks after treatment.

nodes.q: Which immune deficiency makes chronic giardiasis more likely?
nodes.note: Intestinal IgA normally helps clear the organism. Common variable immunodeficiency and X-linked agammaglobulinemia also predispose.

nodes.q: Which test is the most sensitive way to detect it?
nodes.note: Stool microscopy for trophozoites or cysts needs several samples because shedding is intermittent.

nodes.q: Which drug is the usual treatment?
nodes.note: Tinidazole and nitazoxanide are alternatives. Metronidazole causes a metallic taste and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.

nodes.q: How does this drug kill the organism?
nodes.a: It forms toxic free radicals that damage DNA
nodes.note: The nitro group is reduced only inside anaerobic organisms and protozoa, so the radicals form where they are needed.

nodes.q: His diarrhea after travel could suggest amebiasis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bloody stool and fecal white cells; trophozoites that contain red cells; liver abscess**; flask-shaped colonic ulcers
**No blood or white cells; pear-shaped binucleate trophozoites; greasy stool**

nodes.note: The trap: both follow contaminated water and both respond to metronidazole.

nodes.q: His watery diarrhea after water exposure could suggest cryptosporidiosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Acid-fast oocysts in stool**; severe in acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); treated with nitazoxanide
**Negative acid-fast stain; pear-shaped trophozoites**

nodes.q: His greasy diarrhea and weight loss could suggest celiac disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Positive anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies, villous atrophy**; no organisms in stool; improves off gluten
**Negative antibodies; organisms in stool; recent untreated water exposure**

root.stem: A 31-year-old woman has had 2 weeks of sharp, tearing pain during and for hours after bowel movements, with bright red streaks of blood on the toilet paper. She has had constipation for years, and her stools look normal. She has not had trauma or anal intercourse. Gently parting the buttocks shows a linear tear in the skin of the anal canal at the posterior midline, and the sphincter is in spasm. No tissue protrudes, there is no lump or swelling, no discharge or fever, and no warty growth or scaly plaque.
root.oneliner: 31F + 2 weeks of tearing pain with and after defecation + bright red blood on toilet paper + years of constipation + normal-looking stools + no trauma + linear posterior midline tear with sphincter spasm + nothing protrudes, no lump, no discharge or fever, no warts or scaly plaque
highlight: sharp, tearing pain during and for hours after bowel movements
bright red streaks of blood on the toilet paper
linear tear in the skin of the anal canal at the posterior midline
no warty growth or scaly plaque

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A tear in the lining of the anal canal below the dentate line. The clincher: **severe pain with defecation and bright red blood on the paper, with a linear tear at the posterior midline**.

nodes.q: Why does it occur at the posterior midline?
nodes.a: The blood supply there is poor
nodes.note: The posterior commissure is less well perfused than other sites, so tears heal badly.

nodes.q: Why is a tear here so painful?
nodes.a: It lies below the dentate line, where the lining has somatic sensory nerves (inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve)
nodes.note: Above the dentate line the lining has visceral nerves, so internal hemorrhoids are painless.

nodes.q: Spasm of which muscle keeps the tear from healing?
nodes.note: Hard stool tears the lining; sphincter spasm raises resting pressure and squeezes off blood flow, so the tear stays ischemic and does not close.

nodes.q: Which skin finding at the outer end of the tear marks a chronic fissure?
nodes.note: Other signs of chronicity: a hypertrophied anal papilla at the inner end and sphincter fibers visible in the base. They form after about 6 to 8 weeks.

nodes.q: A fissure away from the midline should make you think first of which bowel disease?
nodes.note: Off-midline or multiple painless fissures also suggest sexually transmitted infection, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, tuberculosis or cancer.

nodes.q: What is first-line treatment?
nodes.a: Fiber, fluids and warm sitz baths
nodes.note: Stool softeners and bulk laxatives; most acute fissures heal.

nodes.q: Which drug class applied locally relaxes the sphincter if conservative care fails?
nodes.a: Topical calcium channel blockers (nifedipine or diltiazem)
nodes.note: They relax internal sphincter smooth muscle and improve blood flow. Topical nitroglycerin works through nitric oxide but often gives headache.

nodes.q: Which procedure is used for fissures that persist despite medical therapy?
nodes.note: Botulinum toxin injection is a less permanent alternative; sphincterotomy carries a small risk of incontinence.

nodes.q: Her bright red blood could suggest an internal hemorrhoid. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Painless bleeding with a protruding cushion of tissue**
**Painful defecation with blood on paper; nothing protrudes; linear posterior tear**

nodes.note: The trap: both give bright red blood in a constipated patient.

nodes.q: Her anal pain could suggest a perianal abscess. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Constant throbbing pain, tender fluctuant swelling, fever**
**Pain only with and after defecation; no swelling or fever**

nodes.q: Her anal findings could suggest condyloma acuminatum. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Soft warty growths caused by human papillomavirus types 6 and 11**; usually painless
**Linear tear and pain with defecation, with no warty growths**

nodes.q: Her anal skin change could suggest Bowen disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **A slowly growing scaly or red plaque, squamous cell carcinoma in situ**; chronic and not healing, often linked to human papillomavirus
**Acute tearing pain with a linear tear, no plaque; bleeding after hard stool**

root.stem: A 46-year-old woman with a body mass index of 33 kg/m2 lost 20 kg in 5 months by strict dieting. For 2 days she has had severe right upper abdominal pain that began after a fatty meal and is now constant, spreading to the tip of her right shoulder blade, with nausea and a fever of 38.5°C. She stops inhaling when the examiner presses under her right rib margin. Leukocyte count is 15,000/mm3, total bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 160 U/L and serum lipase is normal. Ultrasonography shows gallstones, a thickened gallbladder wall with fluid around it and a common bile duct of normal width. She has no heartburn, and her stool is negative for occult blood.
root.oneliner: 46F + BMI 33 + lost 20 kg in 5 months + 2 days of severe RUQ pain after a fatty meal, now constant, to the right scapula + nausea + fever 38.5°C + stops inhaling on RUQ palpation + WBC 15,000 + bilirubin 2.1, alk phos 160 + normal lipase + ultrasound: gallstones, thick wall, pericholecystic fluid, normal bile duct + no heartburn, negative occult blood
highlight: lost 20 kg in 5 months by strict dieting
spreading to the tip of her right shoulder blade
stops inhaling when the examiner presses under her right rib margin
gallstones, a thickened gallbladder wall with fluid around it
common bile duct of normal width
stool is negative for occult blood

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Inflammation of the gallbladder, usually from a stone blocking the cystic duct. The clincher: **right upper quadrant pain with fever, a breath halted by right subcostal pressure, and gallbladder wall thickening with stones**.

nodes.q: Which bedside sign is present when she stops inhaling under the right rib margin?
nodes.note: The inflamed gallbladder touches the examiner's hand as it descends with inspiration, and the pain halts the breath.

nodes.q: What starts the inflammation?
nodes.a: A gallstone obstructs the cystic duct, distending the gallbladder and causing chemical and then bacterial inflammation
nodes.note: About 90% of cases are stone-related (calculous).

nodes.q: Which hormone makes the gallbladder contract after a fatty meal, so the pain starts then?
nodes.note: Released by I cells of the duodenum and jejunum in response to fat and protein; it contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi.

nodes.q: Which bile change explains stones after rapid weight loss?
nodes.a: Cholesterol mobilization makes bile supersaturated, with gallbladder stasis
nodes.note: Other cholesterol-stone risks: female sex, obesity, age, pregnancy, estrogen and fertility. Pigment stones come with hemolysis.

nodes.q: Why does the pain spread to the tip of the right shoulder blade?
nodes.a: Referred pain through shared spinal cord segments (about T7 to T9)
nodes.note: Visceral afferents from the gallbladder enter the same segments as skin over the right scapula. If the inflamed gallbladder irritates the diaphragm, pain can also reach the right shoulder through the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5).

nodes.q: Why are her bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase mildly raised when her bile duct is normal width?
nodes.a: Inflammation spreading from the gallbladder to the nearby liver and ducts
nodes.note: Leukocytosis and mild rises in bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase and aminotransferases are common. Marked cholestasis or a dilated duct suggests a common bile duct stone.

nodes.q: Which imaging study is first?
nodes.note: It shows stones, wall thickening above 3 mm, pericholecystic fluid and a sonographic Murphy sign.

nodes.q: Which scan confirms cystic duct obstruction when ultrasound is unclear?
nodes.a: A hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan showing no gallbladder filling
nodes.note: The tracer fills the bile ducts and the intestine but not the gallbladder.

nodes.q: If the distended wall becomes ischemic, which event follows without treatment?
nodes.a: Gangrene with perforation of the gallbladder
nodes.note: Perforation causes bile peritonitis or an abscess. Empyema (pus in the gallbladder) is another complication; gallstone ileus is a late event if a stone erodes into the bowel.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Fluids, analgesia and antibiotics followed by early laparoscopic cholecystectomy
nodes.note: Ceftriaxone with metronidazole is a common choice; operate within about 72 hours. Percutaneous cholecystostomy is used in patients too ill for surgery.

nodes.q: Her upper abdominal pain and nausea could suggest acute pancreatitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Raised lipase**, epigastric pain through to the back, and no wall thickening of the gallbladder
**Normal lipase + Murphy sign + gallbladder wall thickening with pericholecystic fluid**

nodes.note: The trap: gallstones can cause both.

nodes.q: Her raised liver enzymes could suggest fatty liver disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Usually painless; **mildly raised aminotransferases, bright liver on ultrasound**; no fever
**Fever with leukocytosis, Murphy sign and a thick gallbladder wall**

nodes.q: Her upper abdominal pain could suggest peptic ulcer disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Burning epigastric pain related to meals, relieved by antacids; occult blood in stool**
**Right upper quadrant pain after a fatty meal; stool negative for occult blood; stones**

nodes.q: Her pain and nausea could suggest esophageal reflux. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Burning behind the breastbone after meals or lying down**; no fever or leukocytosis
**No heartburn; fever, Murphy sign and gallbladder wall thickening**

nodes.q: Her raised bilirubin could suggest a stone in the common bile duct. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Dilated common bile duct on ultrasound with marked rises in bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase**
**Normal-width common bile duct with only mild liver-test changes and a thick gallbladder wall**

root.stem: A 23-year-old woman has had 6 months of cramping pain in the right lower abdomen, low-grade fevers, a 5-kg weight loss and loose stools that are sometimes streaked with blood. The pain and diarrhea often wake her at night. She smokes 10 cigarettes a day, and her brother has the same illness. Tender red nodules have appeared on both shins. Colonoscopy shows patches of deep ulceration separated by normal-looking mucosa, a cobblestone appearance in the terminal ileum and a normal rectum. Biopsies show inflammation through the full thickness of the wall with non-caseating granulomas. A contrast study shows a narrowed segment of ileum, and she now has a draining opening beside her anus.
root.oneliner: 23F + 6 months right lower quadrant cramps, low-grade fever, 5-kg weight loss, bloody loose stools + woken at night by pain and diarrhea + smoker + brother with the same illness + tender red shin nodules + patches of deep ulcers between normal mucosa, cobblestone terminal ileum, normal rectum + full-thickness inflammation with non-caseating granulomas + narrowed ileum + draining opening beside the anus
highlight: her brother has the same illness
Tender red nodules have appeared on both shins
patches of deep ulceration separated by normal-looking mucosa
cobblestone appearance in the terminal ileum

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gut from mouth to anus. The clincher: **skip lesions with full-thickness inflammation and non-caseating granulomas**, usually in the terminal ileum, with fistulae and strictures.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Also called regional ileitis when only the terminal ileum is involved. Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which feature of her history best separates an inflammatory cause of her diarrhea from a functional one?
nodes.a: Pain and diarrhea that wake her from sleep
nodes.note: Functional symptoms settle during sleep. Other alarm features are blood in the stool, weight loss, fever and anemia.

nodes.q: Which bowel segment is most often inflamed?
nodes.note: Any part of the gut can be involved, often the colon as well. The rectum is usually spared, which fits her normal rectum.

nodes.q: How deep does the inflammation reach into the bowel wall?
nodes.note: Lymphoid aggregates and deep fissures extend into the muscle and the fat. The wall thickens and scars, which explains the fistulae and strictures. On a resected specimen, mesenteric fat wraps around the diseased bowel (creeping fat) and the thick, rubbery loops stick to one another.

nodes.q: Which biopsy finding points to the diagnosis but is seen in only some patients?
nodes.note: Collections of epithelioid macrophages with no central necrosis. Caseating granulomas would suggest tuberculosis instead.

nodes.q: Which gene is the strongest known genetic risk factor?
nodes.note: NOD2 senses bacterial cell wall peptides. Loss of function weakens the handling of gut bacteria and lets the immune system overreact. Her brother's illness fits the familial clustering.

nodes.q: A genome-wide study finds 32 risk loci, each with an odds ratio of only 1.1 to 1.5, that together explain about 10% of the variance in risk, while twin studies suggest 50% heritability. What does this show?
nodes.a: Each locus has a small effect and most of the heritability is still unexplained (missing heritability)
nodes.note: The disease is polygenic and also depends on gut bacteria and environment. No single locus gives simple autosomal dominant inheritance, and more loci keep being found as study size grows.

nodes.q: Inflammation loosens which junction that normally seals the gap between neighbouring intestinal cells, so that a swallowed sugar such as lactulose leaks into the blood?
nodes.note: Cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor (TNF) alpha disrupt the tight junction proteins. Lactulose is normally not absorbed, so more of it in blood or urine shows a leaky gut. Desmosomes and adherens junctions give strength, and gap junctions pass signals.

nodes.q: Which T-helper cell response mainly drives the damage?
nodes.note: Interferon gamma and interleukin 17 recruit macrophages that release tumor necrosis factor alpha and other cytokines, producing granulomas and full-thickness injury. Ulcerative colitis leans more toward a T-helper 2-type response.

nodes.q: Which of her habits makes this disease worse, although it lowers the risk of ulcerative colitis?
nodes.note: Smokers have more flares, fistulae and repeat surgery; stopping smoking is part of treatment.

nodes.q: Prednisone is given during a flare. Which immune function does it mainly suppress?
nodes.note: Glucocorticoids block nuclear factor kappa B and cut the production of interleukin 2 and other cytokines, so T cells are activated and expand less. Antibody binding, complement activity and mast cell degranulation are not the main targets.

nodes.q: Which complication of full-thickness inflammation explains the draining opening beside her anus?
nodes.note: Tracts form between the bowel and the skin, bladder, vagina or another loop of bowel. Perianal fistulae and abscesses are common.

nodes.q: Which acute complication can suddenly follow when a deeply ulcerated, thickened loop gives way?
nodes.note: Bowel contents spill into the peritoneal cavity.

nodes.q: What does this spill cause, which can be fatal?
nodes.note: At autopsy, a fibrinous exudate covers the peritoneal and serosal surfaces, with a punctate opening in a thickened, narrowed loop that is stuck to its neighbours.

nodes.q: Which complication of repeated inflammation and scarring narrows the lumen and causes obstruction?
nodes.note: Fibrosis thickens the wall. On a contrast study the narrowed segment appears as a thin 'string sign'.

nodes.q: What are the tender red nodules on her shins?
nodes.note: An inflammation of the fat under the skin (panniculitis) that tracks with bowel activity. Other extraintestinal signs: uveitis, aphthous mouth ulcers, migratory arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and pyoderma gangrenosum. Primary sclerosing cholangitis is more typical of ulcerative colitis.

nodes.q: Which vitamin is malabsorbed when the terminal ileum is diseased or removed?
nodes.note: It is absorbed only in the terminal ileum, bound to intrinsic factor. Deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neurologic signs. Bile salts are also lost there, causing fat malabsorption, gallstones and calcium oxalate kidney stones (unbound dietary oxalate is absorbed in excess).

nodes.q: Which cancer becomes more likely after years of disease involving the colon?
nodes.note: Risk rises after about 8 years of colitis, so surveillance colonoscopy starts then. It arises from flat dysplasia rather than a polyp.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Computed tomography or magnetic resonance enterography shows the small bowel disease and its complications. Stool cultures and Clostridioides difficile testing exclude infection first; fecal calprotectin tracks inflammation.

nodes.q: A monoclonal antibody is started to heal her fistula. Which cytokine does it neutralize?
nodes.note: Infliximab (chimeric) and adalimumab (fully human) bind soluble and membrane-bound tumor necrosis factor. The same drugs treat ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis. Corticosteroids settle flares but are not used for long-term maintenance.

nodes.q: Which infection must be excluded before the antibody is started?
nodes.note: Tumor necrosis factor keeps granulomas intact, so blocking it can reactivate tuberculosis. Hepatitis B is also screened for.

nodes.q: Her bloody stools could suggest ulcerative colitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Continuous disease from the rectum upward, limited to the mucosa and submucosa, with crypt abscesses and no granulomas**; bloody diarrhea, no fistulae
**Skip lesions, full-thickness inflammation, granulomas, fistulae and strictures**; the rectum is often spared

nodes.note: The trap: both cause cramping pain, diarrhea with blood and weight loss.

nodes.q: Her cramping pain and loose stools could suggest irritable bowel syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Pain relieved by defecation, symptoms that never wake the patient, no blood, fever or weight loss**; normal colonoscopy and biopsy
**Night-time pain and diarrhea, blood in the stool, fever, weight loss** and inflamed bowel on biopsy

nodes.note: Both cause crampy pain and altered stools in a young adult.

nodes.q: Her weight loss and a narrowed bowel segment could suggest colon cancer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Older person with iron-deficiency anemia, occult blood and a mass**; glandular cells invading the wall on biopsy
**Young person with months of cramps, fever, skip ulcers and granulomas**; a smooth stricture rather than a mass

nodes.q: Her diarrhea and weight loss could suggest celiac disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fatty, foul-smelling stools, iron or folate deficiency, dermatitis herpetiformis, and villous atrophy with anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies**; no fever, no fistulae
**Fever, blood in the stool, skip lesions with granulomas and fistulae**

nodes.q: Her right lower quadrant pain and fever could suggest acute appendicitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Pain moving from the umbilicus to the right lower quadrant over hours to a day, with a raised white cell count**; no diarrhea for months, no fistulae
**Six months of cramps, weight loss, bloody loose stools, ileal ulcers and granulomas**
