root.stem: A 3-week-old full-term girl has had 1 week of yellow skin and eyes. Her stools are pale and chalky, her urine is dark enough to stain the diaper, and her liver edge is felt 3 cm below the costal margin. She was not jaundiced at birth, feeds well and is gaining weight. Her blood group is compatible with her mother's and the Coombs test is negative. Total bilirubin is 7 mg/dL, of which 6 mg/dL is direct, the aminotransferases are mildly raised, and gamma-glutamyl transferase is markedly raised. The alpha-1 antitrypsin level is normal. Ultrasonography shows no dilated bile ducts and a small gallbladder.
root.oneliner: 3-week-old F + 1 week of jaundice + pale chalky stools, dark urine + hepatomegaly + not jaundiced at birth, feeding well + compatible blood group, negative Coombs + direct bilirubin 6 of 7 mg/dL + raised gamma-glutamyl transferase + normal alpha-1 antitrypsin + no dilated ducts, small gallbladder
highlight: dark enough to stain the diaper
compatible with her mother's and the Coombs test is negative
no dilated bile ducts and a small gallbladder

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Destruction and scarring of the extrahepatic bile ducts in the first weeks of life, so bile cannot reach the gut. The clincher: **jaundice after the first 2 weeks of life with pale stools, dark urine and mostly direct (conjugated) bilirubin**.

nodes.q: Which form of bilirubin is raised?
nodes.note: The liver conjugates bilirubin normally, but it cannot drain into the intestine and backs up into the blood and urine. Without bile pigment in the gut, stools turn pale.

nodes.q: What would a liver biopsy show?
nodes.a: Bile duct proliferation with portal fibrosis and bile plugs
nodes.note: The hallmark of obstruction to bile flow. Multinucleated giant cells would point to neonatal hepatitis instead.

nodes.q: Which scan shows no bile reaching the bowel?
nodes.a: Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan with no excretion into the intestine
nodes.note: Ultrasonography shows a small or absent gallbladder and a triangular cord at the porta hepatis. A cholangiogram during surgery confirms the diagnosis.

nodes.q: Bile salts do not reach the gut. Which group of vitamins is malabsorbed?
nodes.note: Bile salts form the micelles needed to absorb fat and the vitamins A, D, E and K. The water-soluble vitamins (B6, B12, folate, C) are absorbed normally.

nodes.q: Which bleeding problem can follow deficiency of one of them?
nodes.a: Vitamin K deficiency with a prolonged prothrombin time
nodes.note: Factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S) need vitamin K for carboxylation.

nodes.q: Which of these vitamins, when deficient, causes hemolytic anemia and a spinocerebellar neuropathy with loss of position sense?
nodes.note: It is an antioxidant that protects red cell and nerve membranes from free radical damage.

nodes.q: If it is not treated, what does the liver progress to?
nodes.a: Biliary cirrhosis with end-stage liver failure
nodes.note: Progressive fibrosis from bile stasis leads to portal hypertension within the first years of life. Death usually occurs by about 2 years without surgery.

nodes.q: Which operation, best done before about 8 weeks of age, restores bile flow?
nodes.note: A loop of jejunum is joined to the porta hepatis to drain bile. The earlier it is done, the better the outcome.

nodes.q: What is needed if the operation fails or cirrhosis develops?
nodes.note: Biliary atresia is the most common reason for liver transplantation in children.

nodes.q: Her pale stools and direct hyperbilirubinemia could suggest neonatal hepatitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Giant cell transformation of hepatocytes with patent bile ducts**; some bile reaches the gut on the scan; infection or idiopathic
**Bile duct proliferation with bile plugs and no excretion into the bowel on the scan**; small gallbladder

nodes.note: The trap: both give direct hyperbilirubinemia, pale stools and hepatomegaly in a young infant.

nodes.q: Her jaundice could suggest Crigler-Najjar syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Unconjugated bilirubin from absent glucuronosyltransferase**; normal-coloured stools, no bilirubin in the urine
**Conjugated bilirubin with pale stools and dark urine**

nodes.q: Her jaundice could suggest Gilbert syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in adolescence during fasting or illness**; normal stools and liver tests
**Jaundice at 3 weeks with pale stools, dark urine and conjugated bilirubin**

nodes.q: Her jaundice could suggest hemolytic disease of the newborn. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Unconjugated bilirubin within the first 24 hours, positive Coombs test with mother-infant blood group incompatibility, anemia**; kernicterus risk
**Direct hyperbilirubinemia after 2 weeks, compatible blood groups, negative Coombs test, pale stools**

nodes.q: Her jaundice could suggest physiologic jaundice. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Unconjugated bilirubin that appears after the first day, peaks around days 3 to 5 and clears by 2 weeks**; normal stools and urine
**Jaundice that begins or persists beyond 2 weeks with pale stools and direct bilirubin**

nodes.q: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency also gives neonatal cholestasis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low serum alpha-1 antitrypsin and periodic acid-Schiff-positive globules in hepatocytes**; family history of lung or liver disease
**Normal alpha-1 antitrypsin level, bile plugs and no bile excretion on the scan**

nodes.q: Her jaundice and pale stools could suggest a choledochal cyst. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Cystic dilation of the bile duct on ultrasonography, often with a right upper quadrant mass** and intermittent jaundice
**No dilated ducts, a small gallbladder and a triangular cord at the porta hepatis**

image_prompts.root: A pastel picture of a jaundiced infant with a pale stool in the diaper, beside a liver whose bile ducts end in a scarred, cord-like remnant.

root.stem: A 31-year-old man has had 1 week of nausea, vomiting, aching in the right upper abdomen, dark urine and yellow eyes. Three weeks ago he ate raw oysters on a trip to Mexico. He has never injected drugs, has no tattoos or transfusions, drinks little alcohol and takes no medications. His liver is enlarged and tender, his spleen and lymph nodes are not palpable and he has no sore throat. Aspartate aminotransferase is 1,100 U/L, alanine aminotransferase is 1,600 U/L and the immunoglobulin M antibody to hepatitis A virus is positive.
root.oneliner: 31M + 1 week nausea, vomiting, right upper quadrant ache, dark urine, jaundice + raw oysters in Mexico 3 weeks ago + no injection drugs, tattoos or transfusions, little alcohol + tender hepatomegaly, no splenomegaly, no sore throat + aminotransferases 1,100 and 1,600 U/L + positive immunoglobulin M antibody to hepatitis A virus
highlight: raw oysters on a trip to Mexico
never injected drugs, has no tattoos or transfusions
spleen and lymph nodes are not palpable and he has no sore throat
immunoglobulin M antibody to hepatitis A virus is positive

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An acute viral liver infection spread by the fecal-oral route. The clincher: **jaundice with tender hepatomegaly 2 to 6 weeks after raw shellfish or travel, with immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibodies to hepatitis A virus**.

nodes.q: Which kind of virus causes it?
nodes.a: A non-enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA picornavirus
nodes.note: Hepatovirus A, in the family Picornaviridae. With no envelope, it survives stomach acid and bile.

nodes.q: Why do raw oysters carry the virus?
nodes.a: They filter sewage-contaminated water and concentrate the virus
nodes.note: Spread is fecal-oral, by contaminated food or water, close contact and daycare outbreaks. Travel to endemic areas is a classic exposure.

nodes.q: By which mechanism do his liver cells die?
nodes.a: Apoptosis caused by cytotoxic T cells acting through the death receptor (extrinsic) pathway
nodes.note: The virus is not directly toxic to the cell. CD8 cytotoxic T cells recognise viral antigen on hepatocytes; Fas ligand binds Fas and activates caspase 8, then caspase 3 (perforin and granzyme B add to the killing). It is not necrosis from free radicals or lack of blood supply, and it is not autophagy.

nodes.q: Which change is the characteristic histologic feature of virus-induced liver injury?
nodes.a: Apoptosis: shrunken, bright pink hepatocytes with condensed nuclei (Councilman bodies)
nodes.note: Seen in acute viral hepatitis of any type, with ballooned hepatocytes and lobular lymphocytes. Coagulation necrosis follows ischemia, Mallory hyaline follows alcohol, and smooth endoplasmic reticulum proliferation follows drugs that induce liver enzymes.

nodes.q: Which test confirms acute infection?
nodes.note: Immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibody marks past infection or vaccination and lifelong immunity. Aminotransferases are usually in the thousands.

nodes.q: How does the illness usually end?
nodes.note: There is no chronic infection and no carrier state. Fulminant liver failure is rare, more likely in older adults and those with chronic liver disease.

nodes.q: What is given to a healthy adult household contact exposed a week ago?
nodes.note: Post-exposure prophylaxis works within 2 weeks of exposure. Immune globulin is given instead to infants under 12 months, and added to the vaccine in the immunocompromised and those with chronic liver disease. The inactivated vaccine is also routine in childhood.

nodes.q: His jaundice and raised aminotransferases could suggest acute hepatitis B. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Positive surface antigen and IgM antibody to core antigen after blood, sexual or needle exposure**; incubation 1 to 6 months; can become chronic, with ground-glass hepatocytes
**IgM antibody to hepatitis A virus after raw shellfish or travel**; incubation 2 to 6 weeks; never chronic

nodes.note: The trap: both give an acute jaundiced illness with markedly raised aminotransferases.

nodes.q: His illness could suggest hepatitis C. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Injection drug use or transfusion; usually silent acute illness; most develop chronic infection**; hepatitis C virus RNA in the blood
**Fecal-oral exposure, jaundice with tender liver, full recovery**

nodes.q: His tender liver and jaundice could suggest infectious mononucleosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sore throat, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes and a positive heterophile test**; liver tests only mildly raised
**No sore throat, nodes or spleen enlargement; marked aminotransferase rise with positive IgM antibody to hepatitis A virus**

nodes.q: His raised aminotransferases could suggest alcoholic hepatitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Heavy alcohol use, aspartate aminotransferase to alanine aminotransferase ratio above 2 with values under 300 U/L, neutrophils and Mallory hyaline**
**Little alcohol, alanine aminotransferase above aspartate aminotransferase in the thousands, Councilman bodies**

image_prompts.root: A pastel picture of a plate of raw oysters beside a jaundiced man holding his right upper abdomen, with a small liver cell showing a shrunken, bright pink apoptotic body.

root.stem: A 62-year-old man has had 10 days of mild diffuse abdominal pain and a rapid increase in abdominal girth. He has a 10-year history of cirrhosis from hepatitis C virus infection and alcohol use, and he stopped drinking 8 years ago. Examination shows tense ascites, a small, irregular liver and a firm, discrete 2-cm nodule on the liver surface. He has no fever, and his ascitic fluid contains fewer than 250 neutrophils per microliter. A week after a trial chemotherapy drug is started, a repeat liver biopsy shows shrunken tumor cells with condensed chromatin and membrane-bound cell fragments, and electrophoresis of DNA from the tissue shows a ladder of regularly spaced bands.
root.oneliner: 62M + 10 days abdominal pain, rapidly increasing girth + 10-year cirrhosis from hepatitis C and alcohol, sober 8 years + tense ascites, small irregular liver, discrete 2-cm nodule + no fever, ascitic neutrophils <250/uL + after chemotherapy: shrunken tumor cells, condensed chromatin, DNA ladder
highlight: 10-year history of cirrhosis from hepatitis C virus infection and alcohol use
shrunken tumor cells with condensed chromatin and membrane-bound cell fragments

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The most common primary liver cancer. The clincher: **a new liver nodule or sudden worsening of ascites in a patient with cirrhosis, with a raised alpha-fetoprotein**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: An older name for the same tumor, also called primary liver cancer.

nodes.q: Which background liver condition is present in most patients?
nodes.note: From hepatitis B or C virus, alcohol, hemochromatosis or fatty liver disease. Hepatitis B virus can cause the tumor even without cirrhosis, by integrating into the host genome.

nodes.q: Which mold toxin, found in stored grains and peanuts, also raises the risk?
nodes.a: Aflatoxin B1, made by Aspergillus flavus
nodes.note: It causes a characteristic mutation of the TP53 tumor suppressor gene (codon 249) and acts together with hepatitis B.

nodes.q: Which serum tumor marker is most useful to support the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Made by the fetal liver and yolk sac; a markedly raised level with a liver mass in cirrhosis strongly supports the diagnosis. CA 19-9, carcinoembryonic antigen, CA 125 and prostate-specific antigen point to other tumors; gamma-aminobutyric acid is a neurotransmitter, not a marker.

nodes.q: Which imaging pattern makes the diagnosis in a cirrhotic liver without a biopsy?
nodes.a: Arterial-phase enhancement with washout on multiphasic computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging
nodes.note: The tumor takes its blood from the hepatic artery, the normal liver mostly from the portal vein. A biopsy is usually not needed when the imaging is typical.

nodes.q: How are patients with cirrhosis screened?
nodes.note: Screening aims to find tumors small enough to cure.

nodes.q: Which vein does the tumor tend to invade, suddenly raising the portal pressure and the ascites?
nodes.note: Invasion of the hepatic veins can cause Budd-Chiari syndrome. Spread through the blood goes mainly to the lungs.

nodes.q: Which blood count change can the tumor cause by making erythropoietin?
nodes.note: Other paraneoplastic effects are hypoglycemia and hypercalcemia.

nodes.q: After chemotherapy the tumor shows shrunken cells with condensed chromatin and a DNA ladder. Which form of cell death is this?
nodes.note: Programmed cell death, with cell shrinkage and membrane-bound apoptotic bodies and no inflammation. Necrosis swells the cells and spills their contents.

nodes.q: Which enzyme, activated by caspases, cuts the DNA between nucleosomes to make the ladder?
nodes.note: It cleaves at about 180 base pair intervals. DNA ligase and DNA polymerase repair and copy DNA, transglutaminase cross-links proteins in apoptotic bodies, and phospholipase A2 acts in membrane injury of necrosis.

nodes.q: Which operation can cure a small tumor in a liver that is failing from cirrhosis?
nodes.note: One tumor up to 5 cm, or up to 3 tumors each up to 3 cm, without vascular invasion. Resection suits well-preserved liver function; ablation suits small tumors.

nodes.q: Which drug pair is first-line for tumors that cannot be removed?
nodes.a: Atezolizumab (a programmed death-ligand 1 antibody) plus bevacizumab (a vascular endothelial growth factor antibody)
nodes.note: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as sorafenib and lenvatinib are alternatives.

nodes.q: A liver mass with weight loss could suggest cholangiocarcinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Raised CA 19-9, dilated bile ducts with jaundice and itching**; primary sclerosing cholangitis or liver flukes; glandular cells in dense stroma
**Cirrhosis, raised alpha-fetoprotein and arterial enhancement with washout**

nodes.q: His liver nodule could be a metastasis from a colon cancer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Raised carcinoembryonic antigen, a known colon primary and several nodules in a non-cirrhotic liver**
**A solitary nodule in a cirrhotic liver with raised alpha-fetoprotein**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause liver nodules and ascites in a middle-aged or older adult.

nodes.q: His rapidly increasing ascites with abdominal pain could suggest spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever and an ascitic fluid neutrophil count of 250 per microliter or more**
**No fever, fewer than 250 neutrophils per microliter and a discrete liver nodule**

nodes.q: A liver nodule could be a hepatic adenoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Young woman using oral contraceptives, solitary mass in a non-cirrhotic liver**; normal alpha-fetoprotein; risk of rupture and bleeding
**Man with cirrhosis and raised alpha-fetoprotein**

image_prompts.root: A pastel cross-section of a small, nodular cirrhotic liver with one larger pale tumor nodule, a distended abdomen with fluid, and a tiny inset of a shrunken apoptotic cell.

root.stem: A newborn boy is delivered at 39 weeks after a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios. Within hours he has frothy saliva at the mouth, coughs and turns blue when first fed, and has mild respiratory distress. He has not vomited bile and has no stridor between feeds. A nasogastric tube meets resistance and cannot be passed into the stomach. A chest radiograph shows the tube coiled in the upper chest, a stomach distended with air below the diaphragm and a normal abdominal contour with bowel sounds heard over the abdomen. A holosystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border.
root.oneliner: Newborn boy + polyhydramnios + frothy saliva, coughing and cyanosis at first feed + no bilious vomiting, no stridor + nasogastric tube will not pass, coiled in upper chest + air-distended stomach below the diaphragm + normal abdominal contour with bowel sounds + holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border
highlight: frothy saliva at the mouth, coughs and turns blue when first fed
has not vomited bile and has no stridor
cannot be passed into the stomach
stomach distended with air below the diaphragm
normal abdominal contour with bowel sounds heard over the abdomen

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The upper esophagus ends in a blind pouch and the lower esophagus connects to the trachea (the most common type). The clincher: **a newborn who drools and chokes with feeds, a nasogastric tube that will not pass, and an air-filled stomach**.

nodes.q: Why is the stomach filled with air?
nodes.a: Air passes from the trachea through the fistula into the lower esophagus and stomach
nodes.note: Gas in the stomach shows that there is a fistula to the lower esophagus. With atresia and no fistula the abdomen would have no gas.

nodes.q: Which embryologic error causes it?
nodes.a: Abnormal deviation of the tracheoesophageal septum
nodes.note: The septum splits the foregut into the trachea in front and the esophagus behind during weeks 4 to 5. Deviation leaves the two tubes incompletely separated.

nodes.q: Why did the pregnancy have polyhydramnios?
nodes.a: The fetus could not swallow and absorb the amniotic fluid
nodes.note: The fluid cannot pass the blind upper pouch to be absorbed in the gut.

nodes.q: Which lung complication follows when stomach contents reflux up the fistula into the trachea?
nodes.note: Gastric acid injures the lung, and saliva pooled in the blind pouch is aspirated as well. Feeding is therefore stopped at once.

nodes.q: Which pattern of anomalies often comes with it?
nodes.note: Vertebral defects, Anal atresia, Cardiac defects (often a ventricular septal defect), Tracheoesophageal fistula, Renal anomalies and Limb anomalies. His murmur fits a cardiac defect.

nodes.q: Which tests look for the other defects?
nodes.a: Echocardiography, renal ultrasonography and spine and limb radiographs, with an anal examination
nodes.note: Done once the airway and feeding problem has been dealt with.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Keep him nil by mouth with the head raised and suction the pouch, then surgical ligation of the fistula with end-to-end esophageal anastomosis
nodes.note: Repair is done once he is stable. Long-gap atresia may need staged repair.

nodes.q: Which long-term problem commonly follows repair?
nodes.note: Esophageal stricture and tracheomalacia can also follow because of abnormal motility and weak tracheal cartilage.

nodes.q: Polyhydramnios and an air-filled stomach could suggest duodenal atresia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bilious vomiting after feeds with a double bubble sign; often Down syndrome**; the nasogastric tube passes
**Drooling, choking at the first feed, a tube that will not pass and a single air-filled stomach**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause polyhydramnios because the fetus cannot absorb the fluid.

nodes.q: His breathing trouble could suggest a vascular ring from an aortic arch abnormality. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Stridor, wheezing and trouble swallowing solids that start weeks to months after birth**; barium swallow shows a posterior indentation; the tube passes
**Choking and cyanosis at the first feed and a blocked tube**

nodes.q: His feeding trouble could suggest hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Projectile non-bilious vomiting at 2 to 6 weeks of age with an olive-shaped mass and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis**
**Symptoms from the first feed in a newborn, with a blocked nasogastric tube, because feeds never reach the stomach**

nodes.q: His noisy breathing could suggest tracheomalacia from incomplete tracheal cartilage rings. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Expiratory wheeze or stridor that worsens with crying or feeding**; feeding is otherwise normal and the tube passes
**Choking, frothing at the mouth and cyanosis with a tube that will not pass**

nodes.q: His respiratory distress and cyanosis could suggest congenital diaphragmatic hernia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Scaphoid abdomen, bowel sounds in the chest and bowel loops in the thorax with mediastinal shift** from pulmonary hypoplasia
**Air-filled stomach below the diaphragm, a tube coiled in the upper chest and frothing at the mouth**

image_prompts.root: A pastel picture of a newborn with frothy saliva, beside a diagram of a blind upper esophageal pouch and a lower esophagus joined to the trachea, with air reaching the stomach.

root.stem: A 27-year-old man has had 3 hours of nausea, cramping abdominal pain and diarrhea that began 24 hours after a picnic lunch that included undercooked egg salad; three other guests are also ill. His temperature is 38.2°C, his abdomen is mildly tender and there is no blood or mucus in the stool. Stool culture grows a motile, non-lactose-fermenting, hydrogen sulfide-producing gram-negative rod. He can drink fluids, and his symptoms begin to resolve within 36 hours. He has no sickle cell disease, takes no acid-suppressing drugs, and has no artificial joints or heart valves.
root.oneliner: 27M + 3 hours nausea, cramps, diarrhea starting 24 hours after a picnic with undercooked egg salad + other guests ill + fever 38.2°C + no blood or mucus in stool + culture: motile, non-lactose-fermenting, hydrogen sulfide-producing gram-negative rod + resolving within 36 hours + no sickle cell disease, acid suppression or prostheses
highlight: 24 hours after a picnic lunch that included undercooked egg salad
three other guests are also ill
no blood or mucus in the stool
motile, non-lactose-fermenting, hydrogen sulfide-producing gram-negative rod

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A self-limited infection of the gut after eating contaminated food. The clincher: **diarrhea and cramps 6 to 72 hours after poultry, eggs or reptile contact, with a stool culture growing a non-lactose-fermenting, hydrogen sulfide-producing rod**.

nodes.q: The stool culture report names the species. Which is it?
nodes.note: The nontyphoidal serotypes, mainly Enteritidis and Typhimurium, belong to Salmonella enterica. Typhoid fever is caused by serotype Typhi.

nodes.q: Which features identify the organism on culture?
nodes.a: A motile, gram-negative, non-lactose-fermenting rod that produces hydrogen sulfide
nodes.note: It forms black-centred colonies on Hektoen or xylose-lysine-deoxycholate agar and is oxidase negative.

nodes.q: Which foods and animals carry the organism?
nodes.a: Poultry, eggs and reptiles such as pet turtles
nodes.note: Spread is fecal-oral from animal reservoirs. A large dose is needed unless stomach acid is lowered by antacids or proton pump inhibitors.

nodes.q: Where does it invade the gut to cause fever and inflammatory diarrhea?
nodes.a: M cells overlying the Peyer patches of the ileum
nodes.note: It survives inside macrophages and mostly stays in the gut wall and the nodes draining it, so the illness is usually self-limited.

nodes.q: What is the management of a healthy adult who can drink fluids?
nodes.note: Symptoms settle in 2 to 7 days.

nodes.q: Why are antibiotics withheld in this setting?
nodes.a: They prolong fecal excretion of the organism
nodes.note: They do not shorten the illness. Hypersensitivity is rare, and the chronic carrier state of the gallbladder belongs to typhoid, not to this illness.

nodes.q: Which patients are given antibiotics despite the usual self-limited course?
nodes.a: Infants, older adults, the immunocompromised, those with sickle cell disease or vascular grafts, and those with bacteremia
nodes.note: In these groups the organism can spread beyond the gut.

nodes.q: Which complication follows when the organism seeds bone in a patient with sickle cell disease?
nodes.note: Sickle cell disease causes functional asplenia and bone infarcts, which favours Salmonella infection. Bacteremia can also seed grafts and aneurysms.

nodes.q: Which joint complication can follow 1 to 4 weeks later in a person who carries human leukocyte antigen B27?
nodes.note: An asymmetric arthritis of the knees and ankles, sometimes with urethritis and conjunctivitis. It also follows Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia and Chlamydia infection.

nodes.q: His fever, cramps and diarrhea could suggest shigellosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bloody, mucoid stool with tenesmus after a tiny dose (10 to 100 organisms)**; non-motile, no hydrogen sulfide
**Watery stool after poultry or eggs; a motile, hydrogen sulfide-producing rod**

nodes.note: The trap: both are non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative rods that cause fever and diarrhea.

nodes.q: A meal-related illness could be Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Vomiting and cramps 1 to 6 hours after cream-filled or mayonnaise foods (preformed enterotoxin), no fever, over in 24 hours**
**Onset 6 to 72 hours after the meal, fever, positive stool culture**

nodes.q: Hemolytic uremic syndrome can follow a food-borne diarrhea like his. How do you tell his illness from the one that causes it?

split.note: **Bloody diarrhea after undercooked beef, Shiga toxin and sorbitol non-fermenting colonies**; hemolytic uremic syndrome follows, and antibiotics raise the risk
**Watery diarrhea after poultry or eggs, no hemolytic uremic syndrome**

image_prompts.root: A pastel picnic scene with an egg salad sandwich and a chicken drumstick, and a small inset of a black-centred bacterial colony on agar.

root.stem: A 43-year-old woman has had 1 week of abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and itching. Her sclerae are yellow, her urine is dark and her stools are pale. She is tender in the right upper quadrant, has no rash, and has no fever or chills. Her gallbladder is not palpable. Her hemoglobin, white cell count and reticulocyte count are normal, and the serum total bilirubin is markedly increased, mostly direct. Her aminotransferases are only mildly raised. Abdominal ultrasonography shows a large stone in a dilated common bile duct.
root.oneliner: 43F + 1 week abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, itching + yellow sclerae, dark urine, pale stools + right upper quadrant tenderness + no rash, fever or chills + gallbladder not palpable + normal hemoglobin, white cells, reticulocytes + markedly raised direct bilirubin + mildly raised aminotransferases + large stone in a dilated common bile duct
highlight: dark and her stools are pale
tender in the right upper quadrant
large stone in a dilated common bile duct

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A gallstone lodged in the common bile duct. The clincher: **right upper quadrant pain and jaundice with itching, dark urine and pale stools, and a stone in a dilated common bile duct on ultrasonography**.

nodes.q: Which serum enzyme is most markedly increased?
nodes.note: Blocked bile flow makes the bile duct lining produce more alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase, while aspartate and alanine aminotransferases rise only mildly. Acid phosphatase comes from the prostate, and lactate dehydrogenase rises with hemolysis.

nodes.q: Which form of bilirubin accounts for the jaundice?
nodes.note: It is water-soluble and spills into the urine, making it dark. Bile pigment cannot reach the gut, so stools are pale.

nodes.q: What causes the itching?
nodes.a: Bile salts retained in the blood and deposited in the skin
nodes.note: Cholestyramine binds bile salts in the gut and can ease it.

nodes.q: Where do most of the stones in the common bile duct come from?
nodes.a: The gallbladder, passing through the cystic duct
nodes.note: Primary stones that form in the ducts are mostly brown pigment stones, linked to infection.

nodes.q: Which type of gallstone is most likely in a 43-year-old woman like her?
nodes.note: Risk factors: female sex, age around 40, obesity, pregnancy and estrogen (estrogen raises 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase activity and cholesterol secretion into bile). Most are radiolucent; black pigment stones follow chronic hemolysis.

nodes.q: Which procedure both confirms and removes the stone?
nodes.a: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with sphincterotomy and stone extraction
nodes.note: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography or endoscopic ultrasonography is used first if the chance of a stone is intermediate. A cholecystectomy follows to prevent more stones.

nodes.q: Which dangerous infection occurs when the blocked duct becomes infected?
nodes.note: Charcot triad: fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. Treat with antibiotics and urgent drainage of the duct.

nodes.q: What is the name of the picture when shock and confusion are added to the triad?
nodes.note: It signals suppurative cholangitis with sepsis, which needs urgent decompression of the duct.

nodes.q: Which pancreatic complication follows when a stone blocks the ampulla?
nodes.note: Pancreatic enzymes back up into the pancreas; lipase rises to more than three times normal.

nodes.q: Her jaundice and itching could suggest viral hepatitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Aminotransferases in the hundreds to thousands with a prodrome of malaise**; positive viral serology and no dilated duct
**Alkaline phosphatase out of proportion to the aminotransferases, a stone and a dilated common bile duct**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause jaundice with nausea and right upper quadrant discomfort.

nodes.q: Her jaundice could come from hemolysis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Unconjugated bilirubin, anemia, high reticulocytes and lactate dehydrogenase, with no bilirubin in the urine**
**Conjugated bilirubin with dark urine, pale stools and a normal blood count**

nodes.q: Her pain and vomiting could suggest acute cholecystitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Steady right upper quadrant pain over 6 hours with fever, a positive Murphy sign and a thick-walled gallbladder with a stone in the cystic duct**; bilirubin normal or only mildly raised
**Marked jaundice with a stone in a dilated common bile duct**

nodes.q: Her jaundice with dark urine and pale stools could suggest cancer of the head of the pancreas. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Painless jaundice in an older adult with weight loss and a palpable, non-tender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign)**; raised CA 19-9
**Painful jaundice with right upper quadrant tenderness, a non-palpable gallbladder and a stone in the duct**

image_prompts.root: A pastel picture of a yellow-eyed woman holding her right upper abdomen, beside a bile duct with a round stone blocking it and a dilated duct above.

root.stem: A 17-year-old boy has had several episodes over the past year of large, dark red stools that cause no pain and stop on their own. He had his appendix removed 2 years ago. Tonight he has a fever and pain around the navel that has moved to the right lower abdomen, like his earlier appendicitis. He is pale with a pulse of 112/min and a hemoglobin of 9.1 g/dL. A nuclear medicine scan shows a spot of uptake in the right lower abdomen that lights up at the same time as the stomach. Nobody in his family has polyps or bowel disease, and he has had no diarrhea or weight loss.
root.oneliner: 17M + several episodes of large, dark red painless stools + appendectomy 2 years ago + fever and periumbilical pain moving to the right lower abdomen + pale, pulse 112/min, hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL + nuclear scan: right lower abdominal uptake at the same time as the stomach + no family polyps or bowel disease + no diarrhea or weight loss
highlight: large, dark red stools that cause no pain
had his appendix removed 2 years ago
fever and pain around the navel
lights up at the same time as the stomach
Nobody in his family has polyps or bowel disease

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A small-bowel pouch left over from fetal life and the most common cause of painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding in children. The clincher: **painless dark red rectal bleeding in a child or young adult + a nuclear scan spot in the right lower abdomen that lights up with the stomach**.

nodes.q: Where does the pouch sit?
nodes.a: On the antimesenteric border of the ileum, about 2 feet (60 to 90 cm) from the ileocecal valve
nodes.note: Part of the rule of 2s: about 2% of people, 2 feet from the valve, 2 inches long, 2 kinds of ectopic tissue (gastric and pancreatic), usually symptomatic by age 2, and about twice as common in males.

nodes.q: What layers form the wall of the pouch?
nodes.a: All three layers of the bowel wall (mucosa, muscularis and serosa)
nodes.note: That makes it a true diverticulum, unlike the acquired colonic pouches, which have only mucosa and submucosa.

nodes.q: Which fetal structure failed to disappear?
nodes.note: The duct joins the midgut to the yolk sac and normally closes between the 5th and 7th weeks.

nodes.q: A 6-week-old boy has a swollen umbilical stump that leaks intestinal fluid because the duct stayed open. To which part of the gut does the fistula connect?
nodes.note: The duct arises from the ileum, which is why the pouch sits there too. A fibrous cord, a cyst or a fistula to the umbilicus are other remnants.

nodes.q: That infant's umbilical discharge could be mistaken for a patent urachus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Remnant of the allantois joining the bladder to the navel; **urine** leaks from the umbilicus, especially when the baby cries or strains
Remnant joining the ileum to the navel; **intestinal fluid, mucus or stool** leaks from the umbilicus

nodes.note: The trap: both leave a wet, swollen umbilical stump.

nodes.q: Which tissue inside the pouch causes his bleeding?
nodes.note: Acid-secreting parietal cells in the pouch ulcerate the normal ileal lining next to it. The second most common ectopic tissue is pancreatic tissue; endometrial tissue is rare.

nodes.q: What is the general term for normal tissue found in the wrong place?
nodes.note: Gastric mucosa in the ileum is a choristoma (a hamartoma is a disorganized overgrowth of tissue native to the site).

nodes.q: Which test finds the pouch when bleeding is painless and endoscopy is normal?
nodes.note: Pertechnetate is taken up by the mucus-secreting cells of gastric mucosa, so the pouch lights up at the same time as the stomach.

nodes.q: Which complication explains his fever and right lower abdominal pain after an appendectomy?
nodes.note: It mimics appendicitis with rebound tenderness in the right lower abdomen; in a patient with no appendix, think of this pouch.

nodes.q: In a child, which complication occurs when the pouch is dragged into the bowel as a lead point?
nodes.note: Another cause of obstruction is volvulus around a fibrous band from the pouch to the navel. Untreated, the trapped bowel becomes ischemic and can perforate.

nodes.q: What is the treatment for a bleeding or inflamed pouch?
nodes.a: Surgical resection of the pouch (with the adjacent ileum if the ulcer is there)
nodes.note: Resect all symptomatic pouches; resection of an incidental pouch is debated.

nodes.q: His inflamed terminal ileum and right lower pain could suggest Crohn disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Months of **diarrhea, weight loss, skip lesions with transmural inflammation and granulomas**; bleeding is usually mild; may have fistulae or aphthous ulcers
**Painless large-volume dark red bleeding + a pouch on the antimesenteric ileum** with gastric tissue, without diarrhea or weight loss

nodes.note: The trap: both inflame the terminal ileum and cause right lower abdominal pain.

nodes.q: A tumor in the ileum could also bleed. How do you tell a carcinoid tumor from his pouch?

split.note: Submucosal yellow nodule in the ileum or appendix in an **older adult**; **flushing, diarrhea and high urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid** once it reaches the liver; neuroendocrine cells on biopsy
A pouch in a **teenager** lined by gastric mucosa, not a tumor; no flushing and no diarrhea

nodes.q: A child with currant-jelly stool could have intussusception without a pouch. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Age 6 months to 3 years, **colicky pain with sausage-shaped mass and currant-jelly stool**, often after a viral illness; a target sign on ultrasound
**Painless** bleeding in an older child or teenager; the pouch itself can be the lead point

root.stem: A 38-year-old man has had 8 months of burning pain in the upper abdomen 1 to 2 hours after meals, only partly relieved by omeprazole and not at all by antacids, famotidine or a full course of treatment for Helicobacter pylori. He has had watery, greasy diarrhea for 3 months. For 2 days his stools have been black and he feels light-headed on standing, with a blood pressure of 104/68 mm Hg. Endoscopy shows several ulcers in the second part of the duodenum and thick gastric folds. A computed tomography scan shows a 2-cm mass in the head of the pancreas. The fasting blood level of the hormone that normally drives stomach acid secretion is four times the upper limit of normal. His calcium level is 11.4 mg/dL and his sister had a pituitary tumor removed. He has no skin rash, no jaundice and a normal fasting glucose.
root.oneliner: 38M + 8 months of burning epigastric pain 1-2 hours after meals, partial omeprazole response, no response to antacids, famotidine or Helicobacter pylori treatment + 3 months watery greasy diarrhea + 2 days black stools, light-headed on standing, BP 104/68 + multiple ulcers in the second part of the duodenum, thick gastric folds + 2-cm pancreatic head mass + fasting acid-stimulating hormone 4x normal + calcium 11.4 mg/dL, sister with pituitary tumor + no rash, no jaundice, normal glucose
highlight: not at all by antacids, famotidine or a full course of treatment for Helicobacter pylori
several ulcers in the second part of the duodenum
2-cm mass in the head of the pancreas
four times the upper limit of normal
sister had a pituitary tumor removed
no skin rash, no jaundice and a normal fasting glucose

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A neuroendocrine tumor drives so much stomach acid that ulcers form. The clincher: **ulcers that resist acid-lowering drugs and Helicobacter pylori treatment + a fasting acid-stimulating hormone level several times normal + a pancreatic or duodenal mass**.

nodes.q: Antibodies against which hormone label the tumor cells on immunohistochemistry?
nodes.note: Other pancreatic islet tumors stain for insulin (insulinoma), glucagon or vasoactive intestinal polypeptide; somatostatin and pancreatic polypeptide are made by other islet cells. Amylase and lipase mark acinar cells, not this tumor.

nodes.q: What is the tumor that makes the excess hormone called?
nodes.note: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is the clinical picture; gastrinoma is the tumor that causes it. Answer options may name the tumor.

nodes.q: Where do most of these tumors arise?
nodes.a: In the duodenum or the head of the pancreas, within the gastrinoma triangle
nodes.note: The triangle is bounded by the cystic duct and common bile duct, the junction of the 2nd and 3rd parts of the duodenum, and the neck of the pancreas. Most are in the duodenum.

nodes.q: The hormone released by the tumor makes which stomach cell secrete hydrogen ions?
nodes.note: Gastrin acts directly on parietal cells through the cholecystokinin-B receptor and indirectly by making enterochromaffin-like cells release histamine. Parietal cells then pump out hydrogen ions through the H+/K+ ATPase.

nodes.q: What does the constant gastrin stimulation do to the stomach wall?
nodes.a: Parietal cell hyperplasia with thick gastric folds
nodes.note: Gastrin is trophic for the acid-secreting mucosa.

nodes.q: Why does he have greasy watery diarrhea?
nodes.a: Excess acid inactivates pancreatic lipase and damages the small-bowel lining
nodes.note: Fat is not digested, so stools are fatty. Acid-lowering drugs often stop the diarrhea.

nodes.q: Where do the ulcers lie that point to this diagnosis instead of ordinary ulcer disease?
nodes.a: Beyond the first part of the duodenum, often multiple, and recurring
nodes.note: Ordinary Helicobacter pylori ulcers are usually single and sit in the first part of the duodenum or the stomach.

nodes.q: Which blood test is repeated when he has partly responded to a proton pump inhibitor?
nodes.a: Fasting serum gastrin after the proton pump inhibitor has been stopped
nodes.note: Proton pump inhibitors raise gastrin by removing acid feedback, so a high level on the drug can mislead. Also check gastric pH: high gastrin with high pH points to atrophic gastritis, not a tumor.

nodes.q: What does a secretin injection do to gastrin in this tumor?
nodes.a: It causes a paradoxical rise in gastrin
nodes.note: In healthy people secretin lowers gastrin; a rise of 120 pg/mL or more over baseline confirms a gastrinoma.

nodes.q: Which scan localizes small tumors after the diagnosis is made?
nodes.a: Somatostatin receptor imaging (gallium-68 DOTATATE positron emission tomography) with endoscopic ultrasound
nodes.note: Neuroendocrine tumor cells carry somatostatin receptors.

nodes.q: The tumor occurs in about a quarter of patients with which inherited syndrome?
nodes.note: Caused by loss of the menin tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 11. His high calcium and his sister's pituitary tumor point here.

nodes.q: Which two other glands form tumors or hyperplasia in that syndrome?
nodes.note: Hypercalcemia from parathyroid hyperplasia raises gastrin further; treating the high calcium first can lower acid output.

nodes.q: Which complication explains his black stools and light-headedness on standing?
nodes.note: Loss of blood volume causes the drop in blood pressure on standing.

nodes.q: If an ulcer erodes through the wall, which emergency follows?
nodes.note: A rigid abdomen and free air under the diaphragm on an upright chest x-ray.

nodes.q: Where do malignant gastrinomas usually spread?
nodes.a: To regional lymph nodes and the liver
nodes.note: More than half are malignant; liver metastases decide survival.

nodes.q: Which drug class is first-line?
nodes.note: H2 blockers and antacids fail because they cannot match the acid output.

nodes.q: Which enzyme of the parietal cell do these drugs block irreversibly?
nodes.note: Blocking the final step of acid secretion works whatever the stimulus, so it overrides the hormone drive.

nodes.q: Which treatment can cure a localized tumor?
nodes.note: Without a cure, long-term proton pump inhibitor therapy and treatment of liver metastases.

nodes.q: His ulcers and pain could be ordinary Helicobacter pylori ulcer disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **A single ulcer in the first part of the duodenum or stomach + normal or mildly raised gastrin + heals with acid suppression and eradication therapy**
**Multiple or distal ulcers + gastrin several times normal + failure of acid-lowering drugs and eradication therapy**, often with diarrhea

nodes.note: The trap: both give burning epigastric pain after meals, and a proton pump inhibitor helps both at first.

nodes.q: His watery diarrhea could suggest a tumor secreting vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIPoma). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Large-volume watery diarrhea + low potassium + low stomach acid (achlorhydria)**; no ulcers
**High stomach acid with ulcers**; the diarrhea is greasy and improves with acid suppression

nodes.q: A pancreatic mass could be a glucagonoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Necrolytic migratory erythema rash + diabetes + weight loss**
**Ulcers and high gastrin**; no rash and a normal fasting glucose

nodes.q: A mass in the head of the pancreas could be ductal adenocarcinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Older adult with **painless jaundice, weight loss and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier sign)**, raised CA 19-9
Younger man with **refractory ulcers and high gastrin**; no jaundice

nodes.q: The pancreatic mass could be an acinar carcinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Secretes **lipase**, causing subcutaneous fat necrosis, joint pain and eosinophilia
Secretes **gastrin**, causing ulcers and acid-driven diarrhea

nodes.q: A small pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor could be an insulinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fasting hypoglycemia relieved by glucose (Whipple triad) + high insulin and C-peptide**
**Ulcer pain and bleeding + high gastrin**; his fasting glucose is normal

root.stem: A 56-year-old man who has drunk heavily for 25 years vomits a large amount of bright red blood and becomes light-headed. His blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg and his pulse is 124/min. He has spider-like vessels on his chest, a palpable spleen tip, fluid in the abdomen and dilated veins radiating from the navel. There was no retching before the bleeding, he has no chest pain or pain when swallowing, he takes no anti-inflammatory drugs, and he has never had aortic surgery. His platelet count is 88,000/mm3. Endoscopy shows tortuous blue veins at the lower esophagus.
root.oneliner: 56M + 25 years of heavy drinking + large-volume bright red vomiting, light-headed, BP 84/50, pulse 124 + spider vessels, spleen tip, ascites, dilated veins radiating from navel + no retching, no chest pain, no painful swallowing, no anti-inflammatory drugs, no aortic surgery + platelets 88,000 + tortuous blue veins at the lower esophagus
highlight: vomits a large amount of bright red blood
dilated veins radiating from the navel
no chest pain or pain when swallowing
tortuous blue veins at the lower esophagus

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Swollen submucosal veins in the lower esophagus that rupture. The clincher: **large-volume bright red vomiting + spider vessels, spleen tip, ascites and veins radiating from the navel**.

nodes.q: Which condition raises the pressure in his portal vein?
nodes.note: Alcohol-related and chronic hepatitis B or C cirrhosis are common causes. Bleeding risk rises when the hepatic venous pressure gradient is above 12 mm Hg.

nodes.q: Which two venous systems meet in the lower esophagus?
nodes.a: The left gastric vein (portal system) and esophageal veins draining to the azygos vein (systemic system)
nodes.note: With portal pressure high, blood flows backward from the left gastric vein into the esophageal veins and on to the azygos vein. The thin-walled veins dilate and bulge.

nodes.q: Which layer of the esophageal wall holds the dilated veins seen at autopsy?
nodes.note: Raised pressure in these submucosal veins makes them dilate and rupture under the thin lining. No tumor (carcinoma, hemangioma, angiosarcoma), no fungal plaques, no viral inclusions, no granulomas and no gastric metaplasia.

nodes.q: Which portosystemic connection causes the dilated veins radiating from the navel?
nodes.a: Paraumbilical veins (portal) linking to the superficial epigastric veins (systemic), called caput medusae
nodes.note: The other shunt sites are the esophagus and the rectum.

nodes.q: Which anorectal finding comes from the rectal portosystemic connection?
nodes.a: Anorectal varices, from the superior rectal vein (portal) linking to the middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic)
nodes.note: Internal hemorrhoids are common in everyone and are not caused by portal hypertension.

nodes.q: Why is his spleen big and his platelet count low?
nodes.note: Raised portal pressure backs up into the splenic vein; platelets are trapped in the spleen.

nodes.q: Which state do his blood pressure of 84/50 mm Hg and pulse of 124/min show?
nodes.note: Acute loss of blood volume. Replace volume with blood products and aim for a hemoglobin of about 7 g/dL, because over-transfusion raises portal pressure and rebleeding.

nodes.q: Why can a variceal bleed trigger confusion in a cirrhotic?
nodes.a: Blood in the gut is digested into ammonia that bypasses the failing liver
nodes.note: Blood in the bowel is a protein load; use lactulose to prevent hepatic encephalopathy.

nodes.q: Which procedure screens cirrhotic patients for varices?
nodes.note: Done at diagnosis of cirrhosis and repeated at intervals; also treats the bleeding vessel.

nodes.q: Which drug infusion, started with an antibiotic, lowers portal inflow during the active bleed?
nodes.note: A somatostatin analog that constricts the splanchnic arteries and so lowers portal inflow. Give with ceftriaxone to prevent bacterial infection.

nodes.q: Which endoscopic procedure controls the bleeding?
nodes.note: Within 12 hours of presentation, after resuscitation.

nodes.q: If bleeding continues despite banding, which procedure creates a shunt between the portal and hepatic veins?
nodes.note: Lowers portal pressure but raises the risk of hepatic encephalopathy. A balloon tamponade tube can bridge.

nodes.q: Which drug class prevents first or repeat bleeding?
nodes.note: Beta-1 blockade lowers cardiac output; beta-2 blockade leaves splanchnic vasoconstriction unopposed. Both lower portal inflow.

nodes.q: Vomiting blood after heavy drinking could suggest a Mallory-Weiss tear. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Forceful retching or vomiting first, then blood**; a tear of the mucosa at the gastroesophageal junction; no signs of portal hypertension; bleeding usually stops by itself
**No preceding retching + cirrhosis stigmata and portal hypertension**; massive bleeding

nodes.note: The trap: both bring up bright red blood in someone who drinks heavily.

nodes.q: Massive bleeding from the esophagus could be an aortoesophageal fistula. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Thoracic aortic aneurysm or graft + chest pain + a small sentinel bleed then exsanguination**; no cirrhosis
**Cirrhosis with spleen tip, ascites and veins around the navel**; no aortic surgery or chest pain

nodes.q: Inflammation of the distal esophagus can bleed. How do you tell reflux esophagitis from varices?

split.note: **Heartburn, painful swallowing, erosions at the lower esophagus**; bleeding is small and slow
**Painless large-volume vomiting of blood, blue tortuous veins and portal hypertension**

nodes.q: Esophageal carcinoma could bleed. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Progressive trouble swallowing solids and weight loss**; an irregular mass on endoscopy
**Sudden painless bleeding with no dysphagia**; smooth blue veins

nodes.q: Infectious esophagitis could cause bleeding in an immunosuppressed patient. How do you tell Candida and cytomegalovirus infection from varices?

split.note: **Painful swallowing in an immunosuppressed host; white plaques (Candida) or linear ulcers with intranuclear inclusions (cytomegalovirus)**
**Intact mucosa over dilated veins; no pain on swallowing; portal hypertension**

nodes.q: A bleeding arteriovenous malformation at the gastroesophageal junction could be offered. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Older adult with small, flat red vascular lesions, usually in the right colon, and **painless slow bleeding, associated with aortic stenosis or kidney failure**
**Dilated veins from portal hypertension**, not arteries linked to veins

root.stem: A 68-year-old woman has had constipation for many years and eats little fiber. Last year she passed a large amount of maroon blood without any pain, and it stopped by itself. A screening colonoscopy now shows many round 5- to 10-mm openings in the wall of the left colon, with normal-looking lining around them. She has no fever, no left lower abdominal pain, a normal white blood cell count, and no change in her stool caliber, weight loss or iron deficiency.
root.oneliner: 68F + years of constipation, low-fiber diet + one painless large maroon bleed that stopped alone + colonoscopy: many 5-10 mm round openings in the left colon wall, lining normal + no fever, no left lower pain, normal white count + no change in stool caliber, no weight loss, no iron deficiency
highlight: large amount of maroon blood without any pain
many round 5- to 10-mm openings in the wall of the left colon
no fever, no left lower abdominal pain
no change in her stool caliber, weight loss or iron deficiency

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Acquired pouches of the colon wall. The clincher: **multiple small outpouchings of the colon with normal surrounding lining and no inflammation, in an older person on a low-fiber diet**.

nodes.q: Which colon segment holds most of these pouches in Western patients?
nodes.note: The descending colon is next; the right colon is more often involved in Asian patients.

nodes.q: Why does the sigmoid colon form pouches most often?
nodes.a: It has the narrowest lumen, so wall tension and pressure are highest (Laplace law)
nodes.note: Small hard stool needs strong segmenting contractions that raise the pressure inside the lumen.

nodes.q: Which mechanism makes the pouches form?
nodes.a: Increased pressure inside the lumen pushing the lining out through weak points in the wall
nodes.note: Low-fiber diet makes small, hard stool and constipation; wall weakness increases with age. Connective tissue disorders (Ehlers-Danlos and Marfan syndromes, autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease) cause pouches at younger ages.

nodes.q: Where does the colon wall give way?
nodes.a: Where the vasa recta penetrate the circular muscle, beside the taeniae coli
nodes.note: The muscle layer is interrupted at these points.

nodes.q: Which layers form the wall of each pouch?
nodes.a: Mucosa and submucosa only, with no muscle layer
nodes.note: It is a false (pseudo-) diverticulum, in contrast with a true diverticulum like Meckel.

nodes.q: Which complication explains her painless maroon bleed?
nodes.note: The vasa recta stretched over the dome of the pouch rupture. It is a leading cause of lower gastrointestinal bleeding in older adults; it comes more often from right-sided pouches, and about 80% stop on their own.

nodes.q: Which treatment controls a bleed that continues?
nodes.a: Colonoscopy with clips or cautery, then angiographic embolization if needed
nodes.note: Surgery only for bleeding that cannot be controlled.

nodes.q: Which complication causes left lower abdominal pain and fever when a pouch becomes blocked and infected?
nodes.note: Microperforation of an obstructed pouch. It can lead to abscess, free perforation with peritonitis, stricture or fistula.

nodes.q: Which complication causes air and stool in the urine with repeated urinary tract infections?
nodes.note: Pneumaturia and recurrent urinary tract infection.

nodes.q: Which test shows the pouches and also screens for cancer?
nodes.note: Avoid it during acute inflammation; use computed tomography instead.

nodes.q: Which dietary change reduces pouch formation and bleeding?
nodes.note: Fiber makes bulky soft stool and lowers wall pressure. Avoiding nuts and seeds is not needed.

nodes.q: Her pouches could be inflamed. How do you tell diverticulitis from diverticulosis?

split.note: **Left lower quadrant pain + fever + raised white blood cell count**; inflammation and fat stranding around the pouch on computed tomography
**Pouches without symptoms or inflammation**, or painless bleeding

nodes.note: The trap: same pouches, different state.

nodes.q: Her bleeding could suggest colon cancer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Iron-deficiency anemia, occult blood, a change in stool caliber, weight loss**; a mass or apple-core lesion on colonoscopy
**Painless maroon bleeding with a normal lining and no weight loss or anemia from slow loss**

nodes.q: Pouches in the bowel could be Meckel diverticulum. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Congenital, true pouch of the ileum with all layers**, containing gastric or pancreatic tissue; bleeding in a child or young adult
**Acquired, false pouch with no muscle layer in the sigmoid colon** of an older adult

nodes.q: Another false pouch is the Zenker diverticulum. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Pouch in the posterior hypopharynx above the upper esophageal sphincter**: halitosis, regurgitation of undigested food and trouble swallowing
**Pouches in the sigmoid colon** with constipation and bleeding

nodes.q: Her constipation could suggest Hirschsprung disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Constipation since birth** with absent ganglion cells in the distal colon and a narrow segment before a dilated colon
**Constipation develops with age**; ganglion cells are present, with pouches in the sigmoid colon

root.stem: A 22-year-old man notices yellow eyes on the third day of a stomach illness during which he barely ate. He has had the same mild yellowing before exams and after a fast. He feels well and takes no medicines. Total bilirubin is 3.1 mg/dL with a direct fraction of 0.3 mg/dL. Liver enzymes, alkaline phosphatase and albumin are normal, hemoglobin is normal with no reticulocytosis, and haptoglobin is normal. His urine has no bilirubin and no one in his family has liver disease.
root.oneliner: 22M + yellow eyes on day 3 of a stomach illness with fasting + same mild yellowing before exams and after fasting + well, no medicines + total bilirubin 3.1, direct 0.3 + normal liver enzymes, alkaline phosphatase and albumin + normal hemoglobin, no reticulocytosis, normal haptoglobin + no urine bilirubin
highlight: stomach illness during which he barely ate
same mild yellowing before exams and after a fast
Total bilirubin is 3.1 mg/dL with a direct fraction of 0.3 mg/dL
Liver enzymes, alkaline phosphatase and albumin are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A harmless inherited reduction in bilirubin conjugation. The clincher: **mild isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that appears with fasting, illness or stress, with normal liver tests and no hemolysis**. Fasting, illness, physical or emotional stress and hemolysis all trigger episodes.

nodes.q: Which enzyme activity is reduced?
nodes.a: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (the UGT1A1 enzyme), reduced to about 30% of normal
nodes.note: The enzyme adds glucuronic acid to bilirubin in the liver so it becomes water-soluble (conjugated).

nodes.q: Which genetic change usually causes it?
nodes.a: An extra TA repeat in the promoter of the UGT1A1 gene
nodes.note: Usually autosomal recessive. Common: about 5 to 10% of people. The change reduces production of the enzyme, not its structure.

nodes.q: Why is there no bilirubin in his urine?
nodes.a: Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and is not filtered by the kidney
nodes.note: So the jaundice is acholuric, and the urine is normal in color.

nodes.q: Which anticancer drug is more toxic in these patients because its active metabolite is cleared by the same enzyme?
nodes.note: The active metabolite SN-38 is glucuronidated by UGT1A1; slower clearance causes severe neutropenia and diarrhea.

nodes.q: What is the management?
nodes.note: A benign condition with normal life expectancy. No liver biopsy needed. Avoid unnecessary workup.

nodes.q: His jaundice could be hemolysis, since stress also raises bilirubin. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Anemia, reticulocytosis, low haptoglobin, high lactate dehydrogenase**; bilirubin is also unconjugated
**Normal hemoglobin, reticulocytes and haptoglobin**; bilirubin rises only with fasting or stress

nodes.note: The trap: both give unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver enzymes.

nodes.q: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia could be Crigler-Najjar syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Severe jaundice from the first days of life**, bilirubin often above 20 mg/dL; type 1 (absent enzyme) causes kernicterus and needs phototherapy; type 2 improves with phenobarbital
**Mild, intermittent jaundice, usually first noticed in adolescence or adulthood**; no brain damage

nodes.q: Jaundice with normal liver enzymes could be Dubin-Johnson syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia, a black liver and defective transport of conjugated bilirubin into bile (multidrug resistance-associated protein 2)**; bilirubin in the urine
**Unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinemia; no bilirubin in the urine** and a normal-colored liver

nodes.q: A recent operation could have injured the bile duct. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Conjugated bilirubin, high alkaline phosphatase, pain, fever and a dilated bile duct**; bilirubin in the urine and pale stools
**Almost all unconjugated bilirubin with a normal alkaline phosphatase and no pain**

nodes.q: Hepatitis could cause jaundice. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Raised liver enzymes (often in the hundreds or thousands)**, malaise, dark urine, mixed bilirubin
**Normal liver enzymes** and a bilirubin that rises only with fasting or stress

nodes.q: Liver failure could cause jaundice. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Raised clotting time, low albumin, confusion and ascites**, with high bilirubin
**Normal albumin and clotting time and no symptoms** beyond mild jaundice

nodes.q: Gallstones could cause jaundice. How do you tell them apart?

split.a: Cholelithiasis with a bile duct stone
split.note: **Right upper quadrant pain, raised alkaline phosphatase and conjugated bilirubin**
**Painless; unconjugated bilirubin with a normal alkaline phosphatase**

image_prompts.root: A pastel picture of a young man with mild yellow tint in the whites of the eyes beside a skipped meal and a tired liver cell with a small enzyme; no text

root.stem: A newborn boy, now 2 days old, has not passed any stool since birth. His abdomen is swollen and he has begun vomiting green fluid. His older sister has had repeated lung infections since infancy and needs daily chest physiotherapy. On rectal examination there is no explosive release of stool. An abdominal x-ray shows dilated loops of small bowel with a bubbly, ground-glass pattern. A contrast enema shows a very narrow, unused colon, and a rectal suction biopsy shows normal ganglion cells.
root.oneliner: Newborn boy, 2 days + no stool since birth + swollen abdomen, green vomiting + older sister with lifelong lung infections + no explosive stool release on rectal exam + dilated small-bowel loops with ground-glass pattern + narrow unused colon on contrast enema + normal ganglion cells on rectal biopsy
highlight: not passed any stool since birth

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Thick, sticky meconium blocks the terminal ileum. The clincher: **no stool in the first 48 hours + small-bowel obstruction with a ground-glass bowel pattern in a newborn whose sister has lifelong lung infections**.

nodes.q: Which inherited disease causes almost all cases?
nodes.note: Meconium ileus is often the first sign, in about 15 to 20% of babies with cystic fibrosis.

nodes.q: Which defective protein is responsible?
nodes.a: The CFTR chloride channel (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator), most often with the F508 deletion
nodes.note: Autosomal recessive, on chromosome 7.

nodes.q: Why is the meconium thick and sticky?
nodes.a: Faulty chloride and water secretion dries the intestinal contents, and lack of pancreatic enzymes leaves the meconium undigested
nodes.note: The thick plug blocks the terminal ileum and the colon beyond is unused.

nodes.q: What is the narrow, unused colon on his contrast enema called?
nodes.note: No meconium passed through the colon during fetal life, so it never widened.

nodes.q: Which prenatal event produces calcifications on an abdominal x-ray if the bowel perforates before birth?

nodes.q: Which obstruction of the older patient with cystic fibrosis is called the meconium ileus equivalent?

nodes.note: A highly contagious viral cause of outbreaks. The clincher: **an outbreak with a 1 to 2 day incubation, vomiting and watery diarrhea, no blood or white cells in stool, and recovery in 2 to 3 days**, with spread to contacts.

nodes.q: The exam may list the virus under another name. What is it?

nodes.q: Which virus family does it belong to?
nodes.note: The sapoviruses are close relatives.

nodes.q: What kind of genome does it carry?
nodes.note: Like picornaviruses, its RNA can act directly as messenger RNA.

nodes.q: Which route spreads it?

nodes.note: Very low infectious dose; cruise ships, nursing homes and schools are classic sites.

nodes.q: Why does alcohol hand sanitizer fail against it?

nodes.note: Enveloped viruses are destroyed by alcohol; nonenveloped ones are not.

nodes.q: What damage does the virus do in the small bowel?

nodes.note: Transient malabsorption of fluid and sugars; the lining is not invaded.

nodes.q: Which stool findings result?

nodes.q: Which complication is the main danger, especially in infants and the elderly?
nodes.note: Replace fluid and electrolytes.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Oral rehydration, with supportive care only
nodes.note: Antibiotics do not help. Intravenous fluids if severe.

nodes.q: Which measure limits an outbreak?
nodes.a: Handwashing with soap and water, and excluding sick food handlers until 48 hours after symptoms stop
nodes.note: Contaminated surfaces need bleach-based cleaning. There is no licensed vaccine.

nodes.q: A viral diarrhea could be rotavirus. How do you tell them apart?

nodes.q: Diarrhea after a shared event could be giardiasis. How do you tell them apart?

nodes.q: The fever and diarrhea could be shigellosis. How do you tell them apart?

root.stem: A 48-year-old man vomits bright red blood. no ascites, jaundice or spider-like skin vessels
albumin, liver enzymes and clotting time are normal
varices in the fundus of the stomach and none in the esophagus
normal flow in the portal vein but no flow in one of its tributaries

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Splenic vein thrombosis with gastric varices
nodes.note: A clot blocks the vein that drains the spleen. The clincher: **upper gastrointestinal bleeding from isolated gastric fundal varices + splenomegaly after pancreatitis, with a healthy liver**.

nodes.q: What is the resulting form of portal hypertension, confined to the spleen and stomach, called?
nodes.note: Pressure is high only in the splenic territory; the liver and the main portal vein are normal.

nodes.q: Where does the splenic vein lie in relation to the pancreas?
nodes.a: Along the back of the pancreatic body and tail
nodes.note: So pancreatitis, a pseudocyst or a pancreatic tumor compresses or inflames it and a clot forms.

nodes.q: Which vein joins the splenic vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the portal vein?
nodes.note: The inferior mesenteric vein drains into either of these; the portal vein then enters the liver.

nodes.q: Which veins carry the diverted splenic blood to the stomach?
nodes.a: The short gastric veins (with the gastroepiploic veins) into the gastric fundus
nodes.note: Splenic outflow is blocked, so blood finds a path to the stomach wall and then to systemic veins; the portal vein and liver are normal, so esophageal varices are less common.

nodes.q: Why are his spleen enlarged and platelet count low?
nodes.note: Platelets are trapped in the congested spleen.

nodes.q: Besides Doppler ultrasound, which imaging test shows the clot?
nodes.note: It also shows the pancreatitis, the pseudocyst and the collateral veins. Endoscopy shows isolated gastric varices.

nodes.q: Which operation cures the portal hypertension?
nodes.note: It removes the blood flow that has no outlet. Endoscopic glue injection controls active gastric variceal bleeding.

nodes.q: Which vaccines should be given before the spleen is removed?
nodes.a: Pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccines
nodes.note: They protect against encapsulated bacteria, the cause of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection.

nodes.q: His varices could be from cirrhosis with portal hypertension. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Ascites, jaundice, spider angiomata, low albumin and raised clotting time**; esophageal varices are typical
**Normal liver tests, isolated gastric fundal varices and splenomegaly after pancreatitis**

nodes.note: The trap: both give splenomegaly, low platelets and variceal bleeding.

nodes.q: A clot in the portal vein could be responsible. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Esophageal and gastric varices, with causes such as cirrhosis, thrombophilia or infection of the umbilical stump**; the clot is in the portal vein itself
**Clot in the splenic vein after pancreatic disease; fundal varices, with a patent portal vein**

nodes.q: Bleeding after pancreatitis could come from an artery. How do you tell the splenic artery from the splenic vein?

split.note: **Sudden arterial bleeding into the pseudocyst or pancreatic duct**, pulsatile mass, shock; no gastric varices or splenomegaly
**Venous obstruction causing varices and splenomegaly**; bleeding from gastric varices

nodes.q: Vomiting blood in a heavy drinker could be a Mallory-Weiss tear. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Retching, then blood; a mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction**; normal spleen and platelets
**Splenomegaly, low platelets and fundal varices**

nodes.q: A peptic ulcer could bleed in a patient with pancreatitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Epigastric pain, anti-inflammatory drug use or Helicobacter pylori; an ulcer crater at endoscopy**; normal spleen

root.stem: A 54-year-old man with 20 years of heavy drinking and several episodes of pancreatitis has lost 9 kg in 8 months. He passes three or four large, pale, foul-smelling stools a day that float and are hard to flush. His skin is dry and scaly and he has trouble seeing in dim light. An abdominal x-ray shows calcifications in the upper abdomen. His fasting glucose is normal. He had no childhood lung problems, his small-bowel biopsy is normal, and he has no abdominal fistulae.
root.oneliner: 54M + 20 years of heavy drinking, recurrent pancreatitis + 9 kg weight loss in 8 months + 3-4 large pale foul-smelling floating stools daily + dry scaly skin, poor dim-light vision + upper abdominal calcifications on x-ray + normal fasting glucose + no childhood lung problems, normal small-bowel biopsy, no fistulae
highlight: large, pale, foul-smelling stools a day that float

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The pancreas cannot make enough digestive enzymes. The clincher: **large, pale, greasy, floating stools (steatorrhea) with weight loss after years of drinking and pancreatitis, with a normal small-bowel biopsy**.

nodes.q: Which disease is the most common cause in adults?
nodes.note: Usually from alcohol; the x-ray calcifications show it.

nodes.q: Which inherited disease is the most common cause in children?
nodes.note: Thick secretions block the pancreatic ducts from infancy.

nodes.q: Which enzyme deficiency causes the fatty stools?
nodes.note: Lipase, with its cofactor colipase, digests triglycerides. Steatorrhea appears only after about 90% of function is lost, because protein and carbohydrate digestion have back-up from stomach pepsin, salivary amylase and brush-border enzymes.

nodes.q: Which stain shows fat droplets in the stool?
nodes.note: Quantitative: more than 7 g of fat in a 72-hour stool collection.

nodes.q: Which vitamin deficiency explains his dry scaly skin and poor vision in dim light?
nodes.note: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K) need fat and bile salts for absorption. Vitamin A deficiency causes dry skin and night blindness.

nodes.q: Which other deficiency explains easy bruising in these patients?
nodes.note: Lowers clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and prolongs the prothrombin time.

nodes.q: Which fat-soluble vitamin deficiency softens the bones of adults with long-standing steatorrhea?
nodes.note: Osteomalacia with low calcium and phosphate and raised alkaline phosphatase.

nodes.q: Which water-soluble vitamin may be low because pancreatic proteases are needed to free it from its binding protein?
nodes.note: Pancreatic proteases cleave R-protein from B12 so it can bind intrinsic factor.

nodes.q: Which stool test confirms the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Elastase is stable through the gut and not affected by enzyme supplements.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Pancreatic enzyme replacement (pancrelipase) with every meal
nodes.note: Plus a low-alcohol, normal-fat diet and fat-soluble vitamin supplements.

nodes.q: Why is an acid-lowering drug often added?
nodes.a: Stomach acid inactivates the enzymes, so raising duodenal pH helps them work
nodes.note: Enteric-coated capsules also protect the enzyme.

nodes.q: Which later complication follows loss of the islet cells?
nodes.note: Both insulin and glucagon are lost, so hypoglycemia is easily triggered.

nodes.q: Floating fatty stools and weight loss could be celiac disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Positive anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA, villous atrophy on small-bowel biopsy, HLA-DQ2 or DQ8**, iron-deficiency anemia, dermatitis herpetiformis
**Normal small-bowel biopsy, low fecal elastase and pancreatic calcifications**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.

nodes.q: Malabsorption could be Crohn disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Ileal inflammation with right lower pain, fistulae, diarrhea (sometimes bloody) and vitamin B12 and bile salt malabsorption**; transmural inflammation with granulomas
**Pancreatic calcifications and no fistulae or abdominal inflammation**

nodes.q: The same fatty stools occur in cystic fibrosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Lung infections and salty sweat since childhood, with high sweat chloride**
**Adult onset after years of drinking and pancreatitis; no childhood lung disease**

root.stem: A 51-year-old man with cirrhosis from 20 years of heavy alcohol use is brought in by his wife because of 2 days of confusion and sleeping through the day. He vomited blood 3 days ago. He is jaundiced and has spider angiomata, ascites and prominent veins around the umbilicus. He is disoriented to time and place. When his arms are outstretched, his hands make a flapping, up-and-down motion. He has no eye movement abnormalities, no gait ataxia and no sweating. Serum creatinine is normal and serum bicarbonate is normal.
