root.stem: A 53-year-old man has had a year of a red, scaly rash around his mouth and anus and on his hands and feet, along with hair thinning and cuts that heal slowly. Food tastes bland to him. He has lost 15 kg, his BMI is 17 kg/m2, and his stools are large, greasy and float. He has had chronic pancreatitis from heavy alcohol use. He has no night-vision problems, no bleeding gums, no numbness or tingling and no muscle twitching.
root.oneliner: 53M + 1 year of red scaly rash around the mouth, anus, hands and feet + hair thinning + slow wound healing + bland taste + 15 kg weight loss, BMI 17 + large greasy floating stools + chronic pancreatitis from alcohol + no night-vision problems, bleeding gums, numbness or twitching
highlight: red, scaly rash around his mouth and anus and on his hands and feet
no night-vision problems, no bleeding gums, no numbness or tingling and no muscle twitching

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The clincher: **scaly rash around the mouth, anus and acral skin + hair loss + slow wound healing + loss of taste, with malabsorption**.

nodes.q: What process in his gut explains the deficiency?
nodes.note: Zinc is lost bound to unabsorbed fat in the stool; alcohol also lowers zinc absorption. Other causes: Crohn disease, celiac disease, parenteral nutrition without zinc, and diets high in phytates.

nodes.q: What does zinc do in cells?
nodes.a: It is a cofactor of metalloenzymes and a structural part of zinc-finger transcription factors
nodes.note: So deficiency hits fast-dividing tissues (skin, hair, gut, immune cells) and wound healing. Zinc also helps alkaline phosphatase, carbonic anhydrase and superoxide dismutase. Taste and smell are dulled because taste buds need zinc.

nodes.q: Which inherited disorder blocks zinc absorption in infants?
nodes.note: Autosomal recessive mutation of the intestinal zinc transporter (ZIP4); presents after weaning from breast milk with the same rash, diarrhea and hair loss.

nodes.q: Which endocrine problem can zinc deficiency cause in men?
nodes.note: In children it causes growth delay and delayed puberty.

nodes.q: Which blood tests confirm it?
nodes.a: Low serum zinc with low alkaline phosphatase
nodes.note: Alkaline phosphatase is a zinc-dependent enzyme.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Oral zinc sulfate or gluconate, and treat the cause
nodes.note: Parenteral zinc if the gut cannot absorb it.

nodes.q: Which deficiency can develop if high-dose zinc is given for a long time?
nodes.note: Zinc induces intestinal metallothionein, which traps copper. Causes anemia, neutropenia and neuropathy.

nodes.q: His dry, scaly skin could suggest vitamin A deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Night blindness, Bitot spots and dry eyes (xerophthalmia), follicular hyperkeratosis**; a fat-soluble vitamin lost in steatorrhea
**Rash around the mouth, anus and acral sites + hair loss + poor wound healing + bland taste**; no night blindness

nodes.note: The trap: steatorrhea causes both, and both give dry skin.

nodes.q: His scaly rash with greasy stools could suggest essential fatty acid deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Diffuse dry scaly dermatitis after long fat-free parenteral nutrition or severe fat malabsorption; raised triene-to-tetraene ratio**
**Rash around the mouth and anus and on the hands and feet + bland taste + low alkaline phosphatase**

nodes.q: His scaly rash and weight loss could suggest niacin deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Rash on sun-exposed skin (Casal necklace) + diarrhea + dementia**
**Rash around the mouth and anus + hair loss + slow wound healing + bland taste**

nodes.q: Could this be vitamin B12 deficiency? How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Megaloblastic anemia, numbness and tingling, glossitis**; vitamin B12 is lost with ileal disease
**Acral and periorificial rash, hair loss, no neurologic signs**

nodes.q: Could this be vitamin C deficiency? How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, painful joints**; impaired collagen hydroxylation
**Scaly rash and slow wound healing without bleeding gums**

nodes.q: Could this be magnesium deficiency? How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Muscle twitching, tetany, arrhythmias, low potassium and calcium**; no rash
**Rash, hair loss, bland taste; no twitching**

image_prompts.root: Pastel teaching illustration of a man's face and hands showing red scaly patches around the mouth and on the hands, thin hair, and a small zinc ion symbol; no text.

root.stem: A 72-year-old man has had 1 month of light-headedness and chest tightness on exertion that settle with rest. Two years ago he had painless bleeding from the rectum, and upper endoscopy and colonoscopy at that time found no cause. Pulse is 85/min and blood pressure is 110/75 mm Hg. A systolic ejection murmur is heard at the right upper sternal border. Hemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL with small red cells, stool testing for occult blood is positive and the electrocardiogram is normal. Repeat colonoscopy shows no abnormality. He has had no change in bowel habit, no diarrhea, no weight loss or abdominal pain, and he has no dark spots on his lips.
root.oneliner: 72M + 1 month of light-headedness and exertional chest tightness relieved by rest + prior painless rectal bleeding with negative upper endoscopy and colonoscopy + aortic-area ejection murmur + Hb 8.2 with small red cells + positive stool occult blood + normal ECG + normal repeat colonoscopy + no change in bowel habit, weight loss or lip spots
highlight: systolic ejection murmur is heard at the right upper sternal border
no change in bowel habit, no diarrhea, no weight loss or abdominal pain
no dark spots on his lips

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Fragile dilated blood vessels in the gut wall that bleed slowly. The clincher: **recurrent painless gastrointestinal bleeding with iron-deficiency anemia in an older patient and a normal colonoscopy**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: All describe the same lesion.

nodes.q: What is the lesion?
nodes.a: Dilated, thin-walled submucosal veins and capillaries that form small arteriovenous communications
nodes.note: Believed to be a degenerative change with age, from repeated mild blockage of submucosal veins during muscle contraction.

nodes.q: Where in the colon is it most often found?
nodes.note: The wall is thinnest and wall tension highest here (Laplace law).

nodes.q: Which valve disease explains his murmur and is linked with his bleeding?
nodes.note: Shear stress across the valve destroys the large multimers of von Willebrand factor (acquired von Willebrand disease), so the vessels bleed more easily. Replacing the valve often stops the bleeding.

nodes.q: Which kidney condition also raises the risk of bleeding angiodysplasia?
nodes.note: Uremic platelet dysfunction adds to the bleeding. Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu) gives similar vascular lesions from birth, with nosebleeds and skin telangiectasias.

nodes.q: Which type of anemia does chronic blood loss cause?
nodes.note: Low ferritin, low serum iron and high total iron-binding capacity.

nodes.q: Why does the anemia make his chest tight on exertion?
nodes.a: Reduced oxygen delivery to heart muscle causes demand ischemia, even with a normal electrocardiogram at rest
nodes.note: Heart muscle already extracts most of the oxygen it receives, so it depends on blood oxygen content and flow.

nodes.q: Which test finds the lesions when colonoscopy is normal?
nodes.a: Capsule endoscopy (or CT or mesenteric angiography during active bleeding)
nodes.note: The lesions are small, flat and red, easily missed on colonoscopy, particularly in a cleansed, collapsed bowel; angiography shows early filling veins and a vascular tuft.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Endoscopic cautery (argon plasma coagulation) with iron replacement
nodes.note: Surgery or octreotide is reserved for recurrent bleeding.

nodes.q: His anemia could suggest colon cancer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Occult bleeding, change in bowel habit and weight loss; a mass seen on colonoscopy**
**Normal colonoscopy and stable weight with recurrent bleeding in an older patient**

nodes.note: The trap: right-sided colon cancer also gives iron-deficiency anemia with occult blood.

nodes.q: His past rectal bleeding could suggest diverticulosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sudden large painless bright red bleeding; pouches seen in the sigmoid colon on colonoscopy**
**Slow recurrent occult bleeding with a normal colonoscopy**

nodes.q: Could this be Peutz-Jeghers syndrome? How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Dark spots on the lips and mouth + hamartomatous polyps seen on endoscopy**; presents in the young
**No lip spots, no polyps, older age**

nodes.q: Could this be ulcerative colitis? How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bloody diarrhea with urgency, continuous inflammation from the rectum seen on colonoscopy**
**No diarrhea and a normal colonic mucosa**

image_prompts.root: Pastel teaching illustration of a colon cross-section showing a small cluster of dilated red vessels in the wall of the cecum with a tiny bleeding point; no text.

root.stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has had 1 week of fever, shaking chills and a dull ache in the upper right abdomen. Three weeks ago he was treated for diverticulitis. He has not travelled abroad, has no diarrhea, and has no jaundice or known liver disease. Temperature is 39.5 C. His liver edge is tender and enlarged. CT of the abdomen shows several low-density lesions with enhancing rims in both lobes of the liver, and blood cultures grow Escherichia coli.
root.oneliner: 58M + type 2 diabetes + 1 week of fever, shaking chills, dull RUQ ache + diverticulitis 3 weeks ago + no travel, diarrhea, jaundice or liver disease + T 39.5 C + tender enlarged liver + several rim-enhancing low-density lesions in both lobes on CT + blood cultures grow E. coli
highlight: Three weeks ago he was treated for diverticulitis
not travelled abroad, has no diarrhea
no jaundice or known liver disease
several low-density lesions with enhancing rims in both lobes

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A collection of pus in the liver from bacterial infection. The clincher: **fever and upper right abdominal pain + multiple rim-enhancing liver lesions + enteric organisms in the blood**.

nodes.q: Through which route did the bacteria most likely reach his liver after the diverticulitis?
nodes.a: The portal vein (seeding from an intra-abdominal infection)
nodes.note: The other main route is up the biliary tree in cholangitis, which is the most common source overall; the hepatic artery carries bacteremia from distant sites.

nodes.q: Which organisms usually cause it?
nodes.a: Mixed enteric gram-negative rods (Escherichia coli, Klebsiella) with anaerobes such as Bacteroides
nodes.note: Staphylococcus aureus is seen after bacteremia from distant sites. Klebsiella pneumoniae is linked with diabetes.

nodes.q: What causes the fever and shaking chills?
nodes.a: Endogenous pyrogens (interleukin-1, interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor) released by macrophages raise the hypothalamic set point
nodes.note: The cytokines raise prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus; the body shivers to reach the new set point. There is no abscess in the hypothalamus.

nodes.q: Which enzyme do antipyretics such as acetaminophen and ibuprofen block to lower the fever?
nodes.note: Less prostaglandin E2 resets the hypothalamic set point.

nodes.q: Which tests confirm it?
nodes.a: Contrast CT (or ultrasonography) of the abdomen with blood cultures
nodes.note: Culture of aspirated pus identifies the organism.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Percutaneous drainage plus broad-spectrum antibiotics covering gram-negative rods and anaerobes
nodes.note: For example ceftriaxone plus metronidazole; surgery if drainage fails.

nodes.q: How does metronidazole kill the anaerobes?
nodes.a: It is activated in anaerobes into free radicals that damage their DNA
nodes.note: Covers the Bacteroides and other anaerobes that a cephalosporin misses.

nodes.q: Which complication occurs when bacteria spill from the abscess into the blood?
nodes.note: Rupture can also cause peritonitis.

nodes.q: Which type of shock can follow and is the main cause of death?
nodes.note: Endotoxin-driven cytokines cause widespread vasodilation, low blood pressure and organ failure.

nodes.q: An amebic liver abscess could look the same. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Single large abscess in the right lobe + travel to or from an endemic area**, often in a young man, sometimes after amebic dysentery; anchovy-paste pus, Entamoeba histolytica serology positive; treated with metronidazole and then a luminal agent (paromomycin)
**Multiple abscesses + enteric bacteria in blood or pus + an abdominal source**; needs drainage and antibiotics

nodes.note: The trap: both give fever, a tender liver and a liver cavity on CT.

nodes.q: Could this be hepatocellular carcinoma? How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis, high alpha-fetoprotein, arterial enhancement with washout**; usually no fever
**Fever with chills, rim-enhancing lesions, bacteria in the blood**

nodes.q: Could this be cholangitis? How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever + jaundice + right upper quadrant pain (Charcot triad)** from a blocked bile duct; dilated ducts
**No jaundice; discrete abscesses within the liver tissue**

image_prompts.root: Pastel teaching illustration of a liver with several round pus-filled cavities with enhancing rims, bacteria drifting in from a bowel segment through the portal vein; no text.
